### THE
# English Physician
## ENLARGED:

->With three hundred, sixty, and nine *medicines* made of *English herbs* that were not in any *edition* <note>original: "Impression"</note> until this one: The *Epistle* <note>The introductory letter to the reader.</note> will inform you how to distinguish *this edition* from any other.<-

->*Being an Astrological-Physical Discourse on the Common Herbs of this Nation: Containing a Complete Method of Medicine <note>original: "Physick"</note>, whereby a person may preserve their body in health; or cure themselves, when sick, for three pence charge, using only such things as grow in England, as they are most fit for English bodies.*<-

***

->Herein are also shown these seven things, namely: 1. The way of making plasters, ointments, oils, poultices, syrups, decoctions, juleps, or waters, from all sorts of medicinal herbs, so that you may have them ready for your use at all times of the year. 2. Which planet governs every herb or tree (used in medicine) that grows in England. 3. The time for gathering all herbs, both by common practice and by astrological timing. 4. The way of drying and keeping the herbs all year. 5. The way of keeping their juices ready for use at all times. 6. The way of making and keeping all kinds of useful compounds made of herbs. 7. The way of mixing *medicines* according to the *cause* and *nature* <note>original: "Mixture"</note> of the *disease*, and the *part* of the *body afflicted*.*<-

***

->By NICHOLAS CULPEPER, Gentleman, Student in *Medicine*<-
->and *Astrology*: Living in Spitalfields.<-

***

->*London*, Printed by *Peter Cole* in *Leadenhall*, and are to be sold at his shop at the sign of the *Printing Press* in *Cornhill*,<-
-><insert>August 29.</insert> near the Royal Exchange. 1653.<-

## To the Reader.

Reader,

Take notice, that in this edition, published September 5th, 1653, I have made very many additions to every sheet in the book. Also, be aware that those books of mine printed with the small typeface used for Bibles are very falsely printed; there are usually twenty or thirty gross mistakes in every sheet. Many of these errors are exceedingly dangerous to those who shall venture to use them. Therefore, I do hereby warn you of them; I can do no more at present. Only take notice of these three directions by which you shall be sure to know the true edition from the false.

**The first Direction:** The true edition has this title at the top of every page in the book: [*The English Physician Enlarged*]. The small counterfeit one has only this title: [*The English Physician*].

**The second Direction:** The true edition has these words, [**Government and Virtues**] <note>original: "Government" refers to the astrological ruler of the plant</note>, following the description of the time the plants flower, etc. The counterfeit small one has these words, [**Virtues and Use**], following the time of the plant's flowering.

**The third Direction:** The true edition is in Octavo <note>a book size resulting from folding a sheet into eight leaves</note>, with a larger typeface than the counterfeit one, which is in Twelves <note>Duodecimo; a smaller book size where the sheet is folded into twelve leaves</note>, using the small typeface typically used for Bibles. I shall now speak something regarding the book itself.

All other authors who have written of the nature of herbs gave not a bit of a reason why a specific herb was assigned to a specific part of the body, nor why it cured a specific disease. Truly, my own body being sickly made it easy for me to understand that health was the greatest of all earthly blessings; and truly, he was never sick who does not believe it. Then I considered that all medicines were compounded of herbs, roots, flowers, seeds, etc. This first set me to work studying the nature of simples <note>original: "Simples" are medicinal plants or herbs used on their own, rather than in a compound mixture</note>, most of which I knew by sight before. Indeed, all the authors I could read gave me but little satisfaction in this particular, or none at all. 

I cannot build my faith upon authors' words, nor believe a thing just because they say it. I could wish everyone were of my mind in this: to labor to be able to give a reason for everything they say or do. They say reason makes a man differ from a beast; if that be true, pray, what are they who, instead of providing a reason for their judgment, quote old authors? Perhaps their authors knew a reason for what they wrote, perhaps they did not—what is that to us? Do we know it? 

Truly, in writing this work, first to satisfy myself, I drew out all the virtues of common herbs, plants, and trees, etc., from the best or most approved authors I had or could get. Having done so, I set myself to study the reason for them. I knew well enough that the whole world, and everything in it, was formed of a composition of contrary elements, and in such a harmony as must surely show the wisdom and power of a great God. I knew just as well that this creation, though thus composed of contraries, was one united...

<summary>Nicholas Culpeper warns readers against dangerous counterfeit editions of his work and explains his motivation for writing: to provide a rational, rather than purely traditional, explanation for the medicinal use of plants.</summary>
<keywords>Nicholas Culpeper, The English Physician, herbal medicine, book counterfeiting, medical philosophy, simples, elements, reason vs. authority</keywords>

# TO THE READER.

*...united Body, and* **Man** *an epitome of it; I knew those various affections in* **Man** *in respect of* **Sickness** *and* **Health** *were caused* **Naturally** *(though* **God** *may have other ends best known to himself) by the various operations of the* **Microcosm** <note>original: "Microcosm"; the idea that a human being is a "little world" reflecting the entire universe.</note>; *and I could not be ignorant, that as the Cause is, so must the Cure be. Therefore, he that would know the reason of the operation of Herbs must look up as high as the* **Stars**. *I always found the* **Disease** *vary according to the various motion of the* **Stars**; *and this is enough, one would think, to teach a* **Man** *by the* **Effect** *where the* **Cause** *lay. Then, to find out the reason of the operation of Herbs, Plants, etc., by the* **Stars** *went I; and herein I could find but few* **Authors**, *and those as full of nonsense and contradictions as an egg is full of meat. This being little pleasing and less profitable to me, I consulted with my two brothers,* **Dr. Reason** *and* **Dr. Experience**, *and took a* **Voyage** *to visit my* **Mother Nature**. *By her advice, together with the help of* **Dr. Diligence**, *I at last obtained my desires; and being warned by* **Mr. Honesty**—*a stranger in our days—to publish it to the world, I have done it.*

*But you will say, "Why did I need to have written on this subject, seeing so many famous and learned men have written so much of it in the* **English Tongue** <note>The English language.</note>, *nay, much more than I have done?"*

*To this I* **Answer**:

1. *All those who have written of Herbs, either in the* **English** *or not in the* **English Tongue**, *have in no way answered my intentions in this book. For they have intermixed many—nay, very many—foreign herbs, and many which are hard—nay, impossible—to be obtained; and I am very sensible of what harm this may do. Once a student in* **Medicine** <note>original: "Physick"</note> *in* **Sussex** *sent up to* **London** *to me to buy certain medicines for him and send them down. When I viewed the list, they were medicines quoted by* **Authors** *living in another nation and were not to be had in* **London** *for love nor money. So the poor man had spent much effort and brainpower studying medicines for a disease that were not to be had. Likewise, a man reading* **Gerard's** *or* **Parkinson's Herbal** <note>John Gerard (1545–1612) and John Parkinson (1567–1650) were the authors of the most famous English herbals of the time.</note> *for the cure of a disease may, as likely as not, happen upon an herb that is not to be had here, or not without great difficulty, if at all. But in my book, all the herbs grow near him.*

2. *My last, though not the least of my reasons, is that neither* **Gerard** *nor* **Parkinson**, *nor any who ever wrote in a similar manner, ever gave one wise* **Reason** *for what they wrote. Thus, they did nothing else but train up young novices in* **Medicine** *in the* **School of Tradition**, *teaching them just as a* **Parrot** *is taught to speak: "An author says so, therefore it is true." And if all that* **Authors** *say is true, why do they contradict one another? But in my book, if you view it with the* **Eye of Reason**, *you shall see a* **Reason** *for everything that is written. By this, you may find the very ground and foundation of* **Medicine**; *you may know what you do and why you do it. This work shall call me* **Father**, *as it has (to my knowledge) never been done in the world before.*

*I have now but two things more to write, and then I am finished:*
1. *What the profit and benefit of this work is.*
2. *Instructions in the use of it.*

1. *The profit and benefit arising from it, or that may accrue to a wise man...*

<summary>The author argues that true medicine must be based on astrology and reason rather than just tradition. He critiques previous herbalists like Gerard and Parkinson for including unobtainable foreign plants and failing to explain the underlying causes of why herbs work.</summary>
<keywords>Astrology, Herbalism, Nicholas Culpeper, John Gerard, John Parkinson, Medical Theory, Microcosm, Reason vs Tradition</keywords>

# TO THE READER

The reasons that draw man to this study are many—so many that should I sum up all the particulars, this *Epistle* <note>original: "Epistle"; here meaning the introductory letter or preface</note> would be as large as the *Book* itself. I shall only quote a few general headings.

First, the admirable harmony of the creation is seen herein: in the influence of stars upon herbs and the body of man; how one part of the creation is subservient to another, and all for the use of man. By this, the infinite power and wisdom of God in the creation appears. If I do not marvel at the simplicity of the *Ranters* <note>A radical 17th-century religious sect often accused of pantheism or denying a creator God</note>, never trust me. Who, when viewing the creation, can hold such a foolish opinion as to think it existed from eternity, when its mysteries are so clear to every eye? But that *Scripture* shall be verified to them, *Romans 1:20*: "For the invisible things of Him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even His eternal power and Godhead, so that they are without excuse." *And a poet could teach them a better lesson:*

->*Lest the Author of the Divine gift should slip from your mind,*<-
->*Every herb reveals the present God.*<-
<note>original Latin: "Excideret ne tibi Divini muneris Author / Præsentem monstrat, quælibet Herba Deum."</note>

->*Because out of your thoughts* God *should not pass,*<-
->*His* image *stamped is on every* grass.<-

*This indeed is true:* God *has stamped his* image *upon every* creature, *and therefore the abuse of the* creature *is a great sin. But how much more does the* wisdom *and* excellency *of* God *appear if we consider the* harmony *of the* creation *in the* virtue *and* operation *of every* herb? *This is the first reason.*

*Secondly, by this you may know what infinite knowledge* Adam *had in his* innocence <note>original: "Innocency"; referring to the state of man before the Fall in Eden</note>, *that by looking upon a* creature, *he was able to give it a name according to its* nature. *By knowing that, you may know how great your* fall *was, and be humbled for it even in this respect: because by it you are now so ignorant.*

*Thirdly, here is the right way for you to begin the study of* medicine <note>original: "Physick"</note> *if you intend to begin at the right end, for here you have the reason of the whole* art. *I wrote before in certain* astrological lectures *which I read and printed, entitled* Semeiotica Uranica <note>A Greek-titled work by Culpeper meaning "Uranic Signs" or "Astrological Judgment of Diseases"</note>, *explaining what* planet *caused (as a secondary cause) every* disease, *and how it might be found out which* planet *caused it. Here you have which* planet *cures it by* sympathy *and* antipathy <note>The principle that a plant cures either because it is like the planet causing the illness (sympathy) or opposite to it (antipathy)</note>; *and this brings me to my last promise, namely:*

## Instructions for the right use of the Book.

*And herein let me premise a word or two: the* herbs, plants, *etc., are now in the* book *assigned to their proper* planets. *Therefore,*

*First, consider what* planet *causes the* disease: *that you may find in my* Semeiotica.

*Second, consider what part of the* body *is afflicted by the* disease, *and whether it lies in the* flesh, *or* blood, *or* bones, *or* ventricles <note>original: "Ventricles"; here referring generally to body cavities or chambers, such as the stomach or heart</note>.

*Third, consider by what* planet *the afflicted part of the* body *is governed: my* Semeiotica *will inform you of that also.*

*Fourth, you have in this* book *the* herbs *for* cure *assigned to the various* diseases, *and the* diseases *for your ease are set down in the* margin, *whereby*

<summary>Culpeper argues that studying the astrological virtues of herbs reveals God's wisdom and highlights the knowledge lost by humanity since Adam. He provides a four-step guide for using his book to diagnose and treat illnesses based on planetary influences.</summary>
<keywords>Astrological Medicine, Nicholas Culpeper, Semeiotica Uranica, Sympathy and Antipathy, Creation, Herbalism, Ranters, Adam's Knowledge</keywords>

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page concludes the author's introductory address "To the Reader," following his explanation of the astrological principles of herbal medicine.</meta>

# TO THE READER

*By this method, you may strengthen a specific part of the body with its corresponding element; for example, the brain by herbs of* Mercury, *the breast and liver by herbs of* Jupiter, *the heart and vital organs by herbs of the* Sun, *and so forth.*

*Fifthly, you may oppose diseases by using herbs of the planet opposite to the planet that causes the ailment: such as treating diseases of* Jupiter *with herbs of* Mercury, *and vice versa; diseases of the Luminaries <note>The Sun and the Moon</note> by herbs of* Saturn, *and vice versa; and diseases of* Mars *by herbs of* Venus, *and vice versa.*

*Sixthly, there is a way to cure diseases sometimes by sympathy, where every planet cures its own disease. For instance, the* Sun *and* Moon *cure the eyes with their herbs,* Saturn *cures the spleen,* Jupiter *the liver,* Mars *the gallbladder and diseases of choler <note>original: "choller"; one of the four bodily humors, associated with anger and digestive bile</note>, and* Venus *cures diseases in the reproductive organs.*

*Seventhly, there was a small treatise of mine regarding* Human Virtues <note>original: "Humane Vertues"</note>, *printed at the end of my* Ephemeris <note>An almanac or table of planetary positions</note> *for the year 1651. I believe it would greatly benefit young students to study that alongside this book.*

*Eighthly, young students would help themselves and benefit exceedingly in the study of* Medicine <note>original: "Physick"</note> *if they would take the pains to examine the virtues of the herbs in this book and compare them to these rules. They shall find, to their great satisfaction, that they are all in agreement; thereby, they shall see the reason why a specific herb leads to the cure of a specific disease.*

*Ninthly, I gave you the key to all of this in the entry for the herb* Wormwood. *If anyone thinks that key does not fit the lock because of the complexity of the language there, I have provided it to you again—plainly and without distraction—under another herb of the same planet in this book.*

*That herb is* Carduus Benedictus <note>The Blessed Thistle</note>, *which is located in alphabetical order in the book; I refer you to that place.*

*If you choose to use these rules and apply them to the entry for* Carduus *in this book, you shall find them true throughout the entire work. By paying attention to them, you may be able to provide a reasoned explanation for your judgment to anyone who asks you. I assure you it gave much satisfaction to me, and I wrote it for your benefit. But I must conclude, as my* Letter <note>original: "Epistle"</note> *has already exceeded its* limits. *By this, you see what* logic *can be provided for* medicines, *and the necessity for every* physician *to be an* astrologer. *I suppose you have heard this before, but now you know it. What remains but for you to labor to glorify* God *in your various positions? Do good to yourselves first by increasing your knowledge, and to your* neighbors *afterward by helping their illnesses. I hope this* nation *is worthy of such people, and to such people I shall remain a* friend. *When* publishers <note>original: "Purchaser"</note> *can enjoy their rightful* property *in their* copyrights <note>original: "Copies"</note> *without fear of* thieving rogues, *I shall not fail to produce many more* books *for the* common good *in the* English language *for the benefit of all my* countrymen, *poor or rich.*

***

Spitalfields, next door
to the Red Lion.
September 5, 1653.

->**Nicholas Culpeper.**<-

<summary>Nicholas Culpeper concludes his preface by outlining rules for curing diseases through planetary sympathy and antipathy, urging students to study the astrological "reasons" behind herbal remedies. He asserts that a true physician must also be an astrologer and expresses his intent to publish more works in English for the public good.</summary>

# THE
## English Physician Enlarged.

### Amara-dulcis.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap "C" surrounded by a square border of small floral ornaments.</image-desc>

Considering that various shires in this nation give various names to one and the same herb, and that the common name which it bears in one county is not known in another, I shall take the trouble to set down all the names that I know for each herb. Pardon me for putting that name first which is most common to myself; besides *Amara-dulcis*, some call it *Mortal*, others *Bitter-sweet*, some *Woody-Nightshade*, and others *Felon-wort*.

*Description.*] It grows up with woody stalks even to a man's height, and sometimes higher. The leaves fall off at the approach of winter and spring out again from the same stalk at springtime. The branch is surrounded by a whitish bark and has a pith in the middle of it. The main branch branches itself out into many small ones with tendrils, taking hold of whatever is next to them, as vines do. It bears many leaves; they grow in no order at all, or at least in no common order. The leaves are somewhat long, though fairly broad and pointed at the ends; many of them have two little leaves growing at the end of their leaf-stalk, some of them have but one, and some none. The leaves are of a pale green color. The flowers are of a purple color or of a perfect blue, like violets; and many of them stand together in clusters. The berries are green at first, but when they are ripe, they are very red. If you taste them, you shall find them just like the crab apples which we in *Sussex* call *Bitter-sweet*, namely, sweet at first and bitter afterward.

*Place.*] They grow commonly almost throughout *England*, especially in moist and shady places.

*Time.*] The leaves shoot out about the latter end of *March*, if the

the temperature of the air is ordinary, it flowers in *July*, and the seeds are ripe soon after, usually in the next month.

<margin>Witchcraft</margin>
<margin>Vertigo.</margin>
<margin>Felons.</margin>
Government and Virtues.] It is under the planet *Mercury*, and a notable herb of his as well, if it be rightly gathered under his influence; it is excellently good for removing witchcraft both in men and beasts, as also all sudden diseases whatsoever; being tied around the neck, it is one of the most admirable remedies for vertigo, or dizziness in the head, that exists, and that is the reason (as *Tragus* says) the people in *Germany* commonly hang it about their cattle's necks when they fear any such evil has befallen them. Country people commonly take its berries and, having bruised them, they apply them to felons, and thereby soon rid their fingers of such troublesome guests.

<margin>Obstructions of the liver and spleen, difficulty of breathing, bruises, falls, congealed blood, dropsy, yellow and black jaundice, women after delivery.</margin>
We have now shown you the external use of the herb; we shall speak a word or two of the internal use and then conclude: Take notice that it is a *Mercurial* herb, and therefore of very subtle parts, as indeed all *Mercurial* plants are; therefore take a pound of the wood and leaves together, bruise the wood (which you may easily do, for it is not as hard as oak) then put it in a pot, and add three pints of white wine, put on the pot lid and shut it close, then let it infuse hot over a gentle fire for 12 hours, then strain it out; thus you have a most excellent drink to open obstructions of the liver and spleen, to help difficulty of breathing, bruises, falls, and congealed blood in any part of the body, to help yellow jaundice, the dropsy, and black jaundice, and to cleanse women newly delivered: you may drink a quarter of a pint of the infusion every morning; it purges the body very gently, and not harshly as some hold; and when you find benefit from this, remember me.

## All-heal.

It is called All-heal, Hercules' All-heal, and Hercules' Woundwort, because it is supposed that Hercules learned of the herb and its virtues from *Chiron*, when he learned medicine from him; some call it Panay, and others Opopanay-wort.

Description.] Its root is long, thick, and exceedingly full of juice, with a hot and biting taste; the leaves are great and large, and winged almost like ash-tree leaves, except that they are somewhat hairy, each leaf consisting of five or six pairs of such wings set one against the other upon stalks broad below but narrow toward the end; one of the leaves is a little deeper at the bottom than the other, of a fair, yellowish, fresh, green color; they are

*Place.*] Having given you the description of the herb from the bottom to the top, give me leave to tell you that there are other herbs called by this name; but because they are foreign to England, I gave only the description of this which is easy to find in the gardens of many.

*Time.*] Although *Gerard* says that they flower from the beginning of *May* to the end of *December*, experience teaches those who keep it in their gardens that it flowers not until the later end of *summer*, and sheds its seeds immediately after.

*Government and Virtues.*] It is under the dominion of *Mars*; hot, biting, and choleric: and remedies whatever evils *Mars* afflicts the body of man with by sympathy, as vipers' flesh attracts poison, and the lodestone attracts iron: It kills the worms, helps the gout, cramp, and convulsions; provokes urine, and helps all joint-aches; it helps all cold ailments of the head, the vertigo, falling sickness, and lethargy, the windy colic, obstructions of the liver and spleen, stone in the kidneys and bladder; it *Worms*, provokes the terms, expels the dead birth; it is excellently good *Convulsions.* for the ailments of the sinews, itch, sores, and toothache, the *Cramp,* bites of mad dogs and venomous beasts, and purges choler very gently.

# Water-Agrimony.

It is called in some countries Water Hemp, Bastard Hemp, and Bastard Agrimony, *Eupatorium*, and *Hepatorium*, because it strengthens the liver.

*Description.*] The root continues a long time, having many long, slender strings; the stalks grow up about two feet high, sometimes higher; they are of a dark purple color. The branches are many, growing at distances from one another, one from one side of the stalk, the other from the opposite point. The leaves are winged and much indented at the edges. The flowers grow at the tops of the branches, of a brown-yellow color, spotted with black spots, having a substance within the midst of them like that of a daisy; if you rub them between your fingers, they smell like resin or cedar when it is burnt. The seeds are long and easily stick to any woolen thing they touch.

*Place.*] They do not delight in heat, and therefore they are not so frequently found in the southern parts of *England* as in the north, where they grow frequently. You may look for them in cold grounds, by ponds and ditch sides, as also by running waters; sometimes you shall find them grow in the midst of the waters.

*Time.*] They all flower in *July* and *August*, and the seed is ripe immediately after.

<margin>Cutting, Cleansing, Breast, Cachexia, Dropsy, yellow Jaundice, Obstructions, Liver, Spleen, Imposthumes <note>abscesses</note>, Urine, terms <note>menstruation</note> provokes, the Worms, Itch, Scabs, it drives away flies and wasps.</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] It is a plant of *Jupiter* as well as the other Agrimony, only this belongs to the celestial sign *Cancer*. It heals and dries, cuts and cleanses thick and tough humors of the breast, and for this I hold it inferior to but few herbs that grow. It helps the *cachexia* <note>a general state of ill health and malnutrition</note>, or evil disposition of the body; the dropsy and yellow jaundice. It opens obstructions of the liver and mollifies the hardness of the spleen. Being applied outwardly, it breaks imposthumes <note>abscesses</note>; taken inwardly, it is an excellent remedy for the third-day ague <note>tertian ague</note>. It provokes urine and the terms <note>menstruation</note>; it kills worms and cleanses the body of sharp humors, which are the cause of itch and scabs. The smoke of the herb being burnt drives away flies, wasps, etc.

# Alehoof, Or Ground-Ivy.

Several counties give it several names, so that there is scarcely an herb growing of that size that has received so many; it is called Cat's-foot, Ground Ivy, Gill-go-by-ground, and Gill-creep-by-ground, Tun-hoof, Hay-maids, and Alehoof.

*Description.*] This well-known herb lies, spreads, and creeps upon the ground, shooting forth roots at the corners of the tender jointed stalks, set all along with two round leaves at every joint, somewhat hairy, crumpled, and unevenly dented about the edges with round dents; at the joints likewise with the leaves towards the end of the branches come forth hollow long flowers, of a bluish purple color, with small white spots upon the lips that hang down; the root is small with strings.

*Place.*] It is commonly found under hedges and on the sides of ditches, under houses, or in shadowed lanes, and other waste grounds in almost every part of the land.

*Time.*] They flower somewhat early, and remain so a great while; the leaves continue green until winter, and sometimes last, unless the winter is very sharp and cold.

<margin>Inward wounds, pains, griping, wind, choler, stomach, spleen, belly, liver obstructions, gall, plague, poison, urine, gout, sciatica, sore mouth and throat,</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] It is an herb of **Venus**, and therefore cures the diseases she causes by sympathy, and those of **Mars** by antipathy. You may usually find it all the year long, unless the year is extremely frosty. It is quick, sharp, and bitter in taste, and is thereby found to be hot and dry; it is a singular herb for all inward wounds, ulcerated lungs, or other parts, either by itself or boiled with other similar herbs. When drunk, it in a short time eases all griping pains, windy and choleric humors in the stomach, spleen, or belly; it helps yellow jaundice by opening the obstructions of the gall and liver, and melancholy by opening the obstructions of the spleen; it expels venom or poison, and also the plague; it provokes urine and women's courses. The decoction of it in wine, drunk for some time together, provides ease to those who are troubled with sciatica or hip-gout, as also the gout in the hands, knees, or feet. If you add some honey and a little burnt alum to the decoction, it is excellent for gargling any sore mouth or throat, and for washing sores and ulcers in the

## Alexander.

It is also called Alisander, Horse Parsley, and Wild Parsley, and the black pot-herb; the seed of it is that which is usually sold in the apothecaries' shops as Macedonian parsley-seed.

**Description.**] It is usually sown in all the gardens in Europe, and is so well known that it needs no further description.

**Time.**] They flower in *June* and *July*, and the seed is ripe in *August*.

<margin>Obstructions of the liver and spleen, provokes the periods, afterbirth, wind, provokes urine, biting of serpents.</margin>
**Government and Virtues.**] It is an herb of *Jupiter*, and therefore friendly to nature, for it warms a cold stomach and opens blockages of the liver and spleen. It is good to move women's periods, to expel the afterbirth, to relieve gas, to promote urine, and help the strangury <note>painful or difficult urination</note>; and the seeds will do these things likewise. If either of them be boiled in wine, or being crushed and taken in wine, it is also effective against the biting of serpents. And now you know what Alexander pottage <note>a type of thick soup or stew</note> is good for, so that you may no longer eat it out of ignorance, but out of knowledge.

## The Common Alder-Tree.

<margin>Description.</margin>
It grows to a reasonable height and spreads much if it likes the place. It is so generally well known to country people that I believe it is unnecessary to tell them what is not news.

*Place and Time.*] It delights to grow in moist woods and watery places, flowering in *April* or *May* and yielding ripe seed in *September*.

<margin>Burns, Inflammations.</margin>
*Government and Use.*] It is a tree under the dominion of *Venus* and of some watery sign or other—I suppose *Pisces*—and therefore the decoction or distilled water of the leaves is excellent against burns and inflammation, whether with wounds or without, to bathe the affected place with, and especially for that inflammation in the breast which the common people call an ague <note>likely referring to mastitis or "milk fever"</note>.

If you cannot get the leaves (as it is impossible in winter), use the bark in the same manner.

<margin>Cooling, Drying, Binding, Swellings, Fleas.</margin>
The leaves and bark of the alder tree are cooling, drying, and binding. The fresh leaves laid upon swellings dissolve them and stay the inflammations. The leaves put under bare feet galled <note>sore or chafed</note> from traveling are a great refreshment to them. These leaves, gathered while the morning dew is on them and brought into a chamber troubled with fleas, will draw the fleas to them; when the leaves are suddenly cast out, it will rid the chamber of those troublesome bedfellows.

## Angelica.

To write a description of that which is so well known to be growing in almost every garden, I suppose, is altogether unnecessary; yet for its virtues, it is of admirable use.

In times of heathenism, when men had found any excellent herb, etc., they dedicated it to their gods: as the bay tree to *Apollo*, the oak to *Jupiter*, the vine to *Bacchus*, and the poplar to *Hercules*. The Papists, following these as their patriarchs, dedicate them to their saints, as "Our Lady's Thistle" to the

Alas, poor fools, I am sorry for their folly and grieved at their blasphemy. God send them the rest of their years, for they have their share of ignorance already. Oh! Why must ours be blasphemous because the heathens and Papists were idolatrous? Certainly they have read so much in old, rusty authors that they have lost their understanding of divinity; for unless it were among the Ranters, I never read or heard of such blasphemy. The heathens and Papists were bad, and ours are worse—the Papists giving idolatrous names to herbs for their virtues' sake, not for their fair looks. Therefore, some called this an herb of the Holy Ghost; others, more moderate, called it **ANGELICA** because of its angelic virtues, and that name it retains still, and all nations follow it as closely as their dialect will permit.

*Government and Virtues.*] It is an herb of the *Sun* in *Leo*. Let it be gathered when he is there, the *Moon* applying to his good aspect; let it be gathered either in his hour or in the hour of *Jupiter*, and let *Sol* be angular. Observe the like in gathering the herbs of other plants, and you may happen to do wonders.

</margin>
In all epidemic diseases caused by *Saturn*, this is as good a preventative as grows. It resists poison by defending and comforting the heart, blood, and spirits; it does the same against the plague and all epidemic diseases if the root be taken in powder to the weight of half a dram at a time with some good treacle <note>a medicinal compound, often used as an antidote</note> in Carduus Water, and the patient then laid to sweat in his bed. If treacle is not to be had, take it alone in Carduus or Angelica water. The stalks or roots, candied and eaten while fasting, are good preventatives in times of infection, and at other times to warm and comfort a cold stomach.

# Amaranthus.

Besides this common name, by which it is best known by the florists of our day, it is also called Flower-Gentle, Flower-Velure, Floramor, and Velvet Flower.

*Description.*] Since it is a garden flower and well known to everyone who grows it, I might skip the description; however, because some desire it, I shall provide it. It grows with a stalk a cubit <note>An ancient unit of length, about 18 inches.</note> high, striped and somewhat reddish toward the root, but very smooth, divided toward the top into small branches, among which stand long, broad leaves of a reddish-green color, smooth to the touch. The flowers are not properly flowers but tufts, very beautiful to behold but having no smell, of a reddish color. If you bruise them, they yield juice of the same color. Once gathered, they keep their beauty for a long time. The seed is a shining black color.

*Time.*] They continue to flower from August until the time the frost nips them.

# Arrach, wild and stinking.

Called also Vulvaria from that part of the body upon which its operation is most active; also Dog’s Arrach, Goat’s Arrach, and stinking Mother-wort.

*Description.*] This has small, and almost round leaves, yet slightly pointed, and without any teeth or cuts, of a dusky mealy color, growing on the slender stalks and branches that spread on the ground, with small flowers in clusters set with the leaves, and small seeds succeeding like the rest, perishing yearly, and rising again from its own sowing. It smells like old rotten fish, or something worse.

*Place.*] It usually grows upon dunghills.

*Time.*] They flower in June and July, and their seed is ripe quickly after.

<margin>Mothers</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] Stinking Arrach is used as a remedy to help women pained and almost strangled by the mother <note>This refers to "suffocation of the mother," a condition also known as hysteria, where the patient felt a sensation of choking or fits attributed to the womb.</note>, by smelling it: But taken internally, there is not a better remedy under the moon for that disease. I would be generous in my praise of this herb, if I were only eloquent. It is an herb under the dominion of Venus, and under the sign Scorpio: It is common almost upon every dunghill. The works of God are given freely to man; his medicines are common and cheap, and easy to be found: (it is the medicines of the *College of Physicians* that are so dear, and scarce to find.) 

<margin>womb,</margin>

(And let me tell you this, and I will tell you only the truth: heat of the womb is one of the greatest causes of hard labor in childbirth.) It makes barren women fruitful; it cleanses the womb if it be foul, and strengthens it exceedingly; it provokes the terms <note>Menstruation.</note> if they be stopped, and stops them if they flow immoderately: You can desire no good for your womb but what this herb will effect; therefore if you love children, if you love health, if you love ease, keep a syrup always by you made of the juice of this herb and sugar (or honey if it is to cleanse the womb), and let those who are rich keep it for their poor neighbors, and bestow it as freely as I bestow my studies upon them, or else let them expect to answer for it another day when the Lord shall come to make inquisition of blood <note>A biblical reference meaning to hold individuals accountable for lives lost through neglect or lack of charity.</note>.

Whether this is superstition or folly, I leave to the judicious reader. Others have shown more curiosity than courtesy toward my countrymen in their explanations of both the names and descriptions of this well-known herb. To avoid being guilty of the same, take this short description, starting first with the Red Archangel.

*Description.*] This has various square stalks that are somewhat hairy. At the joints, two dull green leaves grow opposite each other; they are notched around the edges. The lowermost leaves grow on long leaf-stalks, but those toward the tops have none; these top leaves are somewhat round yet pointed, and a little crumpled and hairy. Around the upper joints where the leaves grow thick are several gaping flowers of a pale reddish color; these are followed by the seeds, which are three or four in a husk. The root is small and thread-like, dying every year. The whole plant has a strong scent, but it is not stinking.

White Archangel has various square stalks that do not stand straight and upright but bend downward. Two leaves grow at each joint; these are larger and more pointed than the others, notched around the edges, and greener as well—looking more like Nettle leaves, but they do not sting, though they are hairy. At the joints with the leaves stand larger and more open gaping white flowers, set in husks around the stalks (unlike the other variety, it does not have a bush of leaves among the flowers at the top). These contain small, roundish black seeds. The root is white with many strings; it does not grow downward but lies just under the surface of the earth, and lives for many years, increasing in size. This plant does not have as strong a scent as the former.

Yellow Archangel is like the white variety in its stalks and leaves, except that the stalks are straighter and more upright, and the joints with leaves are further apart. Its leaves are longer than the previous kind, and the flowers are a little larger and more gaping, of a beautiful yellow color in most, though paler in some. The roots are like the white variety, only they do not creep as much under the ground.

*Place.*] They grow almost everywhere (unless it is in the middle of the street). The yellow variety is most usually found in the wet grounds of woods, though sometimes in drier areas, in various parts of this nation.

*Time.*] They flower from the beginning of the spring throughout the summer.

<margin>Spleen</margin>
*Virtues and use.*] The Archangels are somewhat hotter and drier than stinging nettles, and they are used with better success for the stopping and hardness of the spleen. This is done by using a decoction of the herb in wine and afterward applying the hot herb to the region of the spleen as a plaster, or by applying the decoction with sponges. 

<margin>Whites</margin>
The flowers of the white Archangel are preserved or conserved to be used to stop the whites <note>Leukorrhea, or white vaginal discharge.</note>, and the flowers of the

## Ars-smart.

The hot ars-smart is also called water-pepper or culrage. The mild ars-smart is called dead ars-smart, <term>persicaria</term>, or peach-wort, because the leaves are so similar to the leaves of a peach tree; it is also called <term>plumbago</term>.

*Description of the mild.*] This has broad leaves set at the large red joints of the stalks, usually with semicircular blackish marks on them, though sometimes without. The flowers usually grow in long spikes, either blush-colored or whitish, with similar seeds following. The root is long with many strings attached, dying every year. This variety has no sharp taste (unlike another sort which is quick and biting), but is rather sour like sorrel, or else a little drying, or without taste.

*Place.*] It grows in watery puddles, ditches, and the like, which for the most part are dry in summer.

*Time.*] It flowers in June, and the seed is ripe in August.

*Government and Virtues.*] As the virtues of both these are various, so are their planetary rulers; for the variety that is hot and biting is under the dominion of *Mars*, but *Saturn* claims the other, as appears by that lead-colored spot he has placed upon the leaf.

If you see them both together, you may easily distinguish them because the mild one has much broader leaves. ## Asarabacca.

<margin>Description.]</margin> *Asarabacca has many heads rising from the roots, from which come many smooth leaves, each on its own footstalk. These are rounder and larger than violet leaves, thicker also, and of a dark, shining green color on the upper side and a paler yellowish-green underneath, with little or no notches around the edges. From among these rise small, round, hollow, brown-green husks on short stalks about an inch long, divided at the rims into five sections, very like the cups or heads of henbane seed, except they are smaller. These are all the flowers it carries, which are somewhat sweet to the smell. When they are ripe, they contain small, angled, rough seeds, very like the kernels or stones of grapes or raisins. The roots are small and whitish, spreading in various ways in the ground and increasing into several heads, but not running or creeping under the ground like some other creeping herbs. They have a somewhat sweet smell, resembling Nardus <note>spikenard</note>, but more so when they are dry than green; they have a sharp but not unpleasant taste.*

<margin>Place.]</margin> It grows frequently in gardens.

<margin>Time.]</margin> They keep their leaves green all winter but shoot forth new ones in the spring; with these come those heads or flowers which produce ripe seed about Midsummer or shortly after.

<margin>*Causes vomiting, choler, phlegm, urine, obstructions of the liver and spleen, dropsy, jaundice, agues.*</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] It is a plant under the dominion of Mars, and therefore harmful to nature. This herb, when drunk, not only provokes vomiting but purges downward and through the urine also, purging both choler <note>yellow bile</note> and phlegm. If you add to it some spikenard, with the whey of goat's milk or honeyed water, it is made stronger; but it purges phlegm more obviously than choler, and therefore it greatly helps pains in the hips and other parts. Being boiled in whey, it wonderfully helps the obstructions of the liver and spleen, and is therefore profitable for the dropsy and jaundice when steeped in wine and drunk. It helps those continual agues <note>fevers</note> that come from an abundance of stubborn humors. An oil made of it by setting it in the sun, with some laudanum added to it, provokes sweating (the ridge of the back being anointed with it) and thereby drives away the shaking fits of the agues. It will not endure any long boiling, for it loses its chief strength thereby; nor much beating, for the finer powder provokes vomiting and urine, and the coarser purges downwards.

<margin>*Serpents, head, memory.*</margin>
The common use of this is to take the juice of five or seven leaves in a little drink to cause vomiting. The roots also have the same virtue, though they do not operate as forcibly; yet they are very effectual against the biting of serpents, and therefore it is put as an ingredient into both Mithridate and Venice Treacle. The leaves and roots being boiled in lye, and the head often washed with it while it is warm, comforts a head and brain that is ill-affected by taking cold, and helps the memory.

I shall desire ignorant people to forbear the use of the leaves; the roots purge more gently and may prove beneficial for those who have cancers, or old putrified ulcers, or fistulas upon their bodies, by taking a dram of them in powder in a quarter of a pint of white wine in the morning. The truth is, I favor purging and vomiting medicines as little as any man living does, for they weaken nature; nor shall I ever advise them to be used unless out of urgent necessity. If a physician be nature's servant, it is his duty to strengthen his mistress as much as he can, and weaken her as little as possible.

## Asparagus, Sparagus, or Sperage.

IT rises up at first with various whitish-green scaly heads, *very brittle or easy to break while they are young, which afterwards rise up into very long and slender green stalks, of the thickness of an ordinary riding wand at the bottom of most, or larger or smaller, as the roots are grown; on which are set various branches of green leaves, shorter and smaller than fennel to the top; at the joints of which come forth small mossy yellowish flowers, which turn into round berries, green at first, and of an excellent red color when they are ripe, appearing like beads of coral, in which are contained exceedingly hard, black seeds. The roots are dispersed from a spongy head into many long, thick, and round strings, by which it sucks much nourishment out of the ground and increases plentifully thereby.*

# Prickly Asparagus, Sparagus, or Sperage.

<margin>Description.]</margin>
It grows usually in *gardens*, and some of it grows wild in *Appleton Meadow* in *Gloucestershire*, where the poor people gather the buds, or young shoots, and sell them cheaper than our garden *asparagus* is sold at *London*.

<margin>Time.]</margin>
They do for the most part flower and bear their berries late in the year, or not at all, although they are housed in *winter*.

<margin>Government and Virtues.]</margin>
<margin>Bowels, strangury, dysuria, gout, sciatica, eyes, toothache.</margin>
<margin>Kidneys, bladder, womb, cramps, colic, convulsions.</margin>
They are both under the dominion of *Jupiter*. The young buds, or branches, boiled in one's ordinary broth, make the belly soluble and open; and boiled in white wine, it provokes urine when it is stopped and is good against the strangury, or difficulty in urinating; it expels gravel and stones out of the kidneys and helps pains in the kidneys. And boiled in white wine or vinegar, it is prevalent for those that have their arteries loosened or are troubled with hip-gout or sciatica. The decoction of the roots boiled in wine and taken is good to clear the sight, and being held in the mouth, it eases the toothache. Being taken fasting several mornings together, it stirs up bodily lust in man or woman (whatever some have written to the contrary). The garden *asparagus* nourishes more than the wild, yet it has the same effects in all the aforementioned diseases. The decoction of the roots in white wine—and the back and belly bathed therewith, or kneeling or lying down in the same, or sitting therein as a bath—has been found effectual against pains of the kidneys and bladder, pains of the womb and colic, and generally against all pains that happen to the lower parts of the body; it is no less effectual against stiff and benumbed sinews, or those that are shrunk by cramps and convulsions, and it helps the sciatica.

# Ash-tree.

This is so well known that time will be misspent in writing a description of it; and therefore I shall only insist upon its virtues.

<margin>Government and Virtues.]</margin>
<margin>Bites of adders and vipers, dropsy, stones, jaundice, leprosy, scabs, scald heads, stitches, stones, dysuria, rickets.</margin>
It is governed by the *Sun*, and the young tender tops with the leaves taken inwardly, and some of them applied outwardly, are singularly good against the biting of the *viper, adder*, or any other venomous beast. The water distilled therefrom, being taken in a small quantity every morning fasting, is a singular medicine for those who are subject to a dropsy, or to abate the size of those who are too gross or fat. The decoction of the leaves in white wine helps to break the stone and expel it, and cures the jaundice. The ashes of the bark of the ash made into lye, and those heads bathed therewith which are leprous, scabby, or scald, are thereby cured. The kernels within the husks, commonly called *ashen keys*, prevail against stitches and pains in the sides proceeding from wind, and remove the stone by provoking urine.

I can justly disagree with none of all this, except only for the first point, namely: that ash tree tops and leaves are good against the bites of serpents and vipers. I suppose this idea originated from *Gerard* or *Pliny*, both of whom claim there is such an antipathy between an adder and an ash tree that if an adder is surrounded by ash tree leaves, it will sooner run through fire than through the leaves. The opposite of this is actually the truth, as my own eyes have witnessed. The rest of the virtues are likely enough; however, if it is winter and you cannot get the leaves, you may safely use the bark instead. You may easily keep the keys <note>winged seeds of the ash tree</note> all year by gathering them when they are ripe.

## Avens, also called Clovewort and Herb Benet.

<margin>Description</margin> The ordinary avens has many long, rough, dark green, winged leaves rising from the root, each made of many leaves set on each side of the middle rib. The largest three of these grow at the ends and are snipped or dented around the edges. The others are small pieces, sometimes two and sometimes four, standing on each side of the middle rib beneath them. Among these rise up several rough or hairy stalks about two feet high, branching out with leaves at every joint; these are not as long as those below, but are almost as deeply indented on the edges, some into three parts and some into more. On the tops of the branches stand small, pale yellow flowers consisting of five petals, like the flowers of *cinquefoil*, but larger in the middle. In the center of the flower stands a small green head, which, when the flower has fallen, grows to be rough and round, being made of many long greenish-purple seeds (like grains) which will stick to your clothes. The root consists of many brownish strings or fibers, smelling somewhat like cloves, especially those that grow in higher, hotter, and drier grounds, and in the open, clear air.

<margin>Place</margin> They grow wild in many places along hedge-sides and by the pathways in fields, yet they prefer to grow in shady rather than sunny places.

<margin>Time</margin> They flower in *May* and *June* for the most part, and their seed is ripe in *July* at the latest.

<margin>Government and Virtues</margin> It is governed by *Jupiter*, and that gives hope of a wholesome, healthful herb. It is good for diseases of the chest or breast, for pains and stitches in the sides, and to expel crude and raw humors from the belly and stomach by its sweet aroma and warming quality. It dissolves inward congealed blood caused by falls or bruises, and helps the spitting of blood, if the roots, either green or dried, are boiled in wine and drunk. It is also good for all manner of inward or outward wounds if they are washed or bathed with it. The decoction, when drunk, also comforts the heart and strengthens the stomach and a cold brain; therefore, it is good in the springtime to open obstructions of the liver, and helps

# Balm.

<margin>Mind, Heart, Faintings, Melancholy, Indigestion, Obstruction of the Brain, Heart, Arteries, Venomous Beasts, Mad Dogs, Monthly courses, Toothache, Bloody flux, Mushrooms, Difficulty of breathing, Gout, Liver, Spleen</margin>
This herb is so well known as an inhabitant of almost every garden that I shall not need to write any description of it, although its virtues, which are many, must not be omitted.

*Government and Virtues.*] It is an herb of *Jupiter*, and under *Cancer*, and strengthens nature much in all its actions: let a syrup made with its juice and sugar (as you shall be taught at the end of the book) be kept in every gentlewoman’s house to relieve the weak stomachs and sick bodies of their poor sickly neighbors. The herb should also be kept dry in the house so that, with other convenient simples <note>medicinal plants used as single ingredients</note>, you may make it into an electuary <note>a medicinal paste</note> with honey according to the disease, as you shall be taught at the end of the book. It is very good for helping digestion and opening obstructions of the brain, and has such a purging quality (says *Avicen*) that it expels those melancholy vapors from the spirits and blood in the heart and arteries, although it cannot do so in other parts of the body. *Dioscorides* says that the leaves steeped in wine and the wine drunk, with the leaves applied externally, is a remedy against the sting of scorpions and the bites of mad dogs; he also commends its decoction for women to bathe or sit in to provoke their monthly courses. It is good for washing aching teeth and is profitable for those with the bloody flux <note>dysentery</note>. Used with salt, it takes away wens <note>cysts or tumors</note>, kernels, or hard swellings in the flesh or throat; it cleanses foul sores and eases the pains of the gout. ## Barberry.

The shrub is so well known to every boy and girl who has reached the age of seven years that it needs no description.

<margin>

*Government and Virtues.*] *Mars* owns the shrub and presents it for the use of my countrymen to purge their bodies of choler <note>yellow bile</note>. The inner rind of the barberry tree, boiled in white wine and a quarter of a pint drunk each morning, is an excellent remedy to cleanse the body of choleric humors and free it from such diseases as choler causes, such as scabs, itch, tetters <note>skin sores</note>, ringworms, yellow jaundice, boils, etc. It is excellent for hot agues, burns, scalds, heat of the blood, heat of the liver, and bloody flux <note>dysentery</note>; for the berries are as good as the bark and more pleasant. They provide a man with a good appetite for his food by strengthening the attractive faculty, which is under *Mars*, as you may see more at length at the end of my *Ephemeris* for the year 1651. If the hair is washed with the lye made from the ashes of the tree and water, it will make it turn yellow, namely *Mars’s* own color. The fruit and rind of the shrub, the flowers of broom and of heath or furze, cleanse the body of choler by sympathy, just as the flowers, leaves, and bark of the peach tree do by antipathy: because these are under *Mars*, and that is under *Venus*.

## Garden Basil, Or, Sweet Basil.

<margin>*Description.*</margin> *The greater ordinary basil usually rises up with one upright stalk branching out diversely on all sides, with two leaves at every joint, which are somewhat broad and round, yet pointed, of a pale green color, but fresh, a little snipped about the edges, and of a strong heady scent. The flowers are small and white, standing at the tops of the branches, with two small leaves at the joint, in some places green, in others brown, after which comes black seed. The root perishes at the approach of winter, and therefore must be newly sown every year.*

<margin>*Place.*</margin> It only grows in gardens.
<margin>*Time.*</margin> It must be sown late and flowers in the heat of summer, being a very tender plant.
<margin>*Government and Virtues.*</margin> This is the herb which all authors are at odds about and rail at one another like lawyers. Galen and Dioscorides hold it not fitting to be taken internally; and Chrysippus rails at it with downright Billingsgate rhetoric <note>foul or abusive language</note>. Pliny and the Arabian physicians defend it.

For my own part, I soon found that saying true:
> *Non nostrum inter nos tantas componere lites.* <note>Latin: It is not for us to settle such great disputes between us.</note>

And away to Dr. Reason I went, who told me it was an herb of Mars, and under Scorpio, and perhaps therefore called *Basilicon*; and then it is no marvel if it carries a kind of virulent quality with it. <margin>*Venomous beasts, bees, wasps, hornets.*</margin> Being applied to a place bitten by a venomous beast, or stung by a wasp or hornet, it speedily draws the poison to it; *every like draws its like.* Mizaldus affirms that if it is laid to rot in horse dung, it will breed venomous beasts. And Hollerius, a French physician, affirms upon his own knowledge that an acquaintance of his, by frequently smelling it, had a scorpion bred in his brain. Something is the matter that this herb and rue will not grow together,

## Beans.

Both the garden and field beans are so well known that it saves me the labor of writing any description of them: Their virtues follow.

<margin>
Government and Virtues.]
Spots, Stone, Dysuria, Inflammation, Women’s Breasts, Felons or Andicoms, Boils, Bruises, Ears, Eyes, Leeches.

Bean flour is used in poultices to assuage inflammations rising from wounds, and the swelling of women's breasts caused by the curdling of their milk, and it suppresses their milk. The field beans have all the aforementioned virtues as the garden beans.

Beans eaten are extremely windy food; but if, after the Dutch fashion, when they are half-boiled you husk them and then stew them (I cannot tell you how, for I never was a cook in all my life), they are more wholesome food.

## Beets.

<margin>*Description.*</margin>
There are two sorts of *Beets* which are best known generally, and of which I shall principally treat at this time, namely: the *white* and *red beets*, and their *virtues*.

The common white beet has many great leaves next to the ground, somewhat large and of a whitish-green color; the stalk is large, strong, and ribbed, bearing a great store of leaves upon it, almost to the very top of it. The flowers grow in very long tufts, small at the ends and turning down their heads, which are small, pale, greenish-yellow burrs, giving cornered, prickly seed. The root is large, long, and hard, and when it has given seed, is of no use at all.

The common red beet does not differ from the white, except that it is smaller, and the leaves and the roots are somewhat red: The leaves are differently red—in some only with red streaks or veins, some of a fresh red, and others of a dark red. The root of it is red, spongy, and not typically eaten.

<margin>Cleans, digests, dysuria <note>Painful or difficult urination</note>, obstructions of the liver and spleen, vertigo, venomous beasts, burning, St. Anthony's fire <note>Erysipelas, a skin infection</note>, wheals, blisters, chilblains, kibes <note>Ulcerated chilblains on the heels</note>, itch, dandruff, scabs, ulcers, cankers, baldness.</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] The government of these two types of beets is quite different; the red beet being under *Saturn*, and the white under *Jupiter*. Therefore, consider the virtues of them separately. The white beet loosens the belly significantly, is of a cleansing and digesting quality, and provokes urine. The juice of it opens obstructions of both the liver and spleen, and is good for headaches and dizziness, and vertigo; it is also effective against all venomous creatures. Applied to the temples, it stays inflammations in the eyes; it helps burns when used without oil; and with a little alum added to it, it is good for *St. Anthony's fire*. It is also good for all wheals, pustules, blisters, and sores on the skin. The herb boiled and laid upon chilblains or kibes helps them. The decoction of it in water and some vinegar heals the itch if bathed with it, and cleanses the head of dandruff, scurf, and dry scabs; it does much good for fretting and running sores, ulcers, and cankers in the head, legs, or other parts, and is much commended against baldness and the shedding of hair.

<margin>Flux, stopping of menstrual cycles, the whites <note>Leukorrhea</note>, bad breath, noise in the ears, loss of smell.</margin>
The red beet is good to stop the bloody flux <note>Dysentery</note>, women’s menstrual cycles, and the whites, and to help the yellow jaundice. The juice of the root put into the nostrils purges the head, helps the ringing in the ears, and the toothache; the juice snuffed up the nose helps a bad breath if the cause lies in the nose, as it often does if there has been any bruise there, as well as the loss of smell occurring for the same reason.

# Water-Betony.

Called also Brown-Wort, and in *Yorkshire*, *Bishops Leaves*.

*Description.*] First, the *Water-Betony* rises up with square, hard, greenish stalks, sometimes brown, set with broad, dark green leaves, indented around the edges with notches, somewhat resembling the leaves of the *Wood-Betony*, but much larger, with two for the most part set at a joint. The flowers are many, set at the tops of the stalks and branches, being round-bellied and open at the rims and divided into two parts, the uppermost being like a hood and the lowest like a lip hanging down, of a dark red color; which fading away, there come in their places small round heads with small points at the ends, wherein lie small and brownish seeds. The root is a thick bush of strings and threads growing from a head.

*Place.]* It grows by ditch sides, brooks, and other watercourses generally throughout this land, and is seldom found far from the watersides.

*Time.]* It flowers about *July*, and the seed is ripe in *August*.

*Government and Virtues.]* Water-Betony is an herb of *Jupiter* in *Cancer*, and is appropriated more to wounds and hurts in the breast than Wood-Betony which follows. It is an excellent remedy for sick hogs.

<margin>Ulcers,</margin>
It is of a cleansing quality; the leaves bruised and applied are effective for all old and filthy ulcers, and especially if the juice of the leaves be boiled with a little honey, and tents <note>Small plugs of lint or medical material used to keep a wound open</note> dipped therein, and the sores dressed with them: as also for

<margin>Bruises,</margin>
bruises or hurts whether inward or outward. The distilled water of the leaves is used for the same purposes; as also to

<margin>Sunburning.</margin>
bathe the face or hands when spotted, blemished, or discolored by sunburning.

I confess I do not much fancy distilled waters—I mean such waters as are distilled cold. Some virtue of the herb they may perhaps have (it would be a strange thing otherwise), but of this I am confident: that being distilled in a pewter still, as the common and foolish fashion is, both chemical oil and salt are left behind, unless you burn them, and then all is spoiled; and all that was good is as little as can be by such a distillation. You have the best way of distillation in my translation of the *London Dispensatory*. The College of Physicians has as much skill in distillations as an ass has in reading Hebrew.

### Wood-Betony.

<margin>Description.]</margin>
The common or Wood-Betony has many leaves rising from the root, which are somewhat broad and round at the ends, roundly dented about the edges, standing upon long footstalks. From among these rise up small, square, slender, but yet upright hairy stalks, with some leaves on them, two apiece at the joints, smaller than the lower ones. On these are set several spiked heads of flowers like lavender, but thicker and shorter for the most part, and of a reddish or purple color, spotted with white spots both in the upper and lower part. The seeds, being contained within the husks that hold the flowers, are blackish, somewhat long and uneven. The roots are many white, thread-like strings; the stalk perishes, but the root, with some leaves on it, remains all the winter. The whole plant is somewhat small.

*Place.]* It grows frequently in woods, and delights in shady places.

*Time.]* And it flowers in *July*, after which the seed is quickly ripe, yet it is in its prime in *May*.

<margin>Epidemical diseases, witchcraft, Appetite, Indigestion, &c.</margin>

## The Beech-Tree.

In treating of this tree, you must understand that I mean the great Mast Beech, which is by way of distinction from that other small rough sort called in *Sussex* the small Beech, but in *Essex*, Hornbeam.

I suppose it is needless to describe it, as it is already so well known to my countrymen.

<margin>Place.]</margin> It grows in woods among oaks and other trees, and in parks, forests, and chases to feed deer, and in other places to fatten swine.

<margin>Time.]</margin> It blooms in the end of *April* or beginning of *May* for the most part, and the fruit is ripe in *September*.

<margin>Government and Virtues.]</margin> It is a plant of *Saturn*, and therefore performs his qualities and properties in these operations:
<margin>Cools, binds, hot swellings, scurf, scabs, tetters.</margin> The leaves of the Beech-tree are cooling and binding, and therefore good to be applied to hot swellings to dissipate <note>disperse</note> them. The nuts much nourish such beasts as feed on them. The water that is found in the hollow places of decaying beeches will cure both man and beast of any scurf, scab, or running tetters <note>skin eruptions</note>, if they are washed with it. You may boil the leaves into a poultice or make an ointment of them when the season permits.

At the base of the leaves come forth small, hollow, pale, blush-colored flowers, the rims ending in five points with a reddish thread in the middle, which turn into small round berries of the size and color of juniper berries, but of a purple, sweetish-sharp taste; the juice of them gives a purplish color...

## Bifoyl, or Twayblade.

<margin>*Description.*</margin>
This small herb, from a root somewhat sweet, shooting downward many long strings, rises up as a round green stalk, bare or naked near the ground for an inch, two, or three, up to its middle, depending on its age or growth; as also from the middle upward to the flowers, it has only two broad plantain-like leaves (but whiter) set at the middle of the stalk one against another, and encompasses it around at the bottom of them.

<margin>*Place.*</margin>
It is a common inhabitant in woods, copses, and in many other places in this land.

There is another sort that grows in wet grounds and marshes, which is somewhat different from the former: it is a smaller plant and greener, sometimes having three leaves; the spike of flowers is smaller than the former, and the roots of this do run or creep in the ground.

<margin>*Wounds, Ruptures.*</margin>

## The Birch-tree.

<margin>*Description.*</margin> This grows into a handsome, tall, straight tree, filled with many boughs and slender branches bending downward; the old ones are covered with a discolored, cracked bark, and the younger are much browner. The leaves, when they first emerge, are crumpled, and afterward are like beech leaves, but smaller and greener, and notched <note>dented</note> about the edges. It bears small, short catkins, somewhat like those of the hazel-nut tree, which remain on the branches a long time, until, growing ripe, they fall to the ground, and their seed with them.
<margin>*Place.*</margin> It usually grows in woods.
<margin>*Government and Virtues.*</margin> It is a tree of *Venus*. The juice of the leaves while they are young, or their distilled water, or the water that comes out of the tree when it is bored with an auger and distilled after-
<margin>*Stone, sore mouths.*</margin> ward: any of these being drunk for some time together is effective for breaking the stone in the kidneys or bladder, and is also good for washing sore mouths.

## Bird's-Foot.

This small herb grows no more than a span high, with many branches spread on the ground, set with many pairs <note>wings</note> of small leaves. The flowers grow upon the branches; many small ones of a pale yellow color are set in a head together, which afterward turn into small, jointed pods that well resemble the claws of small birds, from which it took its name.
There is another kind of *Bird's-foot* similar to the first in all things but a little larger: the flowers are of a pale whitish-red color, and the pods are distinct by joints like the other, but a little more crooked; the roots carry many small white knots or kernels among the strings.
<margin>*Place.*</margin> These grow on heaths and many open, untilled places in this land.
<margin>*Time.*</margin> They flower and produce seed at the end of summer.
<margin>*Government and Virtues.*</margin> They belong to *Saturn* and are of a drying, binding quality, and thereby very good for use in wound-
<margin>*Dry, bind, wounds, stone, ruptures.*</margin> drinks, as also to be applied outwardly for the same purpose. But the latter *Bird's-foot* is found by experience to break the stones in the back or kidneys and drive them out, if a decoction of it is taken; and it wonderfully helps ruptures <note>hernias</note>, being taken inwardly and outwardly applied to the place.
All salts work best upon the stone, just as ointments and plasters work upon wounds; and therefore you may make a salt of this for the stone. The way to do so may be found in my translation of the *London Dispensatory*, and I may perhaps provide it again in plainer terms at the end of this book.

## Bistort, or Snakeweed.

It is called Snakeweed, English Serpentary, Dragonwort, Oysterloit, and Passions.

*Description.*] This has a thick, short, knobbed root, blackish without, and somewhat reddish within, a little crooked or turned together, of a harsh astringent taste, with various black threads hanging there, from whence spring up every year various leaves standing upon long footstalks, being somewhat broad and long like a dock-leaf, and a little pointed at the ends, except that it is of a bluish green color on the upper side, and of an ash-colored gray, and a little purplish underneath, with various veins therein; from among which rise up various small and slender stalks, two feet high, and almost naked, and without leaves, or with very few, and narrow, bearing a spiky cluster <note>bush</note> of pale flesh-colored flowers, which being past, there remains small seed, somewhat like unto sorrel-seed, but greater.

There are other sorts of Bistort growing in this land, but smaller, both in height, root, and stalks, and especially in the leaves; the root is blackish without, and somewhat whitish within, of an austere binding taste like the former.

*Place.*] They grow in shady moist woods, and at the foot of hills, but are chiefly nourished in gardens. The narrow-leaved *Bistort* grows in the North, in *Lancashire*, *Yorkshire*, and *Cumberland*.

*Time.*] They flower about the end of *May*, and the seed is ripe about the beginning of *July*.

## One-Blade.

<margin>Description.]</margin> *This small plant never bears more than one leaf, except when it rises up with its stalk which then bears another, and seldom more; these are of a bluish green color, broad at the bottom, and pointed with many ribs or veins like plantain. At the top of the stalk grow many small white flowers in a star-shape, smelling somewhat sweet; after which come small reddish berries when they are ripe. The root is small, of the bigness of a rush, lying and creeping under the upper crust of the earth, shooting forth in various places.*

<margin>Place.]</margin> It grows in moist, shadowy, grassy places in woods in many parts of this realm.

<margin>Time.]</margin> It flowers about *May*, and the berries are ripe in *June*, and then it quickly perishes until the next year when it springs from the same root again.

<margin>Government and Virtues.]</margin> It is an herb of the *Sun*, and therefore cordial. Half a dram, or a dram at most, of the roots of this in powder, taken in wine and vinegar of an equal quantity, and the person immediately laid to sweat, is held to be a sovereign remedy for those who are infected with the plague and have a sore upon them, by expelling the poison and
<margin>Pestilence, Wounds, Nerves, Injured Sinews.</margin> pestilence, defending the heart and spirits from danger. It is also accounted a singularly good wound-herb, and therefore used with other herbs in making such balms as are necessary for the curing of wounds, whether fresh or old, and especially if the nerves or sinews are hurt.

## The Bramble, or Black-berry-bush.

This is so well known that it needs no description. The virtues thereof are as follows.

<margin>Government and Virtues.]</margin> It is a plant of *Venus* in *Aries*. You shall have some directions at the end of the book for the gathering of all herbs and plants, etc. If any ask the reason why *Venus* is so prickly? Tell them it is because she is in the house of *Mars*. The buds, leaves, and branches while they are green, are of good use for ulcers and putrid sores of the mouth and throat, and for the <term>Quinsy</term>; and
<margin>Ulcers, Sores, Quinsy, wounds, Flux, Bloody flux, Spitting Blood, Gravel, Stone, Private parts, Menstrual flow.</margin> likewise to heal other fresh wounds and sores. However, the flowers and unripe fruit are very binding, and so profitable for the <term>Bloody-flux</term> and <term>Lasks</term>, and are a fit remedy for spitting of blood. Either the decoction or powder of the root being taken is good to break or drive forth <term>Gravel</term> and the <term>Stone</term> in the <term>Reins</term> and <term>Kidneys</term>. The leaves and brambles, as well green as dry, are excellent good lotions for sores in the mouth or private parts. The decoction of them and of the dried branches much binds the belly and is good for the excessive flowing of a woman's courses. The berries or the flowers are a powerful remedy against the poison of the most venomous serpents, whether drunk or outwardly applied, and helps the sores of the <term>Fundament</term> and the <term>Piles</term>.

# Blites.

<margin>Description.]</margin> Of these, there are two sorts commonly known, namely, *white* and *red*: the *white* has leaves somewhat like those of beets, but smaller, rounder, and of a whitish-green color, each one standing upon a small long stalk. The stalk rises up two or three feet high, with similar leaves on it. The flowers grow at the top in long round tufts or clusters, in which are contained small and round seeds. The root is very full of threads or strings.

The red blite is like the white in all respects, except that its leaves and tufted heads are exceedingly red at first and afterward turn more purplish.

There are other kinds of blites which grow wild, differing very little from the two former sorts, except that the wild ones are smaller in every part.

<margin>Place.]</margin> They grow in gardens, and wild in many places of this land.

<margin>Time.]</margin> They seed in *August* and *September*.

<margin>Government and Virtues.]</margin> They are all of them cooling, drying, and binding, serving to restrain blood flows in either man or woman, especially the red; which also stays the overflowing of women's "reds" <note>menstrual flow</note>, just as the white blite stays the "whites" <note>leucorrhea</note> in women: <margin>Reds and Whites in Women.</margin> It is an excellent secret; you cannot well fail in its use. They are all under the dominion of *Venus*.

There is one other sort of wild blites, like the other wild kinds, but having long and spiked heads of greenish seed, appearing—because they are set so thickly together—to be all seed.

Fish delight in this sort, and it is a good and usual bait; for fish will bite fast enough at them if you only have wit enough to catch them when they bite.

These are so well known to be inhabitants in every garden that I consider it unnecessary to describe them.

To these I may add a third sort, which is not so common nor yet so well known, and therefore I shall give you its name and description.

The name Bugloss, and another by the name Langue-de-beef <note>Ox-tongue</note>, is a question to me, seeing one signifies "ox-tongue" in Greek and the other signifies the same in French.

*Description.*] Its leaves are smaller than those of Bugloss but much rougher; the stalk rises up about a foot and a half high and is most commonly of a red color. The flowers stand in scaly rough heads, being composed of many small yellow flowers, not much unlike those of a dandelion, and the seed flies away in down just as that does. You may easily know the flowers by their taste, for they are very bitter.

*Place.*] It grows wild in many places of the land and may be found plentifully near London, such as between Redrif <note>Rotherhithe</note> and Deptford, by the ditch-sides. Its virtues are held to be the same as Borage and Bugloss, only this is somewhat hotter.

*Time.*] They flower in *June* and *July*, and the seed is ripe shortly after.

*Government and Virtues.*] They are all three herbs of *Jupiter* and under *Leo*; all are great cordials and great strengtheners of nature. They are very cordial <note>invigorating to the heart</note>. The leaves or roots are used to very good purpose in putrid and pestilential fevers to defend the heart and help to resist and expel poison or the venom of other creatures; the seed has a similar effect. Both the seed and leaves are good for increasing milk in women's breasts. The leaves, flowers, and seed—all or any of them—are good for expelling pensiveness and melancholy; they help to clarify the blood and mitigate heat in fevers. The juice made into a syrup is very effective for all the purposes mentioned above and is mixed with other cooling, opening, and cleansing herbs to open obstructions and help the yellow jaundice. Mixed with fumitory, it cools, cleanses, and tempers the blood; thereby it helps the itch, ringworms, and tetters <note>skin sores</note>, or other spreading scabs or sores. The flowers, candied or made into a conserve, help in the aforementioned cases but are chiefly used as a cordial and are good for those who are weak from long sickness, and to comfort the heart and spirits of those who are in a consumption <note>wasting disease</note> or troubled with frequent swooning or heart palpitations. The distilled water is no less effective for all the purposes mentioned above and helps the redness and inflammation of the eyes when washed with it. The dried herb is never used, only the green; yet its ashes, boiled in mead or honeyed water, are useful against inflammations and ulcers in the mouth or throat when used as a wash or gargle. The roots of Bugloss are effective when made into a licking electuary <note>a medicinal paste</note> for the cough and to thicken thin phlegm and rheumatic distillations upon the lungs.
