## Blue-bottle.

It is called Syanus, I suppose from its color; Hurt-sickle, because it turns the edge of the sickles that reap the corn; Blue-blow, Corn-flower, and Blue-bottle.

*Description.*] I shall only describe the most common, and in my opinion most useful: Its leaves spread upon the ground, being of a whitish-green color, somewhat cut on the edges like those of Corn Scabious, among which rises up a stalk divided into various branches, set with long leaves of a greenish color, either very little indented or not at all. The flowers are of a blue color, from which it took its name, consisting of a countless number of small flowers set in a scaly head, not much unlike those of Knapweed. The seed is smooth, bright, and shining, wrapped up in a woolly mantle. The root perishes every year.

*Place.*] They grow in corn fields, among all sorts of corn, peas, beans, and tares excepted; if you please to take them from there and transplant them in your garden, especially toward the full moon, they will grow more double than they are, and many times change color.

*Time.*] They flower from the beginning of *May* to the end of *harvest*.

<margin>Bruises, broken veins, poison, plague, epidemic diseases, wounds, ulcers, inflammations in the eyes.</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] As they are naturally cold, dry, and binding, so are they under the dominion of *Saturn*. The powder of dried leaves of the Blue-bottle, or Corn-flower, is given with good success to those who are bruised by a fall, or have broken a vein inwardly and pass much blood from the mouth, being taken in the water of Plantain, Horsetail, or the greater Comfrey. It is a remedy against the poison of the scorpion, and resists all venoms and poisons. The seed or leaves taken in wine is very good against the plague and all infectious diseases, and is very good for pestilential fevers. The juice put into fresh or green wounds quickly joins their lips together, and is very effective for healing all ulcers and sores in the mouth. The juice dropped into the eyes takes away the heat and inflammation in them. The distilled water of the herb has the same properties and may be used for all the effects mentioned above.

The leaves are parted with various deep gashes on the edge; the leaves remain a long time before any stalk appears. Afterwards, a reasonably large stalk rises up, three or four feet high, and is splendidly adorned with flowers from the middle of the stalk upwards, for on the lower part of the stalk there is neither branch nor leaf. # Briony, or Wild Vine.

It is called Wild Vine, and Wood Vine, *Tamus*, and Our Lady's Seal; the white is called White Vine by some, and the black, Black Vine.
*Description.]* The common white Briony grows climbing upon the hedges, sending forth many long, rough, and very tender branches at the beginning, with many very rough broad leaves thereon, cut (for the most part) into five partitions, in form very like a vine leaf, but smaller, rougher, and of a whitish or hoary green color, spreading very far, and twining with its small tendrils (which come forth at the joints with the leaves) very far on whatever stands next to it. At the several joints also (especially towards the top of the branches) there comes forth a long stalk bearing many whitish flowers together in a long tuft, consisting of five small leaves apiece, laid open like a star. After these come the berries, separated one from another more than a cluster of grapes, green at the first and very red when they are thoroughly ripe, of no good scent, but of a most loathsome taste, provoking vomiting. The root grows to be exceedingly great, with many long twines or branches growing from it, of a pale whitish color on the outside and whiter within, and of a sharp, bitter, loathsome taste.

# Brooklime, or Water-Pimpernel.

<margin>[Description.]</margin>
This sends forth from a creeping root—which shoots out strings at every joint as it runs—various green stalks, round and sappy with some branches on them. It has somewhat broad, round, deep green, and thick leaves set in pairs upon them; from the leaf-axils <note>the junction of the leaf and stem</note> shoot forth long stalks with various small blue flowers on them, each consisting of five small, round, pointed petals.

There is another variety that does not differ from the former except that it is larger and the flowers are a paler blue color.

<margin>[Place.]</margin>
They grow in small standing waters, and usually near watercress.

<margin>[Time.]</margin>
And flower in *June* and *July*, producing seed the following month.

<margin>[Government and Virtues.] Purges the blood, ill humors, scurvy, difficulty in urinating, stone, provokes menstruation, dead child, swellings, inflammations.</margin>
->*Government and Virtues.]*<-

It is a hot and biting <term>Martial Plant</term> <note>a plant ruled by the planet Mars</note>. Brooklime and watercress are generally used together in diet drinks with other ingredients, serving to purge the blood and body of ill humors that would destroy health, and are helpful for <term>scurvy</term>. They also provoke urine and help to break the stone and pass it; they stimulate women’s periods and expel a dead child. Being fried with butter and vinegar and applied warm, it helps all manner of tumors, swellings, and inflammations.

Such drinks ought to be made of various herbs according to the specific illness; I shall give a plain and easy rule for this at the end of this book.

## Broom, and Broomrape.

**To** spend time in writing a description of this is altogether needless, it being so generally used by almost all the good housewives throughout this land to sweep their houses with, and therefore very well known to all sorts of people.
The *broomrape* springs up in many places from the roots of the *broom* (but more often in fields, such as by hedge-sides, and on heaths). The stalk of it is of the thickness of a finger or thumb, over two feet high, having a show of leaves on them and many flowers at the top, of a deadish yellow color, as the stalks and leaves are also.

**Place.]** They grow commonly in many places of this land, and as commonly spoil all the land they grow in.

**Time.]** And flower in the summer months, and produce their seed before winter.

<margin>*Phlegm, joints, dropsy, sides, spleen, bladder.*</margin>
***Government and Virtues.***] The juice or decoction of the young branches or seed, or the powder of the seed taken in a drink, purges downwards and draws phlegmatic and watery humors from the joints, whereby it helps the dropsy, gout, sciatica, and the pains in the hips and joints. It also provokes strong vomiting and helps the pains of the sides and swellings of the spleen; it also cleanses the reins <note>kidneys</note> or kidneys and bladder of the stone, provokes urine abundantly, and hinders the growing again of the stone

# Bucks-horn Plantain.

<margin>Description]</margin>
This being sown of seed, rises up at first with small, long, narrow, hairy, dark green leaves like grass, without any division or notch in them; but those that follow are notched on both sides of the leaves into three or four gashes and pointed at the ends, resembling the tines <note>knags</note> of a buck's horn (from which it took its name), and being well grown round about the root upon the ground in order one by another, they thereby resemble the form of a star. From among these rise up various hairy stalks, about a handbreadth high, each bearing a small long spiky head like those of the common plantain, having similar bloomings and seed after them. The root is single, long, and small, with various strings at it.

<margin>Place.]</margin>
They grow in dry sandy grounds, as in *Tuttle-fields* by *Westminster*, and various other places of this land.

<margin>Time.]</margin>
They flower and seed in *May*, *June*, and *July*, and their green leaves do in a manner remain fresh all the winter.

<margin>Government and Virtues.]</margin>
It is under the dominion of *Saturn* and is of an excellent drying and binding quality. This boiled in wine and drunk, and some-

It is called also Hart's-horn, Herba-stella, and Herba-stellaria, Sanguinaria, Herb-eve, and Herb-ivy, and Wort-cresses and Swine's-cresses.

## Bugle.

Besides the name bugle, it is called middle-confound, and middle-comfrey, brown-bugle, and by some sickle-wort and herb-carpenter, though in *Sussex* we call another herb by that name.
*Description.*] *This has larger leaves than those of the self-heal, but otherwise of the same fashion, or rather a little longer; in some, they are green on the upper side, and in others more brownish, dented about the edges, and somewhat hairy, as is the square stalk also, which rises up to be half a yard high sometimes, with the leaves set in pairs. From almost the middle upward, the flowers stand together, with many smaller and browner leaves than the rest on this stalk below, set at distances, with the stalk bare between them. Among these flowers are also small ones of a bluish, and sometimes of an ash color, fashioned like the flowers of ground-ivy, after which come small, round, blackish seeds.*

# Burnet.

It is also called *Sanguisorba*, *Pimpinella*, *Bipenula*, *Solbastrellia*, etc. The common garden burnet is so well known that it needs no description. There is another sort which is wild, the description of which follows:

*Descript.*] The great wild burnet has winged leaves rising from the roots like the *garden burnet*, but not so many; yet each of these leaves is at least twice as large as the other, and notched in the same manner about the edges, of a grayish color on the underside. The stalks are larger and rise higher, with many such leaves set on them, and larger heads at the tops of a brownish-green color; and out of them come small, dark, purple flowers, like the former, but larger. The root is black and long, like the other, but larger also; it has almost neither scent nor taste in it, unlike the garden kind.

*Place.*] The first grows frequently in gardens. The wild kind grows in various counties of this land, especially in Huntingdon and Northamptonshire in the meadows there; as also near London by *St. Pancras Church*, and by a causeway side in the middle of a field by *Paddington*.

*Time.*] They flower about the end of *June* and beginning of *July*, and their seed is ripe in *August*.

*Government and Virtues.*] This is an herb the Sun claims dominion over, and it is a most precious herb, little inferior to betony. The continual use of it preserves the body in health and the spirits in vigor; for if the Sun is the preserver of life under God, his herbs are the best in the world to do it by. They are accounted to be both of one property,

<margin>*Heart, liver, melancholy, pestilence, epidemic diseases, bleeding, stops menstrual periods and the whites, belching, vomiting, wounds, ulcers, cankers, sores, fluxes.*</margin>

but the lesser is more effective because it is quicker and more aromatic. It is a friend to the heart, liver, and other principal parts of a man's body. Two or three of the stalks with leaves put into a cup of wine, especially claret, are known to quicken the spirits, refresh and cheer the heart, and drive away melancholy. It is a special help to defend the heart from harmful vapors and from infection of the pestilence, the juice thereof being taken in some drink and the patient made to sweat thereupon. They also have a drying and an astringent quality, whereby they are helpful in all manner of fluxes of blood or humors, to staunch bleedings inward or outward, diarrhea <note>lasks</note>, purgings <note>scourings</note>, the bloody flux <note>dysentery</note>, women's too abundant menstrual periods <note>courses</note>, the whites <note>leukorrhea</note>, and the choleric belchings and vomitings of the stomach. And it is a singular wound-herb for all sorts of wounds both of the head and body, either inward or outward; for all old ulcers, or running cankers, and moist sores, to be used either by the juice, or

## The Butter-Bur, or Petasitis.

<margin>Description:]</margin> *This rises up in February with a thick stalk about a foot high, on which are set a few small leaves, or rather pieces, and at the tops, a long spiked head of flowers of a blush or deep red color, according to the soil in which it grows. Before the stalk with the flowers has remained a month above ground, it will be withered and gone, blown away with the wind, and the leaves will begin to spring; these, when full grown, are very large and broad, being somewhat thin and almost round. Their thick red footstalks, about a foot long, stand towards the middle of the leaves. The lower part is divided into two round parts, closing almost one to another, and is of a pale green color and downy underneath. The root is long and spreading underground, being in some places no bigger than one's finger and in others much bigger, blackish on the outside and white within, with a bitter and unpleasant taste.*

<margin>Place and Time:]</margin> They grow in low and wet grounds by rivers and watersides. Their flowers (as has been said) rise and decay in *February* and *March*, before the leaves appear in *April*.

<margin>Government and Virtues.]</margin>
<margin>Plague, epidemic diseases, Poison, Mother, Wheezing, Difficulty of breathing, Dysuria, provokes menses, Flat and broad worms, Blemishes of the skin</margin>
It is under the dominion of the *Sun*, and therefore is a great strengthener of the *heart* and cheerer of the *vital spirits*. The roots of this have been found by long experience to be very effective against the *plague* and *pestilential fevers* by provoking *sweat*; if the powder is taken in *wine*, it also resists the force of any other *poison*. The root taken with *zedoary* and *angelica*, or without them, helps the rising of the *mother* <note>Hysteria or uterine disorders</note>. The decoction of the root in *wine* is exceptionally good for those who *wheeze* much or are *short-winded*. It also provokes *urine* and *women’s courses* <note>menstruation</note>, and kills the *flat and broad worms* in the belly. The powder of the root helps wonderfully to dry up the moisture of sores that are hard to be cured and takes away all spots and blemishes of the skin. It would be well if gentlewomen would keep this root preserved to help their poor neighbors; it is fitting the rich should help the poor, for the poor cannot help themselves.

## The Sea Colewort.

<margin>Description.</margin>
This has several somewhat long and broad, large, thick, wrinkled leaves, somewhat crumpled upon the edges, each growing upon its own thick, very brittle footstalk of a grayish-green color. From among these rises up a strong, thick stalk, two feet high or more, with some leaves on it up to the top, where it branches out extensively; and on every branch stands a large bush of pale, whitish flowers, consisting of four leaves apiece. The root is somewhat large and shoots forth many branches underground, keeping its green leaves all through the winter.

Place.] They grow in many places upon the seacoasts, as well on the *Kentish* as the *Essex* shores; as at *Lydd* in *Kent*, *Colchester* in *Essex*, and various other places and in other parts of this land.

Time.] They flower and seed about the same time that other kinds do.

Government and Virtues.] The *Moon* claims the dominion of these also.

## Calamint, Or Mountain Mint.

<margin>Description.]</margin>
This is a small herb seldom rising above a foot high, with square, hoary, and woody stalks, and two small hoary leaves set at a joint, about the size of Marjoram, or not much bigger, a little dented about the edges, and of a very fierce or quick scent, as the whole herb is. The flowers stand at several spaces of the stalks from the middle almost upwards, which are small and gaping like those of mints, and of a pale blush color; after which follow small, round, blackish seeds. The root is small and woody, with several small sprigs spreading within the ground, and does not die, but remains for many years.

<margin>Place.]</margin>
It grows on heaths and upland dry grounds in many places of this land.

<margin>Time.]</margin>
They flower in *July*, and their seed is ripe quickly after.

<margin>Government and Virtues.]</margin>
It is an herb of *Mercury*, and a strong one too; therefore, it is excellently good for all afflictions of the brain.

# Chamomile.

<margin>*Stitches in the Side, Agues, Liver, Spleen, Weariness, Sinews, Swellings, Colic, Stone, Bellyache, Cold, Ache, Jaundice, Dropsy, Brain, Cramp, Stitch in the Side.*</margin>
This is so well known everywhere that it is but lost time and labor to describe it. Its virtues are as follows: 
A decoction made of *Chamomile* and drunk takes away all pains and stitches in the sides. The flowers of chamomile beaten and made into balls with oil drive away all sorts of agues, if the grieving party is anointed with that oil taken from the flowers, from the crown of the head to the sole of the foot, and is afterwards laid to sweat in his bed, provided that he sweats well. This is *Nicheffor's* (an Egyptian) medicine. It is profitable for all sorts of agues that come either from phlegm or melancholy, or from an inflammation of the bowels, being applied when the humors causing them shall be concocted <note>matured or ripened</note>; and there is nothing more profitable to the sides and the region of the liver and spleen than it. Bathing with a decoction of chamomile takes away weariness and eases pains in whatever part of the body it is applied. It comforts the sinews that are overstrained and softens all swellings. It moderately comforts all parts that have need of warmth, and digests and dissolves whatever needs it by a wonderfully speedy property. It eases all the pains of the colic and stone, and all pains and torments of the belly, and gently provokes urine.

The flowers boiled in posset drink provoke sweat and help to expel colds, aches, and pains anywhere, and they are an excellent help to bring down women's courses <note>menstruation</note>. -># Water-Caltrops.<-

They are also called *Tribulus Aquaticus, Tribulus Lacustris*, and *Tribulus Marinus, Caltrops, Saligot, Water Nuts*, and *water Chestnuts*.

*Description.*] As for the larger kind, or water-caltrop, it is not found here, or very rarely. There are two other kinds which I shall describe here: The first has a long, creeping, and jointed root, sending out tufts at each joint; from these joints arise long, flat, slender, knotted stalks even to the top of the water, divided towards the top into many branches, each carrying two leaves on both sides, being about two inches long and half an inch broad, thin, and almost transparent. They look as though they were torn. The flowers are long, thick, and whitish, set together almost like a bunch of grapes; when these are gone, there usually follow four sharp-pointed grains, which together contain a small white kernel inside them.

The second does not differ much from this, except that it delights in clearer water; its stalks are not flat but round; its leaves are not as long but are more pointed. As for the location, we need not specify it, for their name shows they grow in the water.

<margin>
*Inflammations, cankers, mouth, throat, gums, tonsils <note>almonds of the ears</note>, King's Evil <note>scrofula</note>, stone, gravel, venomous beasts, poison.*
</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] They are under the dominion of the Moon. When made into a poultice, it is excellently good for hot inflammations and swellings, cankers, and sore mouths and throats. When washed with the decoction, it cleanses and strengthens the neck and throat much and helps those swellings which, when people have them, they say the "almonds of the ears" <note>tonsils</note> have fallen down. It is excellently good for the rankness of the gums and is a safe and immediate remedy for the King's Evil. They are excellently good for the stone and gravel, especially if the nuts are dried. They also resist poison and the bites of venomous beasts.

## Carrots.

The garden kind are so well known that they need no description; but because they are of less medicinal <note>physical</note> use than the wild kind (as indeed in almost all herbs the wild are most effective in medicine, being more powerful in operation than the garden kinds), I shall therefore briefly describe the wild carrot.

*Description.*] It grows in a manner almost exactly like the tame, except that the leaves and stalks are somewhat whiter and rougher. The stalks bear large tufts of white flowers with a deep purple spot in the middle, which are drawn together when the seed begins to ripen, so that the middle part being hollow and low, and the outer stalks rising high, it makes the whole umbel <note>flower cluster</note> look like a bird's nest. The root is small, long, and hard, unfit for food <note>meat</note>, being somewhat sharp and strong.

*Place.*] The wild kind grows plentifully in various parts of this land by the field sides and in uncultivated places.

*Time.*] They flower and seed at the end of summer.

<margin>
wind, stitches, provokes urine and the courses, stone, dropsy, colic, barrenness, ulcers.
</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] Wild carrots belong to *Mercury*, and therefore break wind and remove stitches in the sides, provoke urine and women’s courses <note>menstruation</note>, and help to break and expel the stone. The seed of the same also produces the same effect and is good for dropsy and those whose bellies are swollen with wind; it helps the colic, the stone in the kidneys, and the rising of the mother <note>hysteria or uterine disorders</note> when taken in wine, or boiled in wine and taken; it also helps conception. The leaves, being applied with honey to running sores or ulcers, cleanse them.

I suppose the seeds of them perform this better than the roots; and though *Galen* commends garden carrots highly,

# Caraway.

*Description.*] It bears various stalks of finely cut leaves lying upon the ground, somewhat like the leaves of carrots, but not bushing so thick, with a little sharp taste in them. From among these rises up a square stalk, not as high as the carrot, at whose joints are set similar leaves, but smaller and narrower; and at the top are small open tufts or umbels of white flowers, which turn to small blackish seed, smaller than aniseed, and of a quicker and hotter taste. The root is whitish, small, and long, somewhat like a parsnip, but with a more wrinkled bark and much smaller, with a slightly hot and sharp taste, stronger than the parsnip; it remains after seed-time.

*Place.*] It is usually sown with us in gardens.

*Time.*] They flower in June and July, and seed quickly after.

<margin>Wind, Dysuria <note>difficulty urinating</note>, indigestion, head, stomach, bowels, mother <note>the womb</note>, black and blue spots, bruises, colic.</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] This is also a Mercurial plant. Caraway seed has a moderately sharp quality by which it breaks wind and provokes urine, which the herb also does. The root is better food than the parsnip and is pleasant and comforting to the stomach, helping digestion. The seed is conducive to all cold ailments of the head and stomach, the bowels, or the mother <note>the womb</note>, as well as the wind within them; it also helps to sharpen the eyesight. The powder of the seed, put into a poultice, takes away black and blue spots from blows and bruises. The herb itself, or some of the seed bruised and fried and laid hot in a bag or double cloth to the lower parts of the belly, eases the pains of the wind colic.

The roots of caraways, eaten as men eat parsnips, strengthen the stomachs of elderly people exceedingly; they do not even need to make a whole meal of them. They are fit to be planted in everyone's garden.

Caraway comfits, once only dipped in sugar, and half a spoonful of them eaten in the morning while fasting, and as many after each meal, is a most admirable remedy for those who are troubled with wind.

Physicians have another ill-favored trick they use for the eye, and that is worse than the needle; which is to eat away the film by corroding or gnawing medicines. I absolutely protest against this.

1. Because the tunicles <note>membranes</note> of the eye are very thin, and therefore soon eaten through.
2. The *Callus* or film that they would eat away is seldom of an equal thickness in every place, and then the tunicle may be eaten through in one place before the film is consumed in another, and so be a readier way to extinguish the sight than to restore it.

It is called *Chelidonium* from the Greek word <term>χελιδών</term>, which signifies "swallow," because they say that if you prick out the eyes of young swallows when they are in the nest, the old ones will recover their eyes again with this herb. I am confident of this, for I have tried it: if you mar the very apple of their eyes with a needle, she will recover them again; but whether with this herb or not, I do not know.

I have also read (and it seems to me somewhat probable) that if the herb is gathered as I showed before, and the elements drawn apart from it by the art of the alchemist, and after they are drawn apart, rectified—the earthy quality still being added during rectification to the *terra damnata* (as alchemists call it) or *terra sacratissima* (as some philosophers call it)—the elements so rectified are sufficient for the cure of all diseases, provided the offending humor is known and the contrary element is given. It is an experience worth trying, and can do no harm.

# The lesser Celandine, *usually known by the name of* Pilewort and Figwort.

I wonder what ailed the ancients to give this the name of *Celandine*, which resembles it in neither nature nor form. It acquired the name of *Pilewort* from its virtues, and since it is no great matter where I set it down, so long as I set it down at all, I humored Dr. *Tradition* so much as to set it down here.

*Description.*] This Celandine, *then*, or Pilewort (*whichever you please*), spreads many round, pale green leaves set on weak and trailing branches which lie upon the ground; they are fleshy, smooth, and somewhat shining, and in some places (though seldom) marked with black spots, each standing on a long footstalk. Among these rise small yellow flowers, consisting of nine or ten small, narrow leaves <note>petals</note>, upon slender footstalks very much like a crowfoot <note>Ranunculus</note>, to which the seed also is not unlike, being many small ones set together upon a head. The root is made of many small kernels like grains of corn, some twice as long as others, of a whitish color, with some fibers at the end of them.

*Place.*] It grows for the most part in the moist corners of fields and places that are near watersides, yet it will abide in drier grounds if they are but a little shaded.

*Time.*] It flowers early, about *March* or *April*, and is quite gone in *May*, so that it cannot be found until it springs again.

## The Ordinary Small Centaury.

**Description.]** *This grows up most usually with only one round and somewhat crested stalk, about a foot high or more, branching forth at the top into many sprigs, and some also from the joints of the stalks below. The flowers that stand at the tops, as if in an umbel or tuft, are of a pale red tending toward a carnation color, consisting of five, sometimes six small leaves, very like those of St. John's Wort, opening themselves in the daytime and closing at night. After these come seed in little short husks, shaped like wheat grains. The leaves are small and somewhat round. The root is small and hard, perishing every year. The whole plant has an exceedingly bitter taste.*

*There is another sort in all things like the former, except that it bears white flowers.*

**Place.]** They grow ordinarily in fields, pastures, and woods, but the one with white flowers is not as frequent as the other.

**Time.]** They flower in *July* or thereabouts, and seed within a month after.

# The Cherry-Tree.

I suppose there are few who do not know this tree for its fruit's sake, and therefore I shall spare the writing of a description of it.

<margin>Appetite lost, phlegm, gross humors, cool, provoke urine, cough, hoarseness, sight, gravel, wind.</margin>
*Place.*] Regarding the place of its growth, it is given room in every orchard.
*Government and Virtues.*] It is a tree of *Venus*. Cherries, as they are of different tastes, so they are of diverse qualities: The sweet pass through the stomach and belly more quickly, but provide little nourishment. The tart or sour are more pleasing to a hot stomach, procuring an appetite for meat, and help to cut tough phlegm and gross humors; but when these are dried, they bind the belly more than when they are fresh, being cooling in hot diseases, welcome to the stomach, and they provoke urine. The gum of the cherry tree dissolved in wine is good for a cold cough and hoarseness of the throat, improves the color in the face, sharpens the eyesight, provokes appetite, and helps to break and expel the stone. The *black cherries* bruised with the stones and distilled—the water from them is much used to break the stone, expel gravel, and break wind.

## Winter-Cherries.

**Description.]** The Winter-Cherry has a running or creeping root in the ground, often about the size of one’s little finger, shooting forth at several joints in various places, by which it quickly spreads over a large area of ground. The stalk does not rise more than a yard high; on it are set many broad and long green leaves, somewhat like nightshade but larger. At the joints of these, whitish flowers come forth, made of five petals each, which later turn into green berries enclosed in thin skins. These change to reddish when they grow ripe, and the berry is likewise reddish and as large as a cherry, containing many flat and yellowish seeds lying within the pulp. These, being gathered and strung up, are kept all year to be used as needed.

**Place.]** They do not grow naturally in this land, but are cultivated in gardens for their medicinal virtues.

**Time.]** They do not flower until the middle or end of July, and the fruit is ripe about the end of August or the beginning of September.

<margin>Inflammations, dysuria, stone, gravel, ulcers in the kidneys and bladder, passing blood, sharpness of urine.</margin>
**Government and Virtues.]** This is also a plant of *Venus*. They are of great use in medicine. The leaves, being cooling, may be used for inflammations, but they are not "opening" <note>Referring to the ability to open passages or promote flow</note> as the berries and fruit are. These, by drawing down the urine, provoke it to be passed plentifully when it is stopped, or has grown hot, sharp, and painful in the passage. It is also good for expelling stone and gravel from the kidneys and bladder, helping to dissolve the stone and removing it as grit or gravel sent forth in the urine. It also helps much to cleanse inward abscesses or ulcers in the kidneys or bladder, or in those who pass a cloudy or foul urine. The distilled water of the fruit, or the leaves together with them, or the berries green or dry, distilled with a little milk and drunk morning and evening with a little sugar, is effective for all the purposes specified before, and especially against the heat and sharpness of the urine. <margin>A precious recipe.</margin> I shall only mention one way among many others which might be used for preparing the berries to be helpful for the urine and the stone, which is this: Take three or four good handfuls of the berries, either green and fresh or dried, and having bruised them, put them into as many gallons of beer or ale when it is newly tunned <note>Put into a cask or barrel</note>. This drink, taken daily, has been found to do much good to many—both to ease pains and expel urine and the stone, and to prevent the stone from forming. The decoction of the berries in wine or water is the most usual way; but the powder of them taken in drink is more effective.

## Chestnut Tree.

To describe a tree so commonly known would be as vain as telling a man he had a mouth; therefore, take the government and virtues of them as follows.

The tree is absolutely under the dominion of *Jupiter*, and therefore the fruit must certainly breed good blood and yield commendable nourishment to the body; yet if eaten too much, they make the blood thick, cause headaches, and bind the body. The inner skin that covers the nut is of such a binding quality that a <term>scruple</term> of it being taken by a man, or ten grains by a child, soon stops any flux whatsoever. The whole nut being dried and beaten into powder, and a <term>dram</term> taken at a time, is a good remedy to stop the <term>terms</term> in women.

<margin>Flux, terms, stops, cough, spitting blood.</margin>
If you dry chestnuts and beat them into powder (I mean only the kernel, after the bark has been taken away), beat them into powder and make the powder into an <term>electuary</term> with honey; thus you have an admirable remedy for the cough and spitting of blood.

## Earth-Chestnuts.

They are called earth-nuts, earth-chestnuts, ground-nuts, cipper-nuts, and we in *Sussex* call them pig-nuts. A description of them would be needless, for every child knows them.

<margin>Provokes lust, dysuria, spitting blood, urinating blood.</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] They are somewhat hot and dry in quality, under the dominion of *Venus*; they provoke lust exceedingly and stir up those sports of which she is mistress. The seed is excellently good to provoke urine, and so also is the root, but it does not perform it as forcefully as the seed does. The root, being dried and beaten into powder and the powder made into an <term>electuary</term>, is as singular a remedy for spitting and urinating blood as the former chestnuts were for coughs.

# Chickweed.

<margin>Description.]</margin> This is generally known to most people; I shall therefore not trouble you with its description, nor myself with setting forth the several kinds, since only two or three are notable for their usefulness.

<margin>Place.]</margin> These are usually found in moist and watery places, by wood sides, and elsewhere.

<margin>Time.]</margin> They flower about June, and their seed is ripe in July.

<margin>Government and Virtues.]</margin> <margin>Hot liver, abscesses, swellings, red face, welts, pimples, itch, scabs, cramps, convulsions, palsy, red eyes, hemorrhoids, ulcers, tendons.</margin> It is a fine, soft, pleasing herb, under the dominion of the Moon. It is found to be as effective as purslane for all the purposes for which it is used, except for food only. The herb bruised, or the juice applied (with cloths or sponges dipped therein) to the region of the liver—and applying fresh ones as they dry—does wonderfully temper the heat of the liver. It is effective for all abscesses and swellings wherever they may be; for all redness in the face, welts, pimples, itch, and scabs, using the juice either on its own or boiled with hog's grease and applied. The same helps cramps, convulsions, and palsies. The juice or distilled water is of much good use for all heat and redness in the eyes when some is dropped into them, as also into the ears to ease pains in them. It is of good effect to ease the pains, heat, and sharpness of blood in the piles <note>hemorrhoids</note>, and generally all pains in the body that arise from heat. It is used also in hot and virulent ulcers and sores in the private parts of man or woman, or on the legs, or elsewhere. The leaves boiled with marsh-mallows, and made into a poultice with fenugreek and linseed, applied to swellings or abscesses, ripens and breaks them, or soothes the swellings and eases the pains. It helps the tendons when they are shrunk by cramps or otherwise, and helps to extend them and make them pliable again by this medicine: Boil a handful of chickweed and a handful of dried red rose leaves (but not distilled) in a quart of <term>Muscadine</term> until a fourth part is consumed; then add to them a pint of <term>Oil of Trotters</term> (or sheep's-feet oil); let them boil a good while, stirring them well; which being strained, anoint the afflicted place with it while warm near the fire, rubbing it well in with one's hand; also bind some of the herb (if you will) to the place, and with God’s blessing, it will help with three dressings.

## Clary, Or more properly, Cleer-Eye.

*Description.*] Our ordinary garden clary has four-square stalks, with broad, rough, wrinkled, whitish, or hairy green leaves, somewhat evenly cut in on the edges, and with a strong sweet scent, some growing near the ground and some in pairs upon the stalks. The flowers grow at certain distances with two small leaves at the joints under them, somewhat like the flowers of sage, but smaller and of a whitish-blue color. The seed is brownish and somewhat flat, or at least not as round as the wild variety. The roots are blackish and do not spread far, and they perish after the seeding time. It is usually sown, for it seldom grows from its own seeding.
*Place.*] This grows in gardens.
*Time.*] It flowers in June and July, some a little later than others, and its seed is ripe in August, or thereabouts.

We will grant that Clary strengthens the back, but this we deny: that the cause of the running of the reins in men, or the whites in women, lies in the back (though the back may sometimes be weakened by them). Therefore, the medicine is as appropriate as it would be for me, when my toe is sore, to lay a plaster on my nose.

# Wild Clary.

Wild Clary is most blasphemously called Christ's Eye because it cures diseases of the eyes. I could wish from my very soul that blasphemy, ignorance, and tyranny had ceased among physicians, so that they might be happy and I joyful.

*Description.*] It is like the other Clary, but smaller, with many stalks about a foot and a half high; the stalks are square and somewhat hairy; the flowers are of a bluish color. He who knows common Clary cannot be ignorant of this.

*Place.*] It grows commonly in this nation in barren places; you may find it plentifully if you look in the fields near Gray's Inn and the fields near Chelsea.

*Time.*] They flower from the beginning of June to the latter end of August.

*Government and Virtues.*] It is somewhat hotter and drier than the garden Clary is, yet nevertheless it is under the dominion of the Moon, as well as that. The seeds of it, being beaten to powder and drunk with wine, are an admirable help to provoke lust. A decoction of the leaves, being drunk, warms the stomach—and it would be a wonder if it did not, the stomach being Cancer, the house of the Moon. Also, it helps digestion, scatters congealed blood in any part of the body, and helps dimness of sight. The distilled water thereof cleanses the eyes of redness, watering, and heat; it is an excellent remedy for dimness of sight. # Cleavers.

It is also called Aparine, Goose-share, Goose-grass, and Clavers.

<margin>*Description.*</margin> **T**he common Cleavers has various very rough square stalks, not as thick as the tag of a point <note>a lace or string used to fasten clothing</note>, but rising up to be two or three yards high sometimes if it meets with any tall bushes or trees where it may climb (yet without any tendrils), or else much lower and lying upon the ground. They are full of joints, and at every joint it shoots forth a branch in addition to the leaves, which are usually six, set in a round circle like a star or the rowel of a spur. From between the leaves at the joints toward the tops of the branches come forth very small white flowers, each on a small thread-like footstalk. After they have fallen, there appear two small, round, rough seeds joined together like two testicles, which when they are ripe grow hard and whitish, having a little hole on the side somewhat like a navel. Both stalks, leaves, and seeds are so rough that they will cleave to anything that touches them. The root is small and very thread-like, spreading much in the ground, but it dies every year.

<margin>*Place.*</margin> It grows by the hedge and ditch sides in many places of this land, and is so troublesome an inhabitant in gardens that it ramps upon and is ready to choke whatever grows next to it.

<margin>*Time.*</margin> It flowers in *June* and *July*, and the seed is ripe and falls again at the end of *July* or *August*, from which it springs up again, and not from the old roots.

It is under the dominion of the *Moon*.

The juice of the herb and the seed taken together in wine helps those who are bitten by an adder by preserving the heart from the venom. It is commonly taken in broth to keep those lean and lank who are apt to grow fat. The distilled water drunk twice a day helps the yellow jaundice, and the decoction of the herb has been found by experience to do the same, and it stops lasks <note>diarrhea</note> and bloody fluxes <note>dysentery</note>. The juice of the leaves, or the leaves themselves slightly bruised and applied to any bleeding wound, stops the bleeding. The juice is also very good for closing up the lips of green <note>fresh or new</note> wounds, and the powder of the dried herb strewn upon them does the same and likewise helps old ulcers. Being boiled with hog's grease and used as an ointment, it heals all sorts of hard swellings or kernels in the throat. The juice dropped into the ears takes away the pain in them.

It is a good remedy in the spring, eaten (being first chopped small and boiled well) in water-gruel to cleanse the blood and strengthen the liver, thereby keeping the body in health and preparing it for the change of season that is coming.

# Clown's Woundwort.

<margin>Description.</margin> It grows up sometimes to three or four feet high, but usually about two feet, with square, green, rough stalks, but slender, joined somewhat far apart, and two very long and somewhat narrow, dark green leaves, bluntly dented about the edges, ending in a long point. The flowers stand toward the tops, surrounding the stalks at the joints with leaves and ending likewise in a spiked top, having long and very open, gaping hoods of a purplish red color, with whitish spots in them, standing in somewhat rough husks, within which later stand blackish round seeds. The root is composed of many long strings, with some long tuberous knobs growing among them, of a pale yellowish or whitish color; yet at some times of the year these knobby roots are not seen in the plant in many places. The whole plant smells somewhat strong.

<margin>Place.</margin> It grows in various counties of this land, both North and West, and frequently by path sides in the fields near London, and within a three or four-mile distance around it; yet it usually grows in or near ditches.

<margin>Time.</margin> It flowers in June and July, and the seed is ripe soon after.

<margin>Government and Virtues.</margin> <margin>Wounds, ulcers, blood, cancers, bloody flux, broken vessels, ruptures, spitting, urinating, and vomiting blood, swelled muscles, etc.</margin> It is under the dominion of the planet Saturn. It is singularly effective in all fresh and green wounds, and therefore does not bear this name for nothing. It is also very useful in staunching blood and drying up the fluxes of humors in old, fretting ulcers, cancers, etc., that hinder their healing.

A syrup made of its juice is inferior to none for inward wounds, ruptures of veins, bloody flux <note>dysentery or severe diarrhea</note>, broken vessels, and spitting, urinating, or vomiting blood. Ruptures are excellently and speedily—even to wonder—cured by taking a little of the syrup now and then and applying an ointment or plaster of the herb to the place. Also, if any vein be swelled or muscle cut, apply a plaster of this herb to it, and if you add a little comfrey to it, it will do well. I assure you the herb deserves praise though it has been given but a "clownish" <note>meaning rustic or common</note> name, and whoever reads this (if he tries it as I have done) will praise it as well as I.

I have finished, only take notice that it is of a dry, earthy quality.

*Place.]* It grows under hedges, and sometimes in the open fields, in various places of this land.

*Time.]* They flower throughout the months of July and August, and the seed ripens in the meantime.

<margin>Knots and kernels in the flesh, strangury, milk in cattle.</margin>
*Government and Virtues.]* It is under the dominion of Venus. It has the power to rarefy and digest; and therefore the green leaves, bruised and applied as a plaster, disperse knots, nodes, or kernels in the flesh. If the plant is dry and taken in wine, it helps the strangury <note>painful or difficult urination</note>; and when anointed with oil, it provokes sweat. It is an excellent food for cattle to cause them to give a store of milk; why then might it not do the same if boiled in the ordinary drink of nurses?

## Columbines.

These are so well known, growing in almost every garden, that I think I may save the expense of time in writing a description of them.

*Time.]* They flower in May and mostly do not last once June has passed, perfecting their seed in the meantime.

<margin>Sore mouths and throats, obstructions, yellow jaundice, women's labor, stone.</margin>
*Government and Virtues.]* It is also an herb of Venus. The leaves of columbines are commonly used in lotions with good success for sore mouths and throats. *Tragus* says that a dram <note>about 1/8 of an ounce</note> of the seed taken in wine with a little saffron opens obstructions of the liver and is good for the yellow jaundice, if the person, after taking it, is laid in bed to sweat well. The seed also, taken in wine, causes a speedy delivery for women in childbirth; if one draught does not suffice, let her drink a second, and it is effective. The Spaniards are accustomed to eat a piece of the root in the morning while fasting for many days together, to help those who are troubled with the stone in the reins <note>kidneys</note> or kidneys.

## Coltsfoot.

Called also cough-wort, foal's-foot, horse-hoof, and bull's-foot.

*Descript.]* This shoots up a slender stalk with small yellowish flowers somewhat early, which fall away quickly; after they are gone, somewhat round leaves come up, sometimes dented a little about the edges. These are much smaller, thicker, and greener than those of *butterbur*, with a little down or fuzz over the green leaf on the upper side, which may be rubbed away, and they are whitish or mealy underneath. The root is small and white, spreading much underground, so that where it takes hold, it will hardly be driven away again if any little piece remains there; and from there, fresh leaves spring.

*Place.]* It grows in wet grounds as well as in drier places.

*Time.]* It flowers at the end of February, and the leaves begin to appear in March.

## Comfrey.

<margin>*Description.*]</margin>
The common great comfrey has various very large and hairy green leaves lying on the ground, so hairy or prickly that if they touch any tender part of the hands, face, or body, it will cause it to itch. The stalk that rises up from among them, being two or three feet high, hollow and cornered, is very hairy also, having many such similar leaves growing below, but getting smaller and smaller up to the top. At the joints of the stalks, it is divided into many branches with some leaves on them, and at the ends stand many flowers in order one above another, which are somewhat long and hollow like the finger of a glove, of a pale whitish color, after which come small black seeds. The roots are great and long, spreading large branches underground, black on the outside and whitish within, short and easy to break, and full of a glutinous or sticky juice of little or no taste at all.

There is another variety in all things like this, except only that it is somewhat smaller, and with flowers of a pale purple color.

<margin>*Place.*]</margin>
They grow by ditches and watersides, and in various fields that are moist, for therein they especially delight to grow; the first generally through all the land, and the other but in some specific places. With the permission of my authors, I know the first often grows in dry places.

<margin>*Time.*]</margin>
They flower in *June* and *July*, and produce their seed in *August*.

<margin>
*Government and Virtues.*]
Spitting or passing blood, inward wounds and bruises, medicine.
</margin>

The great comfrey helps those who spit blood or pass bloody urine. The root boiled in water or wine, and the decoction drunk, helps all inward hurts, bruises, and wounds, and the ulcers of the lungs, causing the phlegm that oppresses them to be easily spit forth. # Coralwort.

IT is called by some toothwort, toothed violet, dog-teeth violet, and dentaria.

*Description.*] Of the many sorts of this herb, two of them may be found growing in this nation; the first of which shoots forth one or two winged leaves upon long brownish footstalks, which are doubled down at their first coming out of the ground. When they are fully opened, they consist of seven leaves, most commonly of a dark green color, toothed about the edges, set on both sides of the middle rib one against another, like the leaves of the ash tree. The stalk bears no leaves on its lower half; the upper half bears sometimes three or four, each consisting of five leaves, sometimes only three. On the top stand four or five flowers upon short footstalks, with long husks; the flowers are very like the flowers of stock gillyflowers, of a pale purplish color, consisting of four leaves apiece, after which come small pods which contain the seed. The root is very smooth, white, and shining; it does not grow downwards, but creeps along under the upper crust of the ground and consists of several small round knobs set together. Toward the top of the stalk there grow some single leaves, by each of which comes a small round split bulb <note>bulbil</note>, which when it is ripe, if it be set in the ground, will grow to be a root.

As for the other coralwort which grows in this nation, it is more

## Costmary, or Alecost, or Balsam Herb.

This is so frequently known to be an inhabitant in almost every garden that I suppose it needless to write a description of it.

<margin>Time.]</margin> It flowers in *June* and *July*.

<margin>Dysuria, womb, choler, phlegm, putrefaction, corruption, obstructions, daily agues, stomach, liver, headache, rheum, raw humors, cachexia, worms, ulcers. Government and Virtues.]</margin> It is under the dominion of *Jupiter*. The ordinary Costmary, as well as Maudlin, provokes urine abundantly and moistens the hardness of the mother <note>the womb</note>; it gently purges choler and phlegm, thinning that which is thick and cutting through that which is tough and glutinous, cleanses that which is foul, and hinders putrefaction and corruption. It dissolves without attraction <note>drawing in humors</note>, opens obstructions, and heals their evil effects, and is a wonderful help to all sorts of daily agues <note>fevers</note>. It is astringent to the stomach and strengthens the liver and all the other inward parts; and taken in whey, it works the more effectively. Taken fasting in the morning, it is very profitable for continual pains of the head, and to stay, dry up, and consume all thin rheums or distillations from the head into the stomach, and it helps much to digest raw humors that are gathered therein. It is very profitable for those who have fallen into a continual evil disposition of the whole body called *Cachexia* <note>a state of ill health and wasting</note>, being taken especially in the beginning of the disease. It is a special friend and help to evil, weak, and cold livers. The seed is commonly given to children for worms, and so is the infusion of the flowers in white wine, given to them in the quantity of two ounces at a time. It makes an excellent salve to cleanse and heal old ulcers when boiled with olive oil and Adder's Tongue; and after it is strained, a little wax, rosin, and turpentine should be added to bring it into a convenient body <note>consistency</note>.

## Cudweed, or Cottonweed.

**Besides** Cudweed and Cottonweed, it is called Chafweed, Dwarf Cotton, and Petty Cotton.

*Descript.*] The common Cudweed rises up with only one stalk at a time, and sometimes with two or three, thickly set on all sides with small, long, and narrow whitish or woolly leaves, from the middle of the stalk almost up to the top; by every leaf stands a small flower of a dun or brownish-yellow color, or not so yellow as others; in these heads, after the flowers have fallen, come small seeds wrapped up in down, which are carried away by the wind. The root is small and threadlike.
There are other sorts of this which are somewhat smaller than the former and not much different, except that just as the stalk and leaves are shorter, so the flowers are paler and more open.

*Place.*] They grow in dry, barren, sandy, and gravelly grounds in most places of this land.

*Time.*] They flower about *July*, some earlier, some later, and their seed is ripe in *August*.

<margin>
Fluxes
Menstrual issues
Ruptures
Worms
Tenesmus
Wounds

Quinsy
</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] *Venus* is the lady of it. The plants are all astringent, or binding and drying, and therefore useful to bind and dry defluxions of <term>rheum</term> from the head, and to stop fluxes of blood wherever they occur. A decoction made with red wine and drunk, or the powder taken in it, also helps the <term>Bloody Flux</term> <note>dysentery</note> and eases the torments that come thereby; it stops the excessive <term>courses</term> <note>menstruation</note> of women and is also good for inward or outward wounds, hurts, and bruises. It helps children with both ruptures and worms, and the disease called <term>Tenesmus</term>, which is a frequent urge to go to the stool without being able to do anything, whether it is drunk or injected. The green leaves, crushed and applied to any fresh wound, stop the bleeding and heal it quickly. The decoction or juice of it does the same and quickly helps all old and filthy ulcers. The juice of the herb taken in wine and milk is (as *Pliny* says) a sovereign remedy against the mumps and <term>quinsy</term> <note>an abscess in the throat</note>; and he further says that whoever shall take it this way shall never be troubled with that disease again.

The flowers are considered more effective than the leaves, and the roots are of little use. An ointment made with them takes away spots and wrinkles of the skin, and sunburn.

### Sciatica-Cresses.

<margin>Description.]</margin> These are of two kinds. The first rises up with a round stalk about two feet high, spread into various branches, whose lower leaves are somewhat larger than the upper, yet all of them cut or torn on the edges, somewhat like garden-cresses, but smaller. The flowers are small and white, growing at the tops of the branches, where afterwards grow husks with small brownish seed within, very strong and sharp in taste, more so than the cresses of the garden. The root is long, white, and woody.

The other has the lower leaves whole, somewhat long and broad, not torn at all, but only somewhat deeply dented about the edges towards the ends, but those that grow up higher are smaller. The flowers and seed are like the former, and so is the root likewise; and both root and seed are as sharp as the first.

<margin>Place.]</margin> These grow by the way sides in untilled places, and by the sides of old walls.

<margin>Time.]</margin> They flower in the end of *June*, and their seed is ripe in *July*.

<margin>
Sciatica,
Gout,
Headache,
Rheums,
Spleen,
Scars, Leprosy,
Scurf,
Stabs.
</margin>

The leaves, but especially the roots taken fresh in the summer time, beaten and made into a poultice or salve with old hog's grease and applied to the place pained with the sciatica, should continue there for four hours if it be on a man, and two hours on a woman. ## Water-Cresses.

<margin>Description.]</margin>
Our ordinary watercresses spread out with many weak, hollow, sappy stalks, shooting out fibers at the joints, and upwards long, winged leaves, made of various broad, sappy, and round leaves of a brownish-green color. The flowers are many and stand on long footstalks, after which come small yellow seeds contained in small long pods like horns. The whole plant remains green in the water and tastes somewhat hot and sharp.

<margin>Place.]</margin>
They grow (for the most part) in small standing waters, yet sometimes in small rivulets of running water.

<margin>Time.]</margin>
They flower and seed in the beginning of summer.

<margin>Government and Virtues.]</margin>
It is an herb under the dominion of the Moon. They are more powerful against scurvy and for cleansing the blood and humors <note>In the humoral theory of medicine, the four fluids that determine health and temperament</note> than brooklime is, and serve in all the other uses for which brooklime is available—such as breaking the stone <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>, provoking urine, and promoting women's courses <note>menstruation</note>. A decoction of it cleanses ulcers by washing them with it. The bruised leaves, or the juice, is good to apply at night to the face or other parts troubled with freckles, pimples, spots, or the like, and washed away in the morning. The juice mixed with vinegar, used to bathe the forehead, is very good for those who are dull and drowsy or have lethargy.

<margin>Watercress pottage.</margin>
Watercress pottage is a good remedy to cleanse the blood in the spring, to help headaches, and to consume the humors winter has left behind. Those who wish to live in health may use it if they please; if they will not, I cannot help it. If anyone does not like pottage, they may eat the herb as a salad.

## Crosswort.

<margin>Description.]</margin>
Common crosswort grows up with square, hairy, brown stalks, a little over a foot high, having four small, broad-pointed, hairy, yet smooth green leaves growing at every joint, each opposite the other crosswise, which has caused the name. Toward the tops of the stalks at the joints with the leaves, in three or four rows upwards, stand small, pale yellow flowers; after which come small, blackish, round seeds, for the most part set in every husk. The root is very small and full of fibers or threads, taking good hold of the ground and covering a great deal of ground with its branches. These do not perish in winter, although the leaves die every year and spring up again anew.

<margin>Place.]</margin>

# Crowfoot.

**M**any are the names this furious, biting herb has obtained—almost enough to make up a Welshman’s pedigree, if he traces it no further than *John* of *Gaunt* or *William* the Conqueror. For it is called Frog's-foot from the Greek name βάτραχιον <note>Batrachion</note>, Crowfoot, Gold Knobs, Gold Cups, King Kob, Baffinets, Troll Flower, Polts, Locker Goulons, and Butter Flowers.

There are such an abundance of types of this herb that to describe them all would tire the patience even of *Socrates* himself; but because I have not yet attained the spirit of *Socrates*, I shall only describe the most common.

*Descript.]* The most common Crowfoot has many dark green leaves cut into various parts, biting and sharp in taste, biting and blistering the tongue. It bears many flowers, and those of a bright, resplendent yellow color; I do not remember ever seeing anything yellower. In ancient times, virgins used to make powder of them to strew upon bride beds. After these flowers come small heads of seeds, round but rugged like a pineapple.

*Place.]* They grow very commonly everywhere; unless you run your head into a hedge, you cannot help but see some of them wherever you walk.

*Time.]* They flower in *May* and *June*, even until *September*.

*Government and Virtues.]* This fiery and hot-spirited herb of *Mars* is in no way fit to be taken internally, but an ointment of the leaves or flowers will raise a blister, and may thus be appropriately applied to the nape of the neck to draw back rheum <note>excessive watery discharge</note> from the eyes. The herb, being bruised and mixed with a little mustard, raises a blister as well and as perfectly as cantharides <note>Spanish fly, a blistering agent</note>, and with far less danger to the urinary vessels, which cantharides naturally tend to harm. I once knew the herb applied to a pestilential

## Cuckoo-pint.

It is called Aron, Jarus, and Barba-aron, Calves-foot, Ramp, Starch-wort, Cuckoo-pintle, Priest-pintle, and Wake-robin.

*Descript.*] This shoots forth three, four, or five leaves at the most from the root, every one of which is somewhat large and long, broad at the bottom next to the stalk, and forked, but ending in a point, without cuts on the edges, of a full green color, each standing upon a thick round stalk, a hand's breadth long or more. Among these, after two or three months when they begin to wither, rises up a bare, round, whitish-green stalk, spotted and streaked with purple, somewhat higher than the leaves. At the top of this stands a long hollow hose or husk, closed at the bottom but open from the middle upward, ending in a point; in the middle of which stands a small long pestle or clapper, smaller at the bottom than at the top, of a dark purple color like the husk is on the inside, though green on the outside. After it has remained for some time, the husk with the clapper decays, and the foot or bottom of it grows into a small long bunch of berries, green at first, and of a yellowish-red color when they are ripe, of the size of a hazelnut kernel; these remain there almost until winter. The root is round and somewhat long, for the most part lying flat, the leaves shooting forth at the larger end, which when it bears its berries is somewhat wrinkled and loose, with another growing under it that is solid and firm, with many small threads hanging from it. The whole plant is of a very sharp biting taste, pricking the tongue as nettles do the hands, and this remains for a long time without change. The root of this was anciently used instead of starch to starch linen with.

There is another sort of Cuckoo-pint with smaller leaves than the former, and somewhat harder, having blackish spots upon them, which for the most part remain green longer in summer than the former; and both leaves and roots are sharper and more fierce than it. In all other things, it is like the former.

*Place.*] These two sorts grow frequently almost under every hedge side in many places of this land.

*Time.*] They shoot forth leaves in the spring and continue only until the middle of summer, or somewhat later, their husks appearing before they fall away; and their fruit showing in August.

The juice of the herb, taken in the quantity of a spoonful, has the same effect. The green leaves, bruised and laid upon any boil or plague-sore, do wonder-

# Daisies.

These are so well known to almost every child that I suppose it is altogether needless to write any description of them. Take therefore their virtues as follows.

*Government and Virtues.*] The herb is under the sign *Cancer* and under the dominion of *Venus*, and therefore excellently good for wounds in the breast, and very fitting to be kept in oils, ointments, and plasters, as also in syrup. The greater wild daisy is a wound herb of good respect, often used in those drinks or salves that are for
<margin>
Wounds, inward and outward; choler; liver; breast; ulcers; swellings; kernels; bruises; falls; ruptures; burnings; inflammations.
</margin>
wounds, either inward or outward. The juice or distilled water of these, or the small daisies, does much to temper the heat of choler <note>yellow bile</note> and refreshes the liver and other inward parts. A decoction made of them and drunk helps to cure the wounds made in the hollowness of the chest. The same also cures all ulcers and pustules in the mouth or tongue, or in the private parts. The leaves crushed and applied to the testicles, or to any other parts that are swollen and hot, dissolve the swelling and temper the heat. A decoction made of this with walwort and agrimony, if the places are fomented <note>bathed with warm medicinal lotions</note> or bathed with it while warm, gives great ease to those who are troubled with the palsy, sciatica, or the gout. The same also disperses and dissolves the knots or kernels <note>swollen lymph nodes or glands</note> that grow in the flesh of any part of the body, and the bruises and hurts that come from falls and blows. They are also used for ruptures <note>hernias</note> and other inward burnings with very good success. An ointment made of this does wonderfully help all wounds that have inflammations about them, or which, by reason of moist humors having access to them, are kept long from healing; and such are for the most part those that happen in the joints of the arms or legs. The juice of them dropped into the running eyes of anyone helps them much.

# Dandelion, commonly called Piss-a-beds.

<margin>Description.]</margin> This is so well known to have many long and deeply gashed leaves lying on the ground, round about the head of the root; the ends of each gash or jag on both sides look downward towards the root, the middle rib being white; when broken, it yields an abundance of bitter milk, but the root much more. From among the leaves, which always stay green, arise many slender, weak, naked stalks, every one of them bearing at the top one large yellow flower, consisting of many rows of yellow leaves, broad at the points and notched, with a deep spot of yellow in the middle. When it grows ripe, the green husk wherein the flower stood turns itself down to the stalk, and the head of down becomes as round as a ball, with long reddish seed underneath, bearing a part of the down on the head of every one; together, these are blown away with the wind, or may be at once blown away with one's mouth. The root grows downwards exceeding deep; if broken off within the ground, it will notwithstanding shoot forth again, and will hardly be destroyed where it has once taken deep root in the ground.

<margin>Place.]</margin> It grows frequently in all meadows and pasture grounds.

<margin>Time.]</margin> It flowers in one place or other almost all the year long.

<margin>Government and Virtues.]</margin> It is under the dominion of *Jupiter*. It is of an opening and cleansing quality, and therefore very effective
<margin>Opens, Cleanses, Obstructions, Liver, Gall, Spleen, Jaundice, hypochondriac, Melancholy, Dysuria, Consumption, Cachexia, Sleeplessness, heat, ague, Pestilence.</margin> for the obstructions of the liver, gallbladder, and spleen, and the diseases that arise from them, as the jaundice and hypochondriac passion <note>discomfort or distress in the upper abdomen</note>. It wonderfully opens the passages of the urine both in young and old. It powerfully cleanses apostumes <note>abscesses</note> and inward sores in the urinary passages, and by its drying and temperate quality does afterwards heal them; for which purpose the decoction of the roots or leaves in white wine, or the leaves chopped as pot-herbs with a few Alexanders <note>an edible plant, Smyrnium olusatrum</note> and boiled in their broth, is very effective. And whoever is drawing towards a consumption, or an evil disposition of the whole body called *cachexia*, shall find a wonderful help by the use of this for some time together. It also helps to procure rest and sleep to bodies distempered by the heat of ague fits, or otherwise. The distilled water is effective to drink in pestilential fevers and to wash the sores.

You see here what virtues this common herb has, and that is the reason the French and Dutch so often eat them in the spring; and now if you look a little further, you may see plainly without a pair of spectacles that foreign physicians are not so selfish as ours are, but are more communicative of the virtues of plants to people.

# Dill.

<margin>Description.]</margin>
The common Dill grows up with seldom more than one stalk, usually neither so high nor so great as fennel, being round and with fewer joints on it. Its leaves are darker and somewhat long, and so like fennel that it deceives many, but harder in handling and somewhat thicker, and of a stronger, unpleasanter scent. The tops of the stalks have four branches and smaller umbels of yellow flowers, which turn into small seed, somewhat flatter and thinner than fennel seed. The root is somewhat small and woody, perishing every year after it has borne seed; it is also unprofitable, being never put to any use.

Place.] It is most usually sown in gardens and grounds for that purpose, and is also found wild with us in some places.

### Dock.

These are so well known in their many kinds that I shall not trouble you with a description of them; my book grows big too fast.

<margin>Cleanses the blood, strengthens the liver, flux, loathing of food, spitting blood, scabs, itch, freckles, morphew.</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] All docks are under *Jupiter*; of which the red dock, which is commonly called Bloodwort, cleanses the blood and strengthens the liver; but the yellow dock root is best to be taken when either the blood or liver is afflicted by choler <note>yellow bile</note>. All of them have a kind of cooling (though not all alike) and drying quality, the sorrels being the coldest and the bloodworts the most drying. I have spoken of the Burdock already by itself. The seed of most of the other kinds, whether of the garden or field, stops lasks <note>diarrhea</note> or fluxes of all sorts, the loathings of the stomach caused by choler, and is helpful to those who spit blood. The roots boiled in vinegar help the itch, scabs, and breakouts of the skin if it be bathed with it. The distilled water of the herb and roots has the same virtue and cleanses the skin of freckles, morphew, and all other spots and discolorations therein.

All docks, when boiled with meat, make it cook the sooner. Besides, bloodwort is exceedingly strengthening to the liver and produces good blood, being as wholesome a potherb as any that grows in a garden; yet such is the fussiness of our times, forsooth, that women will not put it in the pot because it makes the pottage black; pride and ignorance (a couple of monsters in creation) preferring fussiness over health.

### and other Dodders.

After these strings have risen to such a height that they may draw nourishment from the plant, they seem to be broken off from the ground, either by the strength of their rising or withered by the heat of the sun. And so of the rest.

Sympathy and antipathy are the two hinges upon which the whole model of medicine <note>physick</note> turns, and that physician who does not mind them is like a door off its hinges, more likely to do a man mischief than to secure him. Then all the diseases *Saturn* causes, this helps by sympathy, and strengthens all the parts of the body he rules; such as are caused by *Sol* it helps by antipathy. For what those diseases are, see my *Judgment of Diseases by Astrology*, and if you are pleased to look at the herb wormwood, you shall find a rational way for it.

**Time.]** It flowers in June, July, and August, some earlier and some later, and the seed is ripe quickly after.

# Dragons.

They are so well known to everyone that plants them in their gardens, they need no description; if not, let them look down toward the lower end of the stalk and see how much like a snake they look.

<margin>Scours, cleanses, freckles, morphew, sunburning, wounds, ulcers, cancers, polypus, spots in the eyes, pin and web, helps sight, pestilence, poison, venomous beasts.</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] The plant is under the dominion of *Mars*, and therefore it would be a wonder if it should want some obnoxious quality or other: in all herbs of that quality, the safest way is either to distill the herb in an alembic <note>a distilling apparatus</note>, in what vehicle <note>liquid medium</note> you please, or else to press out the juice and distill that in a glass still in sand; it scours and cleanses the internal parts of the body mightily, and so it does the external parts also, being externally applied for freckles, morphew <note>scurfy skin discoloration</note>, and sunburning: your best way to use it externally is to mix it with vinegar: an ointment of it is held to be good in wounds and ulcers; it consumes cancers, and that flesh growing in the nostrils which they call polypus. ### Eringo, or, Sea-Holly.

<margin>Description.</margin>

The stalk itself is round and strong, yet somewhat crested with joints, and leaves set there, but more divided, sharp, and prickly; and branches rising from there, which likewise have other smaller branches, each of them bearing several bluish round prickly heads, with many small jagged, prickly leaves under them standing like a star, and are sometimes found greenish or whitish. The root grows wonderfully long, even to eight or ten feet in length, set with rings or circles toward the upper part, but smooth and without joints lower down, brownish on the outside and very white within, with a pith in the middle, of a pleasant taste, but much more so being artificially preserved and candied with sugar.*

<margin>Place.</margin>
It is found about the sea coasts, in almost every country of this land which borders upon the sea.

<margin>Time.</margin>
It flowers in the end of summer and produces ripe seed within a month after.

## Eyebright.

*Description.*] The common eyebright is a small, low herb, usually rising up with only one blackish-green stalk, a span <note>about nine inches</note> high or not much more, spread from the bottom into various branches. On these are set small and almost round, yet pointed, dark green leaves, finely notched about the edges, always set two together and very thick. At the joints with the leaves, from the middle upward, come forth small white flowers striped with purple and yellow spots or stripes; after these follow small round heads with very small seed inside. The root is long, small, and stringy at the end.

*Place.*] It grows in many meadows and grassy places in this land.

*Government and Vertues.*] It is under the sign of Leo, and Sol <note>the Sun</note> claims dominion over it. If this herb were used as much as it is neglected, it would half spoil the spectacle-maker’s trade; and a man would think that reason should teach people to prefer the preservation of their natural sight over artificial spectacles. So that they may be instructed how to do this, take the virtues of eyebright as follows:

<margin>
eyes,
dimness,
brain,
memory
</margin>
The juice or distilled water of eyebright, taken inwardly in white wine or broth, or dropped into the eyes for several days together, helps all infirmities of the eyes that cause dimness of sight. Some make a conserve of the flowers for the same effect. Being used in any of these ways, it also helps a weak brain or memory.

# Fern.

<margin>Description]</margin> Of this, there are two kinds principally to be noted: the *Male* and *Female*. The *Female* grows higher than the *Male*, but its leaves are smaller and more divided or indented, and it has as strong a smell as the *Male*. Their *virtues* are both alike, and therefore I shall not trouble you with any further description or distinction of them.

<margin>Place.]</margin> They both grow on heaths and in shady places near the hedge-sides in all parts of this land.

<margin>Time.]</margin> They flourish and produce their seed at Midsummer.

The Female Fern is that plant which in *Sussex* is called Brakes. Some authors hold the seed of this plant to be very rare; I know such a thing exists and may easily be obtained upon *Midsummer Eve*—and for all I know, two or three days before or after, if not more.

<margin>Government and Virtues.]</margin> It is under the dominion of *Mercury*, both the male and the female. The roots of both these sorts of *ferns*, being bruised and boiled in mead <note>honey-wine</note> or honeyed water and drunk, kill both the broad and long worms in the body, and reduce the swelling

# Featherfew.

*Description.*] Common featherfew has many large, fresh, green leaves, very much torn or cut on the edges. The stalks are hard and round, set with many similar leaves but somewhat smaller, and at the tops stand many single flowers upon several small footstalks, consisting of many small white leaves standing around a yellow thrum <note>a tufted center</note> in the middle. The root is somewhat hard and short, with many strong fibers on it. The scent of the whole plant is very strong and pungent, and the taste is very bitter.

*Place.*] This grows wild in some places of this land, but it is for the most part cultivated in gardens.

*Time.*] It flowers in the months of *June* and *July*.

<margin>*Mother, Womb, Menstruation, Dead-birth, After-birth, Cough, Kidneys, Bladder,*</margin>

And if any grumble because they cannot get the herb in winter, tell them, if they please, they may make a syrup of it in summer. It is chiefly used for the diseases of the "mother" <note>the womb; often referring to hysteria or uterine disorders</note>, whether it be the strangling or rising of the mother, or hardness or inflammations of the same, applied outwardly to it. Or a decoction of the flowers in wine, with a little nutmeg or mace put into it and drunk often in a day, is an approved remedy to bring down women's courses <note>menstruation</note> quickly, and helps to expel the dead birth and afterbirth. For a woman to sit over the hot fumes of the decoction of the herb made in water or wine is also effective for the same purpose; and in some cases, to apply the boiled herb warm to the private parts. # Fennel.

<margin>Government and Virtues.</margin>
Every garden affords this so plentifully that it needs no description. One good old fashion is not yet left off, specifically: to boil fennel with fish, for it consumes that phlegmatic humor which fish most plentifully produce and trouble the body with. Therefore, it is a most fit herb for that purpose, though few who use it know why or for what reason they do it; I suppose the reason for its benefit in this way is because it is an herb of *Mercury* and under *Virgo*, and therefore bears an antipathy to *Pisces*.
