*Fennel* is good to break gas, to provoke urine, and ease the pains of the stone, and help to break it. The leaves or seeds boiled in barley-water and drunk are good for nurses to increase their milk and make it more wholesome for the child. The leaves, or rather the seed, boiled in water stops the hiccup and takes away that loathing which often happens to the stomachs of sick and feverish persons, and allays the heat of it. The seed boiled in wine and drunk is good for those who are bitten by serpents or have eaten poisonous herbs or mushrooms. The seed and the root help even more to open obstructions of the liver, spleen, and gall, and thereby help the painful and windy swellings of the spleen and the yellow jaundice, as also the gout and cramps. The seed is of good use in medicines to help shortness of breath and wheezing caused by the stopping of the lungs. It helps also to bring down the menstrual cycles and to cleanse the parts after delivery. The roots are of most use in medicinal drinks and broths that are taken to cleanse the blood, to open obstructions of the liver, to provoke urine, and to improve the unhealthy color in the face after sickness, and to promote a healthy constitution throughout the body. # Sow-Fennel, or Hogs-Fennel.

Besides the common English name *Hogs-fennel* and the Latin name *Peusidanum*, it is called Hoar-strange, Hoar-strong, Sulphur-wort, and Brimstone-wort.

*Description.*] The common *sow-fennel* has several branched stalks of thick and somewhat long leaves, with three for the most part joined together at one place; among these rises a crested straight stalk, smaller than *fennel*, with some joints on it and leaves growing there, and toward the top some branches issue from it. Likewise, on the tops of the stalk and branches stand various tufts of yellow flowers, after which grow somewhat flat, thin, and yellowish seeds, larger than *fennel* seed. The root grows large and deep, with many other parts and fibers about them, having a strong scent like hot brimstone and yielding a yellowish milk or clammy juice, almost like a gum.

*Place.*] It grows plentifully in the salt low marshes near *Feaversham* in *Kent*.

*Time.*] It flowers and seeds in *July* and *August*.

<margin>
Lethargy, frenzy, vertigo, falling sickness <note>epilepsy</note>, headache, palsy <note>paralysis or tremors</note>, sciatica, cramp, sinews, cough, shortness of breath, gas, spleen, childbirth, reins <note>kidneys</note>, bladder, womb, ears, hollow teeth, ulcers, broken bones, thorns, wounds.
</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] This also is an herb of *Mercury*. The juice of *sow-fennel* (says *Dioscorides* and *Galen*), used with vinegar and rose water, or the juice with a little *Euphorbium* applied to the nose, helps those who are troubled with lethargy, frenzy, the turning or giddiness of the head <note>vertigo</note>, the falling sickness, long and chronic headache, palsy, sciatica, and cramp; and it generally helps all diseases of the sinews <note>nerves or tendons</note> when used with oil and vinegar. The juice dissolved in wine or put into an egg is good for a cough or shortness of breath, and for those who are troubled with gas in the body. It purges the belly gently, helps the hardness of the spleen, gives ease to women who have a difficult labor in childbirth, and eases the pains of the reins and bladder, and also of the womb. A little of the juice dissolved in wine and dropped into the ears greatly eases the pains in them; and put into a hollow tooth, it eases the pain there. The root is less effective in all the aforementioned diseases; yet the powder of the root cleanses foul ulcers when applied to them, takes out splinters of broken bones or other objects in the flesh, and heals them up perfectly; it also dries up old and chronic running sores and is of admirable virtue for all fresh wounds.

# Fig-wort, or Throat-wort.

<margin>*Description]*</margin> The common great fig-wort sends forth various great, strong, hard, square, brown stalks, three or four feet high, on which grow large, hard, and dark green leaves, two at a joint, which are larger and harder than nettle leaves, but not stinging. At the tops of the stalks stand many purple flowers set in husks, which are somewhat gaping and open, somewhat like those of *water-betony*. After these come hard round heads with a small point in the middle, in which lie small brownish seeds. The root is large, white, and thick, with many branches growing sideways under the upper crust of the ground; it survives for many years but does not keep its green leaves in winter.

<margin>*Place]*</margin> It grows frequently in moist and shady woods, and in the lower parts of fields and meadows.

<margin>*Time]*</margin> It flowers about *July*, and the seed will be ripe about a month after the flowers have fallen.

<margin>*Government and Virtues]* <margin>*Congealed blood from wounds, bruises, or falls; King's Evil <note>scrofula</note>; wens <note>cysts or tumors</note>; hemorrhoids; fundament <note>the anus</note>; ulcers; scurf; spots; freckles; deformity; leprosy.*</margin></margin> Some Latin authors call it *Cervicaria* because it is associated with the neck, and we call it *Throatwort* because it is associated with the throat. *Venus* owns the herb, and the celestial *Bull* <note>the zodiac sign Taurus, which rules the neck</note> will not deny it; therefore, a better remedy cannot be found for the King's Evil, because the *Moon* (which rules the disease) is exalted there. Nor is there a better remedy for any disease in the neck. Regarding the rest of the diseases specified, you may (if you look) see a very good reason for their cure by this herb. The decoction of the herb taken inwardly, and the bruised herb applied outwardly, dissolves clotted or congealed blood within the body caused by any wound, bruise, or fall. It is no less effective for the King's Evil, or any other knots, kernels, bunches, or wens growing in the flesh anywhere, and for the hemorrhoids, or piles, or other knobs or kernels which sometimes grow about the fundament. An ointment made from this may be used at all times when the fresh herb is not available. The distilled water of the whole plant, roots and all, is used for the same purposes, and dries up the superfluous, virulent moisture of hollow and corroding ulcers. It takes away all redness, spots, and freckles in the face, as well as the scurf or any foul deformity in it, and leprosy likewise.

# The yellow Water-Flag, Or, Flower-de-luce.

<margin>Description.]</margin> **T**his *grows like the* flower-de-luces, *but it has much longer and narrower dark green leaves joined together in that fashion; the stalk also grows oftentimes as high, bearing small yellow flowers shaped like the* flower-de-luce *with three falling leaves, and another three arched that cover their bottoms; but instead of the three upright leaves as the* flower-de-luce *has, this has only three short pieces standing in their places, after which succeed thick and long three-sided heads containing in each part somewhat big and flat seeds like to those of the* flower-de-luces: *The root is long and slender, of a pale brownish color on the outside, and of a pale flesh color on the inside, with many hard fibers thereat, and very harsh in taste.*

<margin>Place.]</margin> *It usually grows in watery ditches, ponds, lakes, and moor sides which are always overflowed with water.*

<margin>Time.]</margin> *It flowers in July, and the seed is ripe in August.*

<margin>Government and Virtues.]</margin> *It is under the dominion of the Moon.*

<margin>Binds, cools, dries, flux, bloody flux, bleeding, stops courses <note>menstrual flow</note>, eyes, spots, blemishes, inflammations, sore breasts, cankers, ulcers. Noli me tangere.</margin>
The root of this water flag is very astringent, cooling, and drying, and thereby helps all lasks <note>diarrhea</note> and fluxes <note>abnormal discharges</note>, whether of blood or humors, such as bleeding at the mouth, nose, or other parts, bloody fluxes, and the immoderate flux of women's courses. The distilled water of the whole herb, flowers, and roots, is a sovereign good remedy for watering eyes, both to be dropped into them and to have clothes or sponges wetted therein and applied to the forehead: It also helps the spots or blemishes that happen in or about the eyes, or in any other parts: The said water applied to swellings and hot inflammations of women's sore breasts, upon cankers also, and those spreading ulcers called *Noli me tangere*, does much good: It helps also foul ulcers in the private parts of man or woman, or elsewhere. An ointment made of the flowers is better for these external applications.

# Fluellin, or Lluellin.

<margin>Description]</margin> *This shoots forth many long branches, partly lying upon the ground and part standing upright, set with almost round leaves, yet a little pointed, and sometimes more long than round, without order thereon, somewhat hoary, and of an unpleasant greenish-white color; at the joints all along the stalks, and with the leaves, come forth small flowers, one at a place, upon a very small short footstalk, gaping somewhat like <term>snapdragons</term>, or rather like <term>toadflax</term>, with the upper jaw of a yellow color and the lower of a purplish color, with a small heel or spur behind, after which come small round heads, containing small black seed. The root is small and threadlike <note>threddy</note>, dying every year, and raises itself again from its own sowing.*

*There is another sort of Lluellin which has longer branches wholly trailing upon the ground two or three feet long, and sometimes more, thinner set with leaves thereon, upon small footstalks. The leaves are a little larger and somewhat round, and cornered sometimes in some places on the edges; but the lower part of them, being the broadest, has on each side a small point, making it seem as if they were ears, somewhat hairy, but not hoary, and of a better green color than the former. The flowers come forth like the former, but the colors therein are more white than yellow, and the purple not so fair; it is a larger flower, and so are the seed and seed vessels. The root is like the other and perishes every year.*

Bees are industrious and go abroad to gather honey from each plant and flower, but drones lie at home and eat up what the bees have taken pains for. Just so do our College of Physicians lie at home and domineer, and suck out the sweetness of other men's labors and studies, being themselves as ignorant in the knowledge of herbs as a child of four years old, as I can make appear to any rational man by their last Dispensatory. Now then, to hide their ignorance, there is not a readier way in the world than to hide knowledge from their countrymen, so that nobody might be able so much as to smell out their ignorance. When simples <note>medicinal herbs</note> were more in use, men's bodies were in far better health by far than they are now, or shall be if the College can help it. The truth is, this herb is of a fine cooling, drying quality, and an ointment or plaster of it might do a man a courtesy who has any hot virulent sores; it is admirable for the ulcers of the French pox <note>syphilis</note>, and if taken inwardly it may cure the disease. It was at first called *Female Speedwell*, but a gentleman of Wales, whose nose was almost eaten off with the pox, and so near the matter that the doctors commanded it to be cut off, being cured by only the use of this herb, to honor the herb for saving his nose whole, gave it one of his own country names, *Lluellin*.

## Fumitory.

*Descript.*] Our common fumitory is a tender, sappy herb, sending forth from one square, slender, weak stalk (which leans downwards on all sides) many branches two or three feet long, with finely cut and jagged leaves of a whitish, or rather bluish, sea-green color. At the tops of the branches stand many small flowers, as if in a long spike, one above another, shaped like little birds of a reddish-purple color with whitish bellies. After these come small round husks containing small black seeds. The root is yellow, small, and not very long, full of juice while it is green, but quickly perishing once the seed is ripe. In the cornfields in Cornwall, this bears white flowers.

*Place.*] It grows in the cornfields almost everywhere, as well as in gardens.

*Time.*] It flowers in May for the most part, and the seed ripens shortly after.

*Government and Virtues.*] *Saturn* owns the herb and presents it to the world as a cure for his own diseases, and a strengthener of the parts of the body he rules. # Garlic.

The offensiveness of the breath of him that has eaten Garlic will lead you by the nose to the knowledge of this, and (instead of a description) direct you to the place where it grows in gardens; these kinds are best and most medicinal.

<margin>
*Urine, menses (terms) provoked, mad dogs, venomous beasts, worms, lethargy, phlegm, pestilence, abscesses (apostumes), mineral vapors, stinking waters, henbane, hemlock, wolf-bane, dropsy, cramps, convulsions, epilepsy (falling-sickness).*
</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] Mars owns this herb. This was anciently counted the Poor Man’s Treacle <note>an apothecary's medicinal compound used as an antidote</note>, it being a remedy for all diseases or hurts (except those which it itself breeds). It provokes urine and women's courses, helps the biting of a mad dog and other venomous creatures; kills worms in children, breaks up and expels tough phlegm, purges the head, helps the lethargy, and is a good preservative against, and a remedy for, any plague-sore or foul ulcer. It takes away spots and blemishes in the skin, eases pains of the ears, and ripens and breaks imposthumes <note>abscesses</note> or other swellings. For all these diseases, onions are also effectual. But garlic has some more peculiar virtues besides the former; namely, it has a special quality to discuss the inconveniences coming by corrupt fevers (agues) or mineral vapors, or by drinking corrupt and stinking waters, as also by the taking of wolf-bane, henbane, hemlock, or other poisonous and dangerous herbs. It is also held good in dropsical (hydropic) diseases, the jaundice, epilepsy (falling-sickness), cramps, convulsions, the piles or hemorrhoids, and other cold diseases.

Many authors quote many diseases this is good for, but conceal its vices: its heat is very vehement, and all vehemently hot things send up ill-favored vapors to the brain. In choleric men it will add fuel to the fire; in men oppressed by melancholy, it will thin the humor and send up strange fancies and as many strange visions to the head. Therefore, let it be taken inwardly with great moderation; outwardly you may be more bold with it.

---

# Gentian, Felwort, or Baldmony.

It is confessed that Gentian, which is most used amongst us, is brought over from abroad; yet we have two sorts of it growing frequently in our nation, which—besides the reasons so frequently alleged, "Why should English herbs not be fittest for English bodies?"—has been proved by the experience of several able physicians to be not a bit inferior in virtue to that which comes from abroad. Therefore, be pleased to take the description of them as follows.

*Description.*] *The greater of the two has many small, long roots thrust down deep into the ground, which remain all the winter. The stalks are sometimes more, sometimes fewer, of a brownish-green color, which are sometimes two feet high if the ground is fruitful, having many long, narrow, dark green leaves set in pairs up to the top. The flowers are long and hollow, of a purple color, ending in five corners.*

**Place.]** The first grows in various places both in the East and West countries, and as well in wet as in dry grounds, as near Longfield and Gravesend, near Cobham in Kent, near Lullingstone in Kent, also in a chalky pit right by a paper mill not far from Dartford in Kent.

The second grows also in various places in Kent, as around Southfleet and Longfield, upon Barton Hills in Bedfordshire: also not far from St. Albans upon a piece of waste chalky ground as you go out of the Dunstable way toward Gorhambury.

**Government and Virtues.]** They are under the dominion of Mars, and it is one of the most principal herbs he rules. They resist putrefaction, poison, and pestilence: nor can a more certain remedy be found to prevent the pestilence than this. It strengthens the stomach exceedingly and helps digestion; it preserves the heart and protects it against fainting and swooning. The powder of the dry roots helps the biting of mad dogs and venomous beasts, opens obstructions of the liver, and restores an appetite for food to those who have lost it. The herb steeped in wine, and the wine drunk, refreshes those who are overweary with travel and have grown lame in their joints either by cold or poor lodgings: it helps stitches and griping pains in the sides, and is an excellent remedy for those who are bruised by falls. It provokes urine and the menses <note>terms</note> exceedingly, therefore let it not be given to women with child. The same is very profitable for those who are troubled with cramps and convulsions to drink the decoction: also they say it breaks the stone and helps ruptures most certainly. It is very excellent in all cold diseases, and for those who are troubled with tough phlegm, scabs, itch, or any fretting sores and ulcers. It is an admirable remedy to kill worms by taking half a dram of the powder in the morning in any convenient liquor; the same is excellent to be taken inwardly for the King's Evil <note>scrofula</note>. It helps agues of all sorts and the yellow jaundice, as also the bots in cattle. When cows are bitten on the udder by any venomous beast, simply stroke the place with the decoction of any of these, and it will instantly help them.

# Clove-gillyflowers.

<margin>Brain, heart, wasting diseases, strengthens nature.</margin>
It is pointless to describe an herb so well known.
**Government and Virtues.]** They are excellent, fine, temperate flowers by nature, and under the dominion of *Jupiter*; indeed, they are so temperate that no excess in heat, cold, dryness, nor moisture can be perceived in them. They are great strengtheners of both the brain and heart, and will therefore serve as either cordials or cephalics <note>medicines for the head or brain</note> as your needs require. There is both a syrup and a conserve made of them, and of them alone, commonly available at every apothecary’s; taking a little of either now and then greatly strengthens nature in those suffering from consumptions <note>wasting diseases</note>. They are also excellent for hot pestilential fevers and for expelling poison.

# Germander.

<margin>Description.]</margin>
**Common Germander** shoots forth various stalks with small and somewhat round *leaves*, toothed around the edges. The flowers stand at the tops and are of a deep purple color. The root is composed of several sprigs, which shoot out a great distance all around, quickly overspreading the ground.

<margin>Place.]</margin>
It usually grows with us in gardens.

<margin>Time.]</margin>
And flowers in June or July.

<margin>Government and Virtues.] Cough, spleen, difficulty of urine, dropsy, induces menstruation, expels stillborn child, poison, ulcers, cramps, agues, epilepsy, headache, melancholy, dullness of spirit, convulsion, palsy, yellow jaundice, worms.</margin>
**Government and Virtues.]** It is a most powerful herb of *Mercury* and strengthens the brain and understanding exceedingly. You may see what human virtues are under *Mercury* in the latter end of my *Ephemeris* for 1651; use this herb to strengthen them when weak and relieve them when drooping. This herb taken with honey (says *Dioscorides*) is a remedy for coughs, for hardness of the spleen, and for difficulty of urine, and it helps those who have fallen into a dropsy, especially at the beginning of the disease, if a decoction is made of it while green and drunk. It also brings down women’s periods and expels a stillborn child. It is most effective against the poison of all snakes when drunk in wine and the bruised herb is applied outwardly. Used with honey, it cleanses old and foul ulcers, and when made into an oil and used to anoint the eyes, it removes their dimness and moisture. It is likewise good for pains in the sides and cramps. A decoction of it taken for several days together drives away and cures both tertian and quartan agues. It is also good against all diseases of the brain, such as continual headache, epilepsy <note>falling-sickness</note>, melancholy, drowsiness, dullness of spirit, convulsions, and palsies. A dram of the seed taken in powder purges by urine and is good against the yellow jaundice. The juice of the leaves dropped into the ears kills the worms in them. The tops of the plant, when in flower, steeped for twenty-four hours in a draft of white wine and drunk, kill worms in the belly.

# Stinking Gladwin.

**Descript.]** This is one of the kinds of *fleurs-de-lis*, having various *leaves* rising from the roots very like a *fleur-de-lis*, except that they are sharp-edged on both sides and thicker in the middle, of a deeper green color, narrower and sharper pointed, and of a strong, unpleasant scent if they are bruised between the fingers. In the middle rises up a reasonably strong stalk at least a yard high, which bears three or four flowers at the top, made somewhat like the flowers of the *fleur-de-lis*, with three upright leaves of a dead purplish ash-color with some discolored veins in them; the other three do not fall down, nor are the three other small ones so arched or cover the lower leaves as the *fleur-de-lis* does, but they stand loose or apart from them. After they have passed, there come up three-square hard husks opening wide into three parts when they are ripe, wherein lie reddish seeds that turn black when they have remained long. The root is like that of the *fleur-de-lis*, but reddish on the outside and whitish within, very sharp and hot in taste, and of as foul a scent as the leaves.

**Place.]** This grows as well on upland grounds as also in moist places, in woods, and shady places by the seaside in many places of this land, and is usually cultivated in gardens.

**Time.]** It does not flower until *July*, and the seed is ripe in *August* or *September*; yet the husks, after they are ripe and open, will hold their seeds within them for two or three months without shedding them.

# Golden Rod.

***Description.]*** This *rises up with small brownish round stalks, two feet high and sometimes more, having on them many narrow and long dark green leaves, very seldom with any dents about the edges, or any streaks or white spots therein; yet they are sometimes found so, divided at the tops into many small branches, with various small yellow flowers on every one of them, all of which are turned one way, and when ripe they turn into down and are carried away with the wind. The root consists of many small fibers which do not grow deep in the ground, but remain there all winter, shooting forth new branches every year, as the old ones die down to the ground.*

***Place.]*** It grows in the open places of woods and copses, in both moist and dry grounds, in many places of this land.

***Time.]*** It flowers about the month of *July*.

<margin>
Lost beauty, stone, gravel, dysuria, wounds, flux, bloody flux, stopping menstruation, ruptures, ulcers, sore mouth and throat, loose teeth.
</margin>
***Government and Virtues.]*** Venus claims this herb, and therefore, to be sure, it restores beauty lost. *Arnoldus de Villa Nova* commends it much against the stone in the reins <note>kidneys</note> and kidneys, and to provoke urine in abundance, whereby also the gravel or stone may be expelled. The decoction of the herb, green or dry, or its distilled water, is very effective for inward bruises, as also when applied outwardly; it stops bleeding in any part of the body, and from wounds as well, the fluxes of humors, the bloody flux, and women's courses; and it is no less prevalent in all ruptures or burstings, being drunk inwardly and applied outwardly. It is a sovereign wound-herb, inferior to none, for both inward and outward hurts; green wounds and old sores and ulcers are quickly cured with it. It is also of especial use in all lotions for sores or ulcers in the mouth, throat, or private parts of man or woman. The decoction also helps to fasten teeth that are loose in the gums.

# Goutwort, or Herb-Gerard.

***Description.]*** This *is a low herb seldom rising half a yard high, having several leaves standing on brownish green stalks in threes, snipped about the edges, and of a strong unpleasant scent. The umbels of flowers are white, and the seed blackish; the root runs in the ground, quickly taking up a great deal of room.*

***Place.]*** It grows by hedge and wall sides, and often in the borders or corners of fields, and in gardens as well.

# Gromel.

Of this I shall briefly describe three kinds, which are principally used in medicine, the virtues of which are alike, though somewhat different in their manner and form of growth.

*Description.] The greater Gromel* grows up with slender, hard, and hairy stalks, trailing and taking root in the ground as it lies upon it, and divided into many other smaller branches with hairy dark green leaves on them. At the joints with the leaves come forth very small blue flowers, and after them hard, stony, roundish seed. The root is long and woody, surviving the winter and shooting forth fresh stalks in the spring.

*The small wild Gromel* sends forth several upright, hard, branched stalks two or three feet high, full of joints, at each of which grow small, long, hard, and rough leaves like the former but smaller; among these leaves come forth small white flowers, and after them grayish round seed like the former. The root is not very long, but has many strings at it.

*The garden Gromel* has several upright, slender, woody, hairy stalks, brown and crested, very little branched, with leaves like the former and white flowers; after which, in rough brown husks, is contained a white, hard, round seed, shining like pearls and larger than either of the former. The root is like the first described, with several branches and strings thereat; which continues (as the first does) all winter.

*Place.]* The first two grow wild in barren or uncultivated places, and by the roadsides in many places of this land. The last is nurtured in the gardens of the curious.

*Time.]* They all flower from *Midsummer* until *September* sometimes, and in the meantime the seed ripens.

*Government and Virtues.]* The herb belongs to Dame *Venus*, and therefore if *Mars* causes the colic or stone, as he usually does if in *Virgo*, this is your cure.

<margin>*Stone, gravel, strangury, labor in women.*</margin>
These are accounted to be of as remarkable a force as any other herb or seed whatsoever to break the stone and to expel it and the gravel, either in the reins <note>kidneys</note> or bladder; as also to provoke urine when it is stopped and to help the strangury. The seed is of greatest use, being bruised and boiled in white wine, or in broth, or the like, or the powder of the seed taken therein. Two drams of the seed in powder, taken with women's breast milk, is very effective for procuring a speedy delivery for such women as have severe pains in their labor and cannot be delivered. The herb itself (when the seed is not to be had), either boiled or its juice drunk, is effective for all the purposes aforesaid, but not so powerful or speedy in operation.

# Gooseberry Bush.

Called also Feapberry, and in *Sussex* Dewberry Bush, and in some countries Wine-berries.

<margin>*Appetite, stomach, women's longings, swellings, inflammations, St. Anthony's fire, stomach, liver, stone, gravel, worms.*</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] They are under the dominion of *Venus*. The berries, while they are unripe, being scalded or baked, are good to stir up a fainting or decaying appetite, especially for those whose stomachs are afflicted by choleric humors. They are excellently good to stay the longings of pregnant women; they may easily be kept preserved with sugar all the year long. The decoction of the leaves of the tree cools hot swellings and inflammations, as also St. Anthony's fire <note>a skin infection, likely erysipelas</note>. When eaten, ripe gooseberries are an excellent remedy to allay the violent heat of both the stomach and liver. The young and tender leaves break the stone and expel gravel from both the kidneys and bladder. All the harm they do to the body of man is that they are supposed to breed crudities <note>indigestion or undigested matter</note>, and by crudities, worms.

# Wintergreen.

*Description.*] This sends forth seven, eight, or nine leaves from a small, brownish, creeping root, every one standing upon a long footstalk. These are almost as broad as long, round-pointed, of a dark green color, and hard to the touch, similar to the leaf of a pear tree. From there arises a slender, weak stalk, yet standing upright, bearing at the top many small, white, and sweet-smelling flowers, laid open like a star, consisting of five round-pointed leaves with many yellowish threads standing in the middle around a green head and a long style with them. In time, this grows to be the seed vessel, which when ripe is found to be five-sided with a small point on it, wherein is contained seed as small as dust.

*Place.*] It grows seldom in the fields, but frequently in the woods northwards, *namely* in *Yorkshire*, *Lancashire*, and *Scotland*.

*Time.*] It flowers about *June* or *July*.

<margin>*Wounds, ulcers, kidneys, bladder, flux, bloody flux, menstruation, stops, inflammations.*</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] Wintergreen is under the dominion of *Saturn* and is a singularly good wound herb and a special remedy for healing green <note>fresh</note> wounds speedily, the green leaves being bruised and applied, or the juice of them. A salve made of the green herbs crushed, or the juice boiled with hog's lard, or with salad oil and wax, and some turpentine added to it, is a sovereign salve and highly extolled by the Germans, who use it much to heal all manner of wounds and sores. The herb boiled in wine and water and given to drink to those who have any inward ulcers in their kidneys or the neck of the bladder helps them wonderfully. It also stays all fluxes, whether of blood or humors, such as the lask <note>diarrhea</note>, bloody flux <note>dysentery</note>, women's courses, and the bleeding of wounds; it also takes away any inflammation

# Groundsel.

*Description.*] **O** *ur common groundsel has a round, green, and somewhat brownish stalk, spread toward the top into branches, set with long, and somewhat narrow green leaves cut in on the edges, somewhat like the oak leaves, but smaller, and round at the ends; at the tops of the branches stand many small green heads, out of which grow small yellow threads or thrums, which are the flowers, and continue many days in bloom in that manner before it passes away into down, and with the seed is carried away in the wind. The root is small and fibrous, and soon perishes, and as soon rises again of its own sowing, so that it may be seen many months in the year, both green, and in flower, and seed, for it will spring and seed twice in a year at least if it is allowed in a garden.*

*Place.*] This grows almost everywhere, as well on the tops of walls, as at the foot among rubbish, and untilled grounds, but especially in gardens.

*Time.*] It flowers as is said before, almost in every month through the year.

## Heart’s-ease.

This is that herb which such physicians as are licensed to blaspheme by authority without danger, having their tongues bored through with a hot iron, call an Herb of the Trinity; it is also called by those that are more moderate, Three Faces in a Hood, Love-in-Idleness, Cull-me-to-you; and in *Sussex* we call them Pansies.

*Place.]* Besides those which are brought up in gardens, they grow commonly wild in the field, especially in such as are very barren; sometimes you may find it on the tops of high hills.

*Time.]* They flower all the spring and summer long.

<margin>*French pox <note>syphilis</note>, convulsions, falling-sickness <note>epilepsy</note>, inflammations in the breast and lungs, pleurisy, scabs, itch.*</margin>
*Government and Virtues.]* The herb is really Saturnine, something cold, viscous, and slimy. A strong decoction of the herbs and flowers (if you will, you may make it into a syrup, or distilled in an alembic <note>a chemical distilling apparatus</note> with whatever vehicle you please) is an excellent cure for the French pox <note>syphilis</note>, the herb being a gallant anti-venereal; and that anti-venereals are the best cure for that disease—far better and safer than to torment them with the flux <note>salivation induced by mercury</note>—several foreign physicians have confessed. The spirit of it is excellently good for convulsions in children, as also for the falling-sickness <note>epilepsy</note>, and a gallant remedy for inflammations of the lungs and breast, pleurisy, scabs, itch, etc. It is under the celestial sign *Cancer*.

## Artichokes.

The Latins call them *Cinera*, only our College <note>The College of Physicians</note> calls them *Artichokus*.

<margin>*Lust provoked, nocturnal emissions, purges.*</margin>
*Government and Virtues.]* They are under the dominion of *Venus*, and therefore it is no marvel if they provoke lust much—indeed they do, being a somewhat windy meat—and yet they stay the involuntary course of natural seed in man, which is commonly called nocturnal emissions. And here I care not greatly if I quote a little of Galen’s nonsense in his treatise of the *Faculties of Nourishments*; he says they contain plenty of choleric <note>relating to yellow bile, one of the four humors</note>...

## Hart’s-Tongue.

<margin>

*Descript.*] **T**his has several leaves rising from the root, each one individually, which fold themselves in their first springing and spreading; when they are full grown, they are about a foot long, smooth and green above, but hard and with little sap in them, and streaked on the back across both sides of the middle rib with small and somewhat long brownish marks; the bottoms of the leaves are a little bowed on each side of the middle rib, somewhat narrow along the length, and somewhat small at the end. *Time.*] It is green all the winter, but new leaves spring every year.

*Government and Virtues.*] *Jupiter* claims dominion over this herb; therefore, it is a singular remedy for the liver, both to strengthen it when weak and ease it when afflicted—it does not matter by what. You would do well to keep it in a syrup all year; for though authors say it is green all year, I scarcely believe it. Hart’s-tongue is much commended against the hardness and blockages of the spleen and liver, and against the heat of the liver and stomach, and against lasks <note>diarrhea</note> and the bloody flux <note>dysentery</note>. The distilled water thereof is also very good against the passions of the heart, and to stop the hiccough, to help the falling of the palate, and to stop the bleeding of the gums when gargled in the mouth. *Dioscorides* says it is good against the stinging or biting of serpents.

As for its use, my directions at the end will be sufficient, and enough for those who are studious in medicine to whet their brains upon for a year or two.

## Hawkweed.

*Descript.*] It has many large leaves lying on the ground, much rent or torn on the sides into many gashes like a dandelion, but with larger parts more like the smooth sow-thistle. From among these arises a hollow, rough stalk two or three feet high, branched from the middle upward, where longer leaves are set at every joint, which are little or not at all rent or cut. It bears at the top various pale yellow flowers consisting of many small, narrow leaves, broad-pointed and notched at the ends, set in a double row or more; the outermost are larger than the inner ones. This form most hawkweeds (for there are many kinds of them) maintain. These turn into down, and along with the small brownish seeds, are blown away with the wind. The root is long and somewhat large, with many small fibers. The whole plant is full of bitter milk.

*Place.*] It grows in various places around field sides and the pathways in dry grounds.

*Time.*] It flowers and flies away in the summer months.

*Government and Vertues.*] Saturn owns it. Hawkweed (says *Dioscorides*) is cooling, somewhat drying and binding, and therefore good for the heat of the stomach and gnawing pains therein, for inflammations, and the hot fits of agues. The juice thereof in wine helps digestion, disperses wind, hinders crudities <note>undigested matter</note> from remaining in the stomach, and helps the difficulty of urinating, the biting of venomous serpents, and the sting of the scorpion, if the herb is also outwardly applied to the place; it is also very good against all other poisons. A scruple <note>a small unit of weight</note> of the dried juice given in wine and vinegar is profitable for those that have dropsy <note>swelling caused by fluid retention</note>. The decoction of the herb taken with honey digests thin phlegm in the chest or lungs, and with hyssop helps the cough. ## The Hawthorn.

It is not my intent to trouble you with a description of this tree, which is so well known that it needs none.

It is ordinarily just a hedge bush, although being pruned and dressed, it grows to be a tree of a reasonable height.

As for the Hawthorn tree at Glastonbury, which is said to flower yearly on *Christmas Day*, it rather shows the superstition of those who observe it for the time of its flowering than any great wonder, since the like may be found in various other places of this land; as in Whey-street in Romney Marsh, and near unto Namptwich in Cheshire by a place called White Green, where if the winter be mild, they will have white blossoms all over before and about *Christmas*; just as in *May*, if the weather be frosty, it flowers not until *January*, or until the hard weather is over.

<margin>Stone, dropsy, flux, inward pains, splinters, thorns.</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] It is a tree of *Mars*. The berries, or the seeds in the berries beaten to powder and drunk in wine, are held singularly good against the stone <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>, and are good for the dropsy. The distilled water of the flowers stops the lask <note>diarrhea</note>. The seeds, cleared from the down, bruised and boiled in wine and drunk, are good for inward tormenting pains. If cloths and sponges are wet in the said distilled water and applied to any place where thorns, splinters, or the like remain in the flesh, it will notably draw them out.

And thus you see the thorn gives a medicine for its own pricking, and so does almost everything else.

## Hemlock.

<margin>*Descript.*]</margin> The common great hemlock grows up with a green stalk, four or five feet high or more, full of red spots sometimes, and at the joints very large winged leaves are set, which are divided into many other winged leaves, set one against another and dented about the edges, of a dark green color. It is branched towards the top where it is full of umbels <note>flat-topped flower clusters</note> of white flowers, and afterwards with whitish flat seed. The root is long, white, and sometimes crooked and hollow within; the whole plant and every part has a strong, heady, and ill-savored scent, which greatly offends the senses.

*Place.*] It grows in all parts of this land by walls and hedge sides, in waste grounds and untilled places.

If the root of it is roasted under the embers, wrapped in double wet papers until it is soft and tender, and then applied to the gout in the hands or fingers, it will quickly help this ailment. If anyone should by mistake eat the herb hemlock instead of parsley, or the root instead of a parsnip (both of which it closely resembles), whereby happens a kind of frenzy or disturbance of the senses as if they were stupefied or drunk, the remedy is, as *Pliny* says, to drink of the best and strongest pure wine before it strikes the heart, or gentian put into wine, or a draught of good vinegar, with which *Tragus* affirms that he cured a woman who had eaten the root.

# Henbane.

<margin>Descript.]</margin>
Our common Henbane has very large, thick, soft, woolly leaves lying upon the ground, much cut in or torn on the edges, of a dark, sickly grayish-green color; among which rise up various thick and short stalks two or three feet high, spread into various smaller branches with lesser leaves on them, and many hollow flowers scarcely appearing above the husks, and usually torn on one side, ending in five round points growing one above another, of a dull yellow color, somewhat paler toward the edges, with many purplish veins therein, and of a dark yellowish purple at the bottom of the flower, with a small pointel <note>pistil</note> of the same color in the middle, each of them standing in a hard close husk, which after the flower is past, grows very like the husk of <term>Asarabacca</term>, and somewhat sharp at the top points, wherein is contained much small seed very like poppy seed, but of a dusky grayish color. The root is great, white, and thick, branching forth various ways underground, so like a parsnip root (except that it is not so white) that it has deceived many. The whole plant, more than the root, has a heavy, unpleasant, sleep-inducing smell that is somewhat offensive.

<margin>Place.]</margin>
It commonly grows by the waysides, and under hedge sides and walls.

<margin>Time.]</margin>
It flowers in *July*, and springs again yearly from its own seed. I suspect my authors mistook *July* for *June*, if not for *May*.

<margin>Government and Virtues.]</margin>
I wonder in my heart how astrologers could take it upon themselves to make this an herb of *Jupiter*, and yet *Mizaldus*, a man of a penetrating brain, was also of that opinion as well as the rest; the herb is indeed under the dominion of *Saturn*, and I prove it by this argument:

All the herbs which delight most to grow in Saturnine places, are Saturnine herbs.

## Black Hellebore.

It is also called Setter-wort, Setter-grass, Bear's-foot, Christmas Herb, and Christmas Flower.

*Description.*] It has various beautiful green leaves rising from the root, each of them standing about a handful high from the earth. Each leaf is divided into seven, eight, or nine parts, indented from the middle of the leaf to the point on both sides, staying green all winter. About Christmas time, if the weather is at all temperate, the flowers appear upon footstalks, also consisting of five large, round, white leaves each, which sometimes are purple toward the edges, with many pale yellow threads <note>thrums</note> in the middle. The seeds are divided into several cells like those of columbines, except they are larger; the seeds are black in color and long and round in form. The root consists of a countless number of blackish strings, all united into one head.

There is another black Hellebore which grows here and there in the woods very much like this one, except that the leaves are smaller and narrower and die in the winter, whereas this one does not.

*Place.*] The first is kept in gardens; the second is commonly found in the woods in *Northamptonshire*.

*Time.*] The first flowers in *December* or *January*; the second in *February* or *March*.

<margin>Melancholy, quartan agues, madness, falling sickness, leprosy,</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] It is an herb of *Saturn*, and therefore it is no wonder if it has some sullen qualities, and it would be far safer if purified by the art of the alchemist than if given raw. If anyone has come to harm by taking it, the common cure is to take goat's milk; if you cannot get goat's milk, you must make do with such as you can get. The roots are very effective against all melancholy diseases, especially those of long standing, such as quartan agues and madness. It helps the falling sickness <note>epilepsy</note> and leprosy; both the yellow and the

# Herb Robert.

*Description.*] This rises up with a reddish stalk two feet high, having various leaves on it upon very long and reddish footstalks, divided at the ends into three or five divisions, each of them cut in on the edges, some deeper than others, and all dented likewise about the edges, which often turn reddish. At the tops of the stalk come forth various flowers made of five petals <note>leaves</note>, much larger than the Dove's-foot, and of a more reddish color, after which come beak-heads as in others. The root is small and thready, and the whole plant smells very strong, almost stinking.

*Place.*] This grows frequently everywhere by waysides, upon ditch banks, and waste grounds wherever one goes.

*Time.*] It flowers chiefly in June and July, and the seed is ripe shortly after.

<margin>Stone, bleeding, stops menstrual flow, wounds, ulcers in the private parts.</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] It is under the dominion of Venus. Herb Robert is commended not only against the stone, but to stop bleeding <note>stay blood</note>, wherever or however it is flowing. It speedily heals all green wounds and is effective in old ulcers in the private parts or elsewhere. You may persuade yourself this is true, and also conceive a good reason for it, if you only consider it is an herb of Venus, even though it has a man's name.

# Herb Truelove, or Oneberry.

The whole plant is without any manifest taste.

The roots in powder taken in wine ease the pains of the colic speedily. The leaves or the juice applied to whitlows <note>felons</note>, or those nails of the hands or toes that have abscesses <note>imposthumes</note> or sores gathered at their roots, heals them in a short time.

The herb is not to be described only for the reasons mentioned above, but is fit to be nurtured in every good woman's garden.

These are so well known that they need no description—I mean the cultivated kind, with which every good husband or housewife is acquainted.
*The wild hop grows up as the other does, climbing upon trees or hedges that stand next to them, with rough branches and leaves like the former; but it produces smaller heads, and in far less plenty than the cultivated kind, so that there is scarcely a head or two seen in a year on various plants of this wild kind, which is the chief difference.*
Place.] They delight to grow on low moist grounds, and are found in all parts of this land.

# Horehound.

# Horse-Tail.

<margin>Description]</margin> **O**f this there are many kinds, but I shall not trouble you nor myself with any large description of them, which to do, would be but as the proverb is, *To find a knot in a rush*: All the kinds hereof being nothing else but knotted rushes, some with leaves, and some without: Take the description of the most eminent sort as follows:

The great *horse-tail* at the first springing has heads somewhat like those of asparagus, and after they grow to be hard, rough, hollow stalks, jointed at various places up to the top, a foot high, so made as if the lower part were put into the upper, whereat grow on each side a bush of small, long, rush-like hard leaves, each part resembling a horse's tail (from whence it was so called). At the tops of the stalks come forth small catkins like those of trees. The root creeps underground, having joints at various places.

<margin>Place]</margin> This (as most of the other sorts hereof) grows in wet grounds.

<margin>Time]</margin> They spring up in *April*, and their blooming catkins in *July*, seeding for the most part in *August*, and then perish down to the ground, rising afresh in the spring.

## Houseleeks, or Sengreen.

Both these are so well known to my countrymen that I shall not need to write any description of them.

**Place.]** It grows commonly on walls and house-sides, and flowers in *July*.

<margin>Heat, eyes, agues, thirst, salt rheums, ears, stops menstrual terms, fluxes, inflammations, St. Anthony's fire, burns, scalds, tetters, ringworms, corns on the hands and feet, headache, frenzy, insomnia, bleeding, nettles, bees, etc.</margin>
**Government and Virtues.]** It is an herb of *Jupiter*, and it is reported by *Mizaldus* to preserve what it grows upon from fire and lightning. Our ordinary Houseleek is good for all inward heats as well as outward, in the eyes or other parts of the body. A posset made with the juice of Houseleek is singularly good in all hot agues <note>fevers</note>, for it cools and tempers the blood and spirits, and quenches the thirst; it is also good to stay all hot defluxions of sharp and salt rheums in the eyes, the juice being dropped into them; or dropped into the ears, it helps them. It also helps other fluxes of humors into the bowels, and the immoderate courses <note>menstrual periods</note> of women. It cools and restrains also all other hot inflammations, St. Anthony's fire <note>erysipelas, a skin infection</note>, scaldings and burnings, the shingles, fretting ulcers, cancers, tetters, ringworms, and the like; and much eases the pain of the gout proceeding from a hot cause. The juice also takes away warts and corns in the hands or feet, if they are often bathed with it and the skin of the leaves is laid on them afterwards. It also eases the headache and distempered heat of the brain in frenzy, watching <note>insomnia or wakefulness</note>, frenzies, or through want of sleep, being applied to the temples and forehead. The leaves bruised and laid upon the crown or seam of the head stay bleeding at the nose very quickly. The distilled water of the herb is profitable for all the purposes aforesaid. The leaves being gently rubbed on any place stung with nettles or bees, quickly take away the pain.

# St. Johns-wort.

**Descript.]** The common *Saint John's Wort* shoots forth brownish, upright, hard, round stalks, two feet high, spreading many branches from the sides up to the tops of them, with two small leaves set opposite one another at every point, which are of a deep green color, somewhat like the leaves of the <term>lesser Centaury</term>, but narrower and full of small holes in every leaf, which cannot be as well perceived except when they are held up to the light. At the tops of the stalks and branches stand yellow flowers made of five leaves apiece, with many yellow threads in the middle, which, when bruised, yield a reddish juice like blood; after these come small round heads wherein is contained small blackish seed smelling like resin <note>Rozin</note>. The root is hard and woody, with various strings and fibers at it, and of a brownish color, which remains in the ground many years, shooting anew every spring.

**Place.]** This grows in woods and copses, as well as those that are shady as those open to the sun.

**Time.]** They flower about Midsummer and in *July*, and their seed is ripe in the latter end of *July* or *August*.

<margin>Wounds, bruises, obstructions, swellings, spitting and vomiting blood, venomous beasts, dysuria, choler, agues, sciatica, falling-sickness, palsy.</margin>
**Government and Vertues.]** It is under the celestial sign *Leo* and under the dominion of the *Sun*. It may be if you meet with a Papist that is an astrologer, he will tell you *Saint John* made it over to him by a power of attorney <note>Letter of Atturny</note>, especially if he also happens to be a lawyer. *Saint John's Wort* is as singular a wound-herb as any other whatsoever, whether for inward wounds, hurts, or bruises, to be boiled in wine and drunk, or prepared into oil or ointment, bath or lotion, outwardly. It has power to open obstructions, to dissolve swellings, to close up the edges of wounds, and to strengthen the parts that are weak and feeble. The decoction of the herb and flowers, but of the seed especially in wine, being drunk; or the seed made into powder and drunk with the juice of <term>Knotgrass</term>, helps all manner of spitting and vomiting of blood, whether it be by any vein broken inwardly, by bruises, falls, or otherwise. The same helps those who are bitten or stung by any venomous creature; and is good for those who are troubled with the stone in their kidneys or who cannot urinate <note>make Water</note>; and being applied, it provokes women's courses <note>menstruation</note>. Two drams of the seed of *Saint John's Wort* made into powder and drunk in a little broth gently expels choler <note>yellow bile</note> or congealed blood in the stomach. The decoction of the leaves and seeds being drunk somewhat warm before the fits of agues <note>fevers</note>, whether they be *tertians* or *quartans*, alters the fits and

## Ivy.

**Descript.]** IT is so well known to almost every child to grow in woods upon the trees, and upon the stone walls of churches, houses, etc., and sometimes to grow alone by itself, though but seldom.

**Time.]** It flowers not until *July*, and the berries are not ripe until Christmastide, after they have felt the winter frosts.

<margin>

**Government and Vertues.]** It is under the dominion of **Saturn**. A <term>pugil</term> <note>a pinch of material held between the thumb and two fingers</note> of the flowers, which may be about a dram (says *Dioscorides*) drunk twice a day in red wine, helps diarrhea <note>the lask</note> and bloody flux. It is an enemy to the nerves and sinews when much taken internally, but very helpful to them being outwardly applied. *Pliny* says that the yellow berries are good against the jaundice, and taken before one is set to drink hard, preserves from drunkenness and helps those that spit blood; and that the white berries, being taken internally or applied externally, kill the worms in the belly. The berries are a singular remedy to prevent the plague, as also to free those from it who have caught it, by drinking the berries thereof made into powder for two or three days together. They being taken in wine, certainly help to break the stone, provoke urine, and women's courses <note>menstruation</note>. The fresh leaves of *Ivy* boiled in vinegar and applied warm to the sides of those that are troubled with the spleen, ache, or stitch in the sides, gives them much ease; the same applied with some rosewater and oil of roses to the temples and forehead eases the headache, even if it be of long continuance. The fresh leaves boiled in wine, and used to wash old filthy ulcers that are hard to be cured, wonderfully help to cleanse and heal them. It also quickly heals green wounds, and is effective to heal all burnings and scaldings, and all kind of ulcerations coming thereby, or by salt phlegm or hot humors in other parts of the body. The juice of the berries or leaves snuffed up into the nose purges the head and brain of thin rheum that causes discharges <note>defluxions</note> into the eyes and nose, and cures the ulcers and stench therein; the same dropped into the ears helps the old and running sores in them. Those that are troubled with the spleen shall find much ease by continual drinking out of a cup made of *Ivy*, provided the drink stands some small time in it before it is drunk. *Cato* says that wine put into such a cup will soak through it, by reason of the antipathy that is between them.

There seems to be a very great antipathy between wine and ivy, for if any have got a surfeit <note>illness from overindulgence</note> by drinking wine, his speediest cure is to drink a draught of the same wine wherein a handful of ivy leaves, being first bruised, have been boiled.

# Juniper-Bush.

TO give a description of a bush so commonly known is needless.
*Place.*] They grow plentifully in various woods in *Kent*, upon *Warley* Common <note>Warny-Common</note> near *Brentwood* in *Essex*, upon *Finchley* Common outside *Highgate*, close by the *New-found-wells* near *Dulwich*, upon a common between *Mitcham* and *Croydon*, on the highway near *Amersham* in *Buckinghamshire*, and in many other places.
*Time.*] The berries are not ripe the first year, but continue green for two summers and one winter before they are ripe; at which time they are of a black color, and therefore you shall always find green berries upon the bushes: the berries are ripe about the fall of the leaf.

<margin>
Counter-poison,
Pestilence, Venomous beasts,
Provokes urine,
Dysuria, Strangury, Dropsy,
Provokes terms, Fits of the mother,
Stomach, Expels wind, Colic,
Cough, shortness of breath, Consumption, pains in the belly, ruptures, Cramps, Convulsions,
Speedy delivery to women, brain, Memory, Sight,
Agues, Gout, Sciatica, Strengthens limbs,
Scurvy, Fluxes, Hemorrhoids, Piles,
Worms, Itch, Scab, Leprosy, Stone, Provokes appetite, Palsies, Falling-sickness.
</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] This admirable *Solar* shrub is scarcely to be paralleled for its virtues. The berries are hot in the third degree and dry only in the first: being a most admirable counter-poison, and as great a resister of the pestilence as any that grows; they are excellent against the bitings of venomous beasts, they provoke urine exceedingly, and therefore are very available for dysuria <note>painful urination</note> and strangury: it is so powerful a remedy against the dropsy that the very lye made of the ashes of the herb being drunk cures the disease: it provokes the terms <note>menstruation</note>, helps the fits of the mother <note>hysteria</note>, strengthens the stomach exceedingly, and expels wind: indeed, there is scarcely a better remedy for wind in any part of the body, or to expel the colic, than the chemical oil drawn from the berries: such country people as do not know how to draw the chemical oil may content themselves by eating ten or a dozen of the ripe berries every morning fasting. They are admirably good for the cough, shortness of breath, and consumption, pains in the belly, ruptures, cramps, and convulsions: They give safe and speedy delivery to women with child, they strengthen the brain, exceedingly help the memory, and fortify the sight by strengthening the optic nerves: They are excellent in all sorts of agues, they help the gout and sciatica, and strengthen all the limbs of the body: The ashes of the wood are a special remedy for those who have the scurvy to rub their gums with: the berries stay all fluxes, help the hemorrhoids or piles, and kill worms in children: A lye made of the ashes of the wood, when the body is bathed with it, cures the itch, scabs, and leprosy: The berries break the stone, provoke appetite when it is lost, and are excellent for palsies and falling-sickness <note>epilepsy</note>.

# Kidney-wort, or Wall-Pennyroyal,
## Or Wall Pennywort.

<margin>Description.]</margin>
It has many thick, flat, and round leaves growing from the root, every one having a long footstalk fastened underneath about the middle of it, and a little unevenly waved sometimes about the edges, of a pale green color, and somewhat hollow on the upper side like a saucer; from among which rise one or more tender smooth hollow stalks half a foot high, with two or three small leaves thereon, usually not round as those below, but somewhat long and divided at the edges: The tops are sometimes divided into long branches, bearing a number of flowers, set round about a long spike one above another, which are hollow and like a little bell, of a whitish-green color, after which come small heads containing very small brownish seed, which falling on the ground, will plentifully spring up before winter, if it has moisture. The root is round, and most usually smooth, grayish without and white within, having small fibers at the head of the root, and bottom of the stalk.

<margin>Place.]</margin>
It grows very plentifully in many places of this land, but especially in all the West parts thereof, upon stone and mud walls, upon rocks also, and in stony places upon the ground, at the bottom of old trees, and sometimes on the bodies of those that are decayed and rotten.

<margin>Time.]</margin>
It usually flowers in the beginning of *May*, and the seed, ripening quickly after, sheds itself: so that about the end of *May* usually the leaves and stalks are withered, dry, and gone until *September*, when the leaves spring up again, and so abide all winter.

<margin>Government and Virtues.]</margin>
*Venus* claims the herb under *Libra*.

<margin>Inflammations, pimples, redness, St. Anthony's fire, kidneys, hurt by the stone, dysuria, stone, bloody flux, piles, hemorrhoids, gout, sciatica, scrotum, King's Evil, kibes, chilblains.</margin>
The juice or the distilled water being drunk is very effectual for all inflammations and unnatural heats, to cool a fainting hot stomach, or a hot liver, or the bowels: The bruised herb, or the place bathed with the juice or distilled water thereof, and outwardly applied, heals pimples, redness, St. Anthony's fire <note>erysipelas</note>, and other outward heats and inflammations. The said juice or water also helps much to heal sore kidneys, torn or chafed by the stone, or ulcerated within, and eases the pains; it also provokes urine, and is available for the dropsy, and helps to break the stone, cooling the inflamed parts and other pains of the bowels, and the bloody flux <note>dysentery</note>; it is singularly good to cool the painful piles, or hemorrhoidal veins, the juice being used as a bath for them, or made into an ointment: it is no less effectual to give ease of pains to the hot gout, the sciatica, and the inflammations and swellings in the scrotum <note>cods</note>; it helps the kernels or knots in the neck or throat, called the King's Evil <note>scrofula</note>; it heals kibes <note>ulcerated chilblains</note> and chilblains if they be bathed with the juice, or anointed with an ointment made thereof, and some of the skin of the leaf laid upon them; it is also used in green wounds to stay the blood, and to heal them quickly.

# Knapweed.

*Description.]* The common sort of this has many long and somewhat broad dark green leaves, rising from the root deeply dented about the edges, and sometimes a little rent or torn on both sides in two or three places, and somewhat hairy withal; among which rises up a strong round stalk four or five feet high, divided into many branches; at the tops of which stand great scaly green heads, and from the middle of them thrust forth a number of dark purplish red thrums or threads, which after they are withered and past, there are found various black seeds, lying in a great deal of down, somewhat like a thistle seed, but smaller: The root is white, hard, and woody, with various fibers attached to it, which does not perish but abides with leaves on it all the winter, shooting out fresh every spring.

*Place.]* It grows in most fields and meadows, and about their borders and hedges, and in many waste grounds also, almost everywhere.

*Time.]* It usually flowers in *June* and *July*, and the seed is ripe shortly after.

<margin>*Fluxes, bleeding, broken veins, phthisic, falls, blows, ruptures, sores, cancers, fistulas, scabby head, sore throat, uvula, jaws.*</margin>
*Government and Virtues.]* Saturn claims the herb for his own. This knapweed helps to stay fluxes, both of blood at the mouth or nose, or other outward parts, and those veins that are inwardly broken, or inward wounds, as also the fluxes of the belly; it stays the distillations of thin and sharp humors from the head upon the stomach and lungs: it is good for those that are bruised by any fall, blows, or otherwise. It is very profitable for those that are ruptured and have a hernia, by drinking the decoction of the herb and roots in wine, and applying the same outwardly to the place: It is singularly good in all running sores, cancerous and fistulous, drying up the moisture and healing them up gently, without sharpness; it does the same to running sores or scabs of the head or other parts. It is of special use for the soreness of the throat, swelling of the uvula and jaws; and excellently good to stay bleeding and heal up all green wounds.

It is generally so well known that it needs no description.

*Place.]* It grows in every country of this land, by the highway sides, and by footpaths in fields, as also by the sides of old walls.

*Time.]* It springs up late in the spring, and abides until winter, when all the branches perish.

<margin>*Bleeding, heat, flux.*</margin>
*Government and Virtues.]* Saturn seems to me to own the herb; and yet some hold the Sun; without doubt it is *Saturn*. The juice of the common kind of knot-grass is most effectual to stay bleeding at the mouth, being drunk in steeled or red wine: and the bleeding at the nose, to be applied to the forehead and temples,

# Ladies-Mantle.

<margin>Description.]</margin> It has many leaves rising from the root, standing upon long hairy leaf-stalks, being almost round, but a little cut in on the edges into eight or ten parts more or less, making it seem like a star with so many corners and points, and dented round about; it is of a light green color, somewhat hard to the touch, and as if it were folded or pleated at first and then crumpled in various places, and a little hairy like the stalk is also. The stalk rises up among them to the height of two or three feet with similar leaves upon it, but smaller; and being weak, it is not able to stand upright but bends down to the ground, divided at the top into two or three small branches with small yellowish-green heads and flowers of a whitish color breaking out of them. When these are past, there comes a small yellow seed like poppy seed. The root is somewhat long and black, with many strings or fibers attached to it.

<margin>Place.]</margin> It grows naturally in many pastures and wood sides in Hertfordshire, Wiltshire, and Kent, and other places of this land.

<margin>Time.]</margin> It flowers in May and June, and remains green all through the winter after seed time.

## Lavender.

It is so well known, being an inhabitant in almost every garden, that it needs no description.

***Time.***] It flowers about the end of June and the beginning of July.

It strengthens the stomach and frees the liver and spleen from obstructions, provokes women's courses <note>Menstrual cycles.</note>, and expels the dead child and afterbirth. The flowers of lavender steeped in wine help those to pass water who are blocked, or who are troubled with gas <note>Historically "the Wind".</note> or colic, if the affected areas are bathed with it. A decoction made with the flowers of lavender, horehound, fennel, and asparagus roots, and a little cinnamon, is very profitably used to help the falling-sickness and the giddiness or vertigo <note>Historically "turning of the Brain".</note>. Gargling the mouth with its decoction is good against toothache. Two spoonfuls of the distilled water of the flowers helps those who have lost their voice, as well as the tremblings and passions of the heart, and faintings and swoonings—not only when drunk, but also when applied to the temples or held to the nostrils to be smelled. However, it is not safe to use it when the body is overfull <note>Historically "replete".</note> with blood and humors, because of the hot and subtle spirits with which it is possessed. # Lavender Cotton.

Since it is a common garden herb, I shall omit the description, only noting that it flowers in *June* and *July*.

<margin>Poison, putrefaction, venomous beasts, running of the reins, whites in women, worms, scabs, itch.</margin>
***Government and Virtues.***] It is under the dominion of *Mercury*. It resists poison and putrefaction, and helps the bites of venomous beasts. A dram of the powder of the dried leaves taken every morning while fasting in any suitable vehicle <note>A substance used to administer a medicine.</note>, stops the running of the reins <note>A discharge, often associated with gonorrhea.</note> in men, and the whites <note>Leukorrhea.</note> in women. The seed being beaten into powder and taken like wormseed, it kills worms, not only in children, but also in people of older years; the same is done by the herb itself being boiled in milk and the milk drunk. The body bathed with the decoction of it helps scabs and itch.

# Ladies-Smocks, or Cuckoo-Flowers.

***Description.***] The root is composed of many small white threads, from which spring several long stalks of winged leaves consisting of many round, tender, dark green leaves set opposite one another on a middle rib, the largest being at the ends. Among these rise up several tender, weak, round green stalks, somewhat streaked, with longer and smaller leaves upon them; on the tops of these stand flowers almost like stock-gilliflowers, but rounder and not so long, of a blushing white color. The seed is reddish and grows in small pouches, having a sharp, biting taste, as does the herb itself.

***Place.***] They grow in moist places and near brook sides.

***Time.***] They flower in *April* or *May*, and the lower leaves remain green all winter.

<margin>Scurvy, provokes urine, stone, stomach, lost appetite, indigestion.</margin>
***Government and Virtues.***] They are under the dominion of the *Moon*, and are very little inferior to watercresses in all their operations. They are excellent for the scurvy; they provoke urine and break the stone <note>Kidney or bladder stones.</note>, and excellently warm a cold and weak stomach, restoring lost appetite and helping digestion.

## The Water-Lily.

<margin>*Description*]</margin>
Of these there are two principally noted kinds, namely, the *white* and the *yellow*.

<margin>*Description*]</margin>

<margin>*Place*]</margin>
They are found growing in great pools and standing waters, and sometimes in slow-running rivers and smaller ditches of water in various places across this land.

<margin>*Time*]</margin>
They flower most commonly about the end of *May*, and their seed is ripe in *August*.

*Government and Virtues.*]
*Inflammations,
Agues,*
</margin>

## Lily of the Valley.

Called also Conval-Lily, May-Lilies, and Lily-Constancy.
*Descript.*] The root is small and creeps far in the ground as grass roots do; the leaves are many, among which arises up a stalk half a foot high, with many white flowers like little bells, with turned edges, of a strong though pleasing smell; the berries are red, not much unlike those of asparagus.
*Place.*] They grow plentifully upon Hampstead Heath, and in many other places in this nation.
*Time.*] They flower in May, and the seed is ripe in September.
<margin>Brain, Memory, inflammations in the eyes, pin and web, lost speech, Palsy, Apoplexy, Heart, Vital Spirits, Gout.</margin> *Government and Virtues.*] It is under the dominion of *Mercury*, and therefore there is no question to be made but it strengthens the brain, recruits a weak memory, and makes it strong again. ### Liquorice.

**Description.]** *Our English liquorice rises up with various woody stalks, whereon are set at several distances many narrow, long, green leaves, set together on both sides of the stalk and an odd one at the end, very well resembling a young ash tree sprung up from the seed. This, by many years' continuance in a place without removing, and not otherwise, will bring forth flowers; many standing together in a spike fashion one above another upon the stalks, in the form of pea-blossoms but of a very pale blue color, which turn into long, somewhat flat, and smooth pods, wherein is contained small, round, hard seed. The root runs down exceedingly deep into the ground, with various other smaller roots and fibers growing with them, and shoots out suckers from the main roots all around, whereby it is much increased; it is of a brownish color on the outside and yellow within.*

**Place.]** It is planted in fields and gardens in various places of this land, and therefore good profit is made from it.

<margin>
Cough, hoarseness, phthisic, consumption, reins, strangury, heat of urine, eyes, bladder.
</margin>
**Government and Virtues.]** It is under the dominion of **Mercury**. Liquorice boiled in fresh water with some maidenhair and figs makes a good drink for those who have a dry cough or hoarseness, wheezing, shortness of breath, and for all the ailments of the breast and lungs, <term>phthisic</term> or consumptions caused by the distillation of salt humors on them. It is also good in all pains of the <term>reins</term> <note>kidneys</note>, the <term>strangury</term> <note>painful or difficult urination</note>, and heat of urine. The fine powder of liquorice blown through a quill into the eyes that have a <term>pin and web</term> <note>a film or cataract on the eye</note> (as they call it) or rheumatic distillations into them cleanses and helps them. The juice of liquorice is as effective in all the diseases of the breast and lungs, the reins and bladder, as the decoction. The juice dissolved in rose-water with some gum tragacanth is a fine licking medicine for hoarseness, wheezing, etc.

## Liver-wort.

**Description.**] The common Liver-wort grows close and spreads much upon the ground in moist and shadowy places, with many dark green leaves, or rather (as it were) sticking flat one to another, very unevenly cut in on the edges and crumpled; from among these arise small slender stalks an inch or two high at most, bearing small starlike flowers at the tops. The roots are very fine and small.

<margin>Liver, inflammation, yellow jaundice, spleen, running of the reins, whites, tetters, ringworms, surfeits.</margin>
**Government and Virtues.**] It is under the command of **Jupiter**, and under the sign **Cancer**. It is a singularly good herb for all the diseases of the liver, both to cool and cleanse it, and it helps inflammations in any part, as well as the yellow jaundice. Being bruised and boiled in small beer and drunk, it cools the heat of the liver and kidneys, and helps the <term>running of the reins</term> <note>a discharge from the urinary tract</note> in men, and the <term>whites</term> <note>leukorrhea or vaginal discharge</note> in women. It is a singular remedy to stay the spreading of <term>tetters</term> <note>various skin eruptions</note>, ringworms, and other fretting and running sores and scabs. It is an excellent remedy for those whose livers are corrupted by <term>surfeits</term> <note>excessive eating or drinking</note>, which causes their bodies to break out, for it fortifies the liver exceedingly and makes it impregnable.

## Loosestrife, or Willow-Herb.

**Description.**] The common yellow Loosestrife grows to be four or five feet high or more, with great round stalks a little ridged, diversely branched from the middle of them to the tops into great and long branches; on all of these at the joints there grow long and narrow leaves but broader below, and usually two at a joint, yet sometimes three or four, somewhat like willow leaves, smooth on the edges, and of a faint green color. From the upper joints of the branches, and at the tops of them also, stand many yellow flowers of five leaves apiece, with various yellow threads in the middle, which turn into small round heads containing small cornered seeds. The root creeps underground, almost like couch grass but larger, and shoots up every spring brownish heads which afterwards grow up into stalks. It has no scent nor taste but is only astringent.

**Place.**] It grows in many places of this land in moist meadows and by watersides.

**Time.**] It flowers from June to August.

<margin>Bleeding, flux, bloody flux, terms stops, wounds, sore mouth, privities, gnats.</margin>
**Government and Virtues.**] This herb is good for all manner of bleeding at the mouth or nose, or from wounds, and all <term>fluxes</term> <note>abnormal fluid discharges</note> of the belly and the <term>bloody flux</term> <note>dysentery</note>; given either to drink or taken by <term>clyster</term> <note>enema</note>, it also stays the abundance of <term>women's courses</term> <note>menstrual periods</note>. It is a singularly good wound-herb for <term>green wounds</term> <note>fresh or recent wounds</note> to stay the bleeding and quickly close together the lips of the wound, if the herb is bruised and the juice only applied. It is often used in gargles for sore mouths, as also for the secret
