# Loosestrife, with Spiked Heads of Flowers.

**Description.**] *This grows with many woody square stalks, full of joints, at least three feet high; at every joint stand two long leaves, shorter, narrower, and of a deeper green color than the former, and some brownish. The stalks are branched into many long stems of spiked flowers, half a foot long, growing in <term>rundles</term> <note>circles or clusters around a stem</note> one above another, out of small husks very like the spiked heads of lavender; each of these flowers has five round-pointed leaves of a purple-violet color, or somewhat inclining to redness. In these husks stand small round heads after the flowers have fallen, wherein is contained small seed. The root creeps underground like the yellow, but is larger than it; and so are the heads of the leaves when they first appear out of the ground, being more brown than the other.*

Place.] It grows usually by rivers and ditch-sides in wet grounds, as about the ditches at and near Lambeth, and in many other places of this land.

Time.] It flowers in the months of June and July.

<margin>Eyes, blindness, wounds, ulcers, inflammations, quinsy, King's Evil, spots, marks, scars.</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] The herb is an herb of the Moon, and under the sign Cancer. I do not know a better preserver of the sight when it is well, nor a better curer of sore eyes than eyebright taken inwardly and this used outwardly; it is cold in quality. This herb is not at all inferior to the former; it has not only all the virtues which the former has, but some particular virtues of its own found out by experience. Namely, the distilled water is a present remedy for hurts and blows on the eyes and for blindness, provided the <term>crystalline humor</term> <note>the lens of the eye</note> is not destroyed or hurt; and this has been sufficiently proved true by the experience of a man of judgment, who kept it long to himself as a great secret. It also clears the eyes of dust or any other thing gotten into them, and preserves the sight. It is also very helpful against wounds and thrusts, being made into an ointment in this manner: To every ounce of the water, add two drams of <term>May-butter</term> <note>unsalted butter made in May, traditionally used in medicinal ointments</note> without salt, and of sugar and wax an equal amount also; let them boil gently all together. Let <term>tents</term> <note>small plugs of lint or medical material used to keep a wound open or apply medicine</note> be dipped in the liquor that remains after it is cold and put into the wounds, and the place covered with a linen cloth doubled and anointed with the ointment; this is also an approved medicine. It likewise cleanses and heals all foul ulcers and sores wherever they may be, and stays their inflammations by washing them with the water and laying on them a green leaf or two in the summer, or dry leaves in the winter. This water gargled warm in the mouth, and sometimes drunk also, cures the <term>quinsy</term> <note>a peritonsillar abscess or severe throat inflammation</note> or <term>King's Evil</term> <note>scrofula, a form of tuberculosis of the neck lymph nodes</note> in the throat. The said water applied warm takes away all spots, marks, and scars in the skin. And a little of it drunk quenches thirst when it is extraordinary.

# Lovage.

**Description.**] It has many long and large stalks of large winged leaves divided into many parts like <term>Smallage</term> <note>Wild celery</note>, but much larger and greater, each leaf being cut about the edges, broadest toward the tip and smallest at the stalk, of a dark green color, smooth and shining; from among which rise up several strong hollow green stalks, five or six feet—yes, sometimes seven or eight feet high—full of joints, but with smaller leaves set on them than those that grow below; and with them toward the tops come forth long branches, bearing at their tops large <term>umbels</term> <note>clusters of flowers forming a flat or curved surface</note> of yellow flowers; and after them flat brownish seed. The root grows thick, large, and deep, spreading much and enduring long, of a brownish color on the outside and whitish within. The whole plant, and every part of it, smells strong and aromatically, and is of a hot, sharp, biting taste.

**Place.**] It is usually planted in gardens, where, if it is allowed, it grows huge and large.

**Time.**] It flowers in the end of *July*, and seeds in *August*.

<margin>
Humors, menstrual cycles, difficulty urinating, cold stomach, indigestion, wind, poison, epidemic diseases, agues, bellyache, quinsy, pleurisy, spots, freckles, boils.
</margin>
**Government and Virtues.**] It is an herb of the *Sun* under the sign *Taurus*; if *Saturn* offends the throat (as he always does, if he is the cause of the malady, and *Taurus* is in the <term>Genesis</term> <note>The birth chart</note>), this is your cure. It opens, cuts, and digests humors, and powerfully provokes women's menstrual cycles and urine. Half a dram at a time of the dried root in powder taken in wine wonderfully warms a cold stomach, helping digestion and consuming all raw and superfluous moisture therein; it eases all inward griping and pains, dissolves wind, and resists poison and infection. It is a known and much-practiced remedy to drink the decoction of the herb for any sort of ague, and to help the pains and torments of the body and bowels coming from cold. The seed is effective for all the purposes aforesaid (except the last) and works more powerfully. The distilled water of th<unclear>e herb</unclear> helps the quinsy in the throat, if the mouth and th<unclear>roat b</unclear>e gargled and washed with it, and helps pleurisy when drunk three or four times. Being dropped into the eyes, it takes away the redness or dimness of them; it likewise takes away spots or freckles from the face. The leaves bruised and fried with a little hog's lard, and applied hot to any botch or boil, will quickly break it.

# Madder.

**Description.]** *Garden Madder shoots forth many very long, weak, four-square, reddish stalks trailing on the ground a great way, very rough or hairy, and full of joints; at every one of those joints come forth several long and somewhat narrow leaves, standing like a star about the stalks, also rough and hairy, toward the tops of which come forth many small pale yellow flowers. After these come small round heads, green at first and reddish afterwards, but black when they are ripe, in which the seed is contained. The root is not very large, but exceedingly long, running down half a man's length into the ground, red and very clear while it is fresh, spreading in various ways.*

**Place.]** *It is only cultivated in gardens or larger fields for the profit that is made from it.*

**Time.]** *It flowers toward the end of summer, and the seed is ripe quickly after.*

**Government and Virtues.]** <margin>Yellow jaundice, obstructions of the liver and gall, spleen, melancholy, palsy, sciatica, bruises inward and outward, provokes menstrual cycles, freckles, morphew, scurf.</margin> It is an herb of *Mars*. It has an opening quality, and afterwards binds and strengthens. It is a reliable remedy for the yellow jaundice by opening the obstructions of the liver and gall and cleansing those parts. It also opens the obstructions of the spleen and diminishes the <term>melancholic</term> <note>one of the four humors, associated with sadness and the spleen</note> humor. It is available for <term>palsy</term> <note>paralysis or tremors</note> and <term>sciatica</term> <note>nerve pain in the leg</note>, and effective for bruises inward or outward, and is therefore much used in <term>vulnerary</term> <note>wound-healing</note> drinks. The root, for all those aforesaid purposes, is to be boiled in wine or water, as the cause requires, and some honey or sugar put into it afterward. Its seed taken with vinegar and honey helps the swellings and hardness of the spleen. The decoction of the leaves and branches is a good <term>fomentation</term> <note>a warm, medicated soak or compress</note> for women to sit over who do not have their <term>courses</term> <note>menstrual cycles</note>. The leaves and roots, beaten and applied to any part that is discolored with freckles, <term>morphew</term> <note>a skin disease causing scurfy eruptions</note>, white <term>scurf</term> <note>scales or flakes on the skin</note>, or any such deformity of the skin, cleanses them thoroughly and takes them away.

# Wall-Rue, or ordinary White Maidenhair.

**Description.]** This has very fine pale green stalks, almost as fine as hairs, set haphazardly with various pale green leaves on very short footstalks, somewhat near the color of Garden Rue and not much different in form, but more diversely cut on the edges and thicker, smooth on the upper part and finely spotted underneath.

**Place.]** It grows in many places of this land, such as at Dartford and the bridge at Ashford in Kent, at Beaconsfield in Buckinghamshire, at <unclear>Wipley</unclear> in Huntingdonshire, on Framlingham Castle in Suffolk, on the church walls at Mayfield in Sussex, in Somersetshire, and various other places of this land, and it is green in winter as well as in summer.

**Government and Virtues.]** Both this and the former are under the dominion of Mercury, as is also the one that follows; and the virtues of both these are so nearly alike that, although I have described them and their places of growth separately, I shall join them both together in writing their virtues as follows:

# Mallows, and Marsh-Mallows.

Common Mallows are generally so well known that they need no description.

*Our common Marsh-Mallows have various soft, grayish-white stalks rising to be three or four feet high, spreading forth many branches; the leaves are soft and hairy, somewhat smaller than the other mallow leaves, but with longer points; for the most part, they are cut into a few deep divisions. The flowers are numerous, but also smaller than the other mallows, and white or tending toward a blush color. After these come round cases and seeds similar to those in the other mallows. The roots are many and long, shooting from one head, about the thickness of a thumb or finger, very pliant, tough, and bending like liquorice; they are of a whitish-yellow color on the outside and whiter within, full of a slimy juice which, when laid in water, will thicken it as if it were jelly.*

**Place.]** Common Mallows grow in every county of this land.

The Common Marsh-Mallows grow in most of the salt marshes from Woolwich down to the sea, on both the Kentish and Essex shores, and in various other places of this land.

**Time.]** They flower during the summer months, even until the winter pulls them down.

**Government and Virtues.]** Venus owns them both. The leaves of either of the sorts specified before, and the roots also, boiled in wine or water, or in broth with parsley or fennel roots, help to open the body; and it is very convenient in hot agues or other distempers of the body to apply the leaves, boiled and warm, to the belly. It not only voids hot choleric and other offensive humors, but eases the pains and torments of the belly caused by them; they are therefore used in all clysters <note>enemas</note> serving those purposes. The decoction of the seed of any of the common mallows, made in milk or wine, marvelously helps excoriations, phthisis, pleurisy, and other diseases of the chest and lungs that proceed from hot causes, if it is taken continuously for some time. The leaves and roots produce the same effects. They also help much with excoriations of the guts and bowels, hardness of the "mother" <note>the uterus</note>, and in all hot and sharp

The green leaves (says *Pliny*), beaten with nitre <note>saltpeter</note> and applied, draw out thorns or pricks in the flesh.

The leaves are likewise used to loosen the belly gently, and in decoctions for clysters <note>enemas</note> to ease all pains of the body, opening the narrow passages and making them slippery, so that the stone may descend more easily and without pain from the reins <note>kidneys</note>, kidneys, and bladder, and to ease the torturing pains thereof. You may remember that not long since there was a raging disease called the bloody flux <note>dysentery</note>; the College of Physicians, not knowing what to make of it, called it "The Plague in the Guts," for their wits were at *ne plus ultra* <note>their furthest limit</note> about it. The only thing I gave him was mallows, bruised and boiled both in milk and drink; in two days (the blessing of God being upon it) it cured him, and I, here to show my thankfulness to God in communicating it to His creatures, leave it to posterity.

<margin>*Government and virtues.*</margin>

# Wild Marjoram.

Called also organ, origanum, bastard marjoram, wild marjoram, and grove marjoram.

<margin>*Description.*</margin>
Description.] Wild or field marjoram has a root which creeps much underground and continues for a long time, sending up various brownish, hard, square stalks with small dark green leaves very like those of sweet marjoram, but harder and somewhat broader. At the tops of the stalks stand tufts of flowers of a deep purplish red color; the seed is small and somewhat blacker than that of sweet marjoram.

## Marigolds.

These being so plentiful in every garden, they are so well known that they need no description.

<margin>Time.]</margin>
They flower all the summer long, and sometimes in winter if it be mild.

<margin>Government and Virtues.] Heart, vital spirits, pestilence, smallpox, measles, hot swellings, fevers, pestilence.</margin>
It is an herb of the Sun, and under *Leo*: They strengthen the heart exceedingly and are very expulsive, and little less effectual in the smallpox and measles than saffron. The juice of marigold leaves mixed with vinegar, when any hot swelling is bathed with it, instantly gives ease and assuages it. The flowers, either green or dried, are used much in smallpox, possets, broths, and drinks as a comforter of the heart and spirits, and to expel any malignant or pestilential quality which might annoy them. A plaster made with the dry flowers in powder, hog's grease, turpentine, and rosin, and applied to the breast, strengthens and succors the heart infinitely in fevers, whether pestilential or not pestilential.

## Masterwort.

<margin>Description.]</margin>
*Common masterwort has various stalks of winged leaves divided into several parts, usually three standing together at a small footstalk on both sides of the larger one, and three likewise at the end of the stalk, somewhat broad and cut in on the edges into three or more divisions, all of them dented about the brims; of a dark green color, somewhat resembling the leaves of Angelica, except that these grow lower to the ground and on smaller stalks; among which rise up two or three short stalks about two feet high and slender, with such leaves at the joints as grew below, but with smaller and fewer divisions, bearing umbels of white flowers, and after them small, thin, flat, blackish seed bigger than dill seeds: The root is somewhat larger and grows sideways rather than deep into the ground, shooting forth several heads, which taste sharp and bite the tongue, and is the hottest and sharpest part of the plant; the seed is next to it.*

# Melilot, or Kings-Claver.

# French, and Dogs Mercury.

<margin>Description.]</margin> This rises up with a square green stalk full of joints, two feet high or thereabouts, with two leaves at every joint, and branches likewise from both sides of the stalk, set with fresh green leaves somewhat broad and long, about the size of the leaves of basil, finely toothed about the edges: towards the tops of the stalks and branches, there come forth at every joint in the *Male Mercury* two small round green heads, standing together upon a short foot-stalk, which when ripe are the seeds, not having any flower: In the *Female*, the stalk is longer, in a spike fashion, set round about with small green husks, which are the flowers made like small bunches of grapes which give no seed, but stay long upon the stalks without shedding: The root is composed of many small fibers, which perishes every year at the first approach of winter, and rises again from its own sowing; and where it is once allowed to sow itself, the ground will never lack it afterwards, even both sorts of it.

## Mint.

<margin>Spearmint, near unto Basil;</margin>
*Description.*] Of all the kinds of mints, the spearmint, *or* heart-mint, *being most useful: I shall only describe it as follows:*

*Spearmint has several round stalks and long but narrowish leaves set on them, of a dark green color. The flowers stand in spiked heads at the tops of the branches, being of a pale blush color. The smell or scent of it is somewhat near to basil; it increases by the root underground, as all the others do.*

*Place.*] It is a common inhabitant in gardens; and because it seldom gives any good seed, the defect is compensated by the plentiful increase of the root, which being once planted in a garden, will hardly be gotten rid of again.

*Time.*] It does not flower until the beginning of *August*, for the most part.

<margin>
Provokes venery, stays vomiting, allays choler, abscesses, great breasts, mad dog bites, pains of the ears, good for the stomach, pains of the head, sores and scabs, cracks of the fundament <note>the anus</note>, liver and stomach, stops vomiting and hiccups, provokes lust,
</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] It is an herb of *Venus*. *Dioscorides* says it has a heating, binding, and drying quality; and therefore the juice taken with vinegar stops bleeding. It stirs up venery, or bodily lust. Two or three branches of it taken with the juice of four pomegranates stops the hiccups and vomiting, and allays the choler. It dissolves abscesses when applied with barley meal. It is good to repress the milk in women's breasts, and for those who have swollen, sagging, or large breasts. Applied with salt, it helps the bite of a mad dog; with mead or honeyed water, it eases the pains of the ears and takes away the roughness of the tongue when rubbed upon it. The virtues of the wild or horse mints, such as grow in ditches (the description of which I purposely omitted because they are well enough known), are especially to dissolve wind in the stomach, to help the colic, and those that are short-winded; they are an especial remedy for those who have venereal dreams and nightly pollutions, being outwardly applied to the testicles or scrotum. The juice dropped into the ears eases their pains and destroys the worms that breed there. They are good against the venomous biting of serpents. The juice applied warm helps the King’s Evil, or kernels in the throat. The decoction or distilled water helps a stinking breath resulting from the corruption of the teeth; and snuffed up into the nose, it purges the head. Pliny says that eating the leaves has been found by experience to cure leprosy, and applying some of them to the face with vinegar helps the scurf or dandruff of the head.

They are extremely bad for wounded people; and they say if a wounded man eats mints, his wound will never be cured; and that is a long time.

*Place.*] It grows very rarely on oaks with us, but upon various others, as well timber as fruit trees, plentifully in woods, groves, and the like, throughout all this land.

*Time.*] It flowers in the springtime, but the berries are not ripe until October and remain on the branches all winter, unless the blackbirds and other birds devour them.

*Government and Virtues.*] That it is under the dominion of the *Sun*, I do not question; and I can also take for granted that that which grows upon oaks participates something in the nature of *Jupiter*, because an oak is one of his trees; as also that which grows upon pear trees and apple trees participates something in his nature, because he rules the trees it grows upon, having no root of its own. But why that which grows upon oaks should have the most virtues, I know not, unless because it is rarest and hardest to come by; and our College's opinion in this is contrary to the Scripture, which says, *God's tender mercies are over all his works*; and so it is, let the College of Physicians walk as contrary to him as they please, and that is as contrary as the East is to the West. *Clusius* affirms that which grows upon pear trees to be just as effective, and gives orders that it should not touch the ground after it is gathered; and he also says that being hung a-

## Money-wort, or Herb-Twopence.

**Description.]** *The common Money-wort sends forth from a small thready root various long, weak, and slender branches lying and running upon the ground, two or three feet long or more, set with leaves two at a joint, one against another at equal distances; these are almost round but pointed at the ends, smooth, and of a good green color. At the joints with the leaves, from the middle forward, there come forth at every joint sometimes one yellow flower, and sometimes two, each standing on a small footstalk and made of five leaves, narrow and pointed at the ends, with some yellow threads in the middle. When these have passed, small round heads of seed stand in their places.*

**Place.]** *It grows plentifully in almost all places of this land, commonly in moist grounds by hedge sides and in the middle of grassy fields.*

**Time.]** *They flower in June and July, and their seed is ripe quickly after.*

<margin>
Fluxes,
Ulcers,
Green wounds,
Old ulcers
</margin>
**Government and Virtues.]** *Venus owns it. Money-wort is singularly good to stay all fluxes in man or woman, whether they be diarrhea <note>lasks</note>, bloody fluxes, the flowing of women's courses, bleedings inwardly or outwardly, and the weakness of a stomach that is prone to vomiting <note>casting</note>. It is very good also for all ulcers or excoriations of the lungs or other inward parts. It is exceedingly good for all wounds, either fresh or green, to heal them speedily, and for old ulcers that are of a spreading nature. For all these purposes, the juice of the herb or the powder drunk in water wherein hot steel has been often quenched, or the decoction of the green herb in wine or water drunk, or the seed, juice, or decoction used on outward places to wash or bathe them, or to have <term>tents</term> dipped therein and put into them, are effective.*

## Moon-wort.

**Description.]** *It usually rises up with only one dark green, thick, and fleshy leaf standing upon a short footstalk, not above two fingers' breadth; but when it will flower, it may be said to bear a small slender stalk about four or five inches high, having but one leaf set in the middle of it. This leaf is much divided on both sides into sometimes five or seven parts on a side, sometimes more; each of these parts is small next to the middle rib but broad forward and round-pointed, resembling a half-moon, from which it took its name; the uppermost parts or divisions are smaller than the lowest. The stalk rises above this leaf two or three inches, bearing many branches of small long tongues, every one like the spiky head of <term>Adder's-tongue</term>, of a brownish color; whether I shall call them flowers or the seed, I do not well know; after they have continued a while, they resolve into a mealy dust. The root is small and fibrous. This plant sometimes has various such leaves as are described before, with many branches or tops arising from one stalk, each divided from the other.*

*Place.*] It grows on hills and heaths, yet where there is much grass, for it delights to grow therein.

*Time.*] It is to be found only in *April* and *May*, for in *June*, when any hot weather comes, for the most part it is withered and gone.

The leaves boiled in red wine and drunk stay the immoderate flux of *women's courses*, and the whites <note>leukorrhea</note>. It also stays bleeding, vomitings, and other fluxes. It helps all blows and bruises, and helps to consolidate all fractures and dislocations. It is good for ruptures. But it is chiefly used by most with other herbs to make oils or balsams to heal fresh or green wounds (as I said before), either inward or outward, for which it is excellently good.

Moon-wort is an herb which they say will open locks and unshoe such horses as tread upon it; some laugh this to scorn, and those are no small fools either. But country people whom I know call it [*Unshoe the Horse*]. Besides, I have heard commanders say that on White Down in *Devonshire* near *Tiverton*, there were found thirty horseshoes pulled off from the feet of the Earl of *Essex's* horses being there drawn up in a body, many of them being but newly shod, and no known reason for it, which caused much wonder; and the herb described usually grows upon heaths.

## Mosses.

I shall not trouble the reader with any description of these, since my intent is to speak only of two kinds as the most principal, namely, *Ground-moss* and *Tree-moss*, both of which are very well known.

*Place.*] The *Ground-moss* grows in our moist woods, and the bottoms of hills, in boggy grounds, and in shadowy ditches, and many other such places.

The *Tree-moss* grows only on trees.

<margin>*Stone, inflammations.*</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] All sorts of mosses are under the dominion of *Saturn*. The *Ground-moss* is held to be singularly good to break the stone and to expel and drive it forth by urine, being boiled in wine and drunk. The herb bruised and boiled in water and applied eases all inflammations and pains coming from a <margin>*hot gout.*</margin> hot cause; and is therefore used to ease the pains of the hot gout.

<margin>*Fluxes, vomiting, bleeding, women's courses.*</margin>
The *Tree-mosses* are cooling and binding, and partake of a digesting and mollifying quality as well, as *Galen* says. But each moss partakes of the nature of the *tree* from which it is taken; therefore, that of the oak is more binding and is of good effect to stay fluxes in man or woman, as also vomitings or bleedings, the powder thereof being taken in wine. The decoction thereof in wine is very good for women to be bathed with, or to sit in

# Mother-wort.

<margin>*Description*]</margin>
This has a hard, square, brownish, rough, strong stalk, rising three or four feet high at least, spreading into many branches; whereon grow leaves on each side with long footstalks, two at every joint, which are somewhat broad and long, appearing rough or crumpled, with many great veins therein, of a dark green color, and deeply dented about the edges, and almost divided: From the middle of the branches up to the tops of them (which are very long and small) grow the flowers round about them at distances, in sharp-pointed rough hard husks, of a more red or purple color than balm or horehound, but in the same manner or form as the horehound’s: after which come small round blackish seeds in great plenty. The root sends forth a number of long strings and small fibers, taking strong hold in the ground, of a dark yellowish or brownish color, and remains as the horehound does, the smell of this being not much different from it.

<margin>*Place.*]</margin>
It grows only in gardens with us in *England*.

<margin>*Government and Virtues.*]</margin>
*Venus* owns the herb, and it is under *Leo*: There is no better herb to drive melancholy vapors from 
<margin>*Melancholy vapors, swoonings, painful labor, the womb, urine, women's courses, phlegm, cold phlegm, cramps, convulsions.*</margin> 
the heart, to strengthen it, and make a merry, cheerful, blithe soul, than this herb: It may be kept in a syrup or conserve, therefore the Latins called it *Cardiaca*. Besides, it makes women joyful mothers of children, and settles their wombs as they should be; therefore we call it *Motherwort*. It is held to be of much use for the trembling of the heart, and in faintings and swoonings, from which it took the name *Cardiaca*. The powder thereof to the quantity of a spoonful drunk in wine is a wonderful help to women in their painful labors, as also for the suffocations or risings of the mother <note>the womb</note>; and from these effects it is likely it took the name of *Motherwort* with us. It also provokes urine and women's courses, cleanses the chest of cold phlegm oppressing it, and kills the worms in the belly: It is of good use to warm and dry up the cold humors, to digest and disperse those that are settled in the veins, joints, and sinews of the body, and to help cramps and convulsions.

# Mouse-Ear.

*Description*] Mouse-Ear is a low herb that creeps upon the ground by small runners like the strawberry plant, by which it shoots forth small roots. On the ground grow many small and somewhat short leaves arranged in a round shape; they are hollowish in the middle where they are broadest, of a grayish color all over, and very hairy. When broken, they produce a white milk. From among these leaves spring up two or three small grayish stalks about a span <note>about 9 inches</note> high, with a few smaller leaves on them. At the tops usually stands only one flower, consisting of many pale yellow petals broad at the points and slightly notched, set in three or four rows—the larger ones being outermost—very similar to a dandelion flower and a bit reddish underneath around the edges, especially if it grows in dry ground. After they have flowered for a long time, they turn into down, which, along with the seed, is carried away by the wind.

*Place*] It grows on ditch banks, and sometimes in ditches if they are dry, and in sandy grounds.

*Time*] It flowers about June and July and stays green all winter.

belly-ache,

*Government and Virtues*] The Moon also rules this herb. Although authors criticize alchemists for attempting to fix quicksilver <note>mercury</note> with this herb and moonwort, a Roman would not have judged a thing by the outcome; if it is to be fixed at all, it is by lunar influence. The juice of this taken in wine, or the decoction of it drunk, helps jaundice even of long duration, if drunk morning and evening while abstaining from other drinks for two or three hours afterward. It is a special remedy against the stone <note>kidney or bladder stones</note> and its tormenting pains, as well as other tortures and griping pains of the bowels. The decoction of it with succory and centaury is held to be very effective in helping dropsy <note>edema</note> and those inclined toward it, as well as diseases of the spleen. It stops fluxes of blood, whether from the mouth or nose, and internal bleeding as well, for it is an exceptional wound-herb for wounds both internal and external. It helps the bloody flux <note>dysentery</note> and excessive menstrual flow. There is a syrup made from its juice and sugar by the apothecaries of Italy and other places, which they value highly for those troubled with a cough or phthisic <note>a wasting disease, usually pulmonary tuberculosis</note>. The same is also exceptionally good for ruptures or burstings <note>hernias</note>. The green herb, bruised and immediately bound to any fresh cut or wound, quickly heals the edges of it. The juice, decoction, or powder of the dried herb is most exceptional at stopping the malignancy of spreading and eroding cankers and ulcers anywhere, even in the mouth or private parts. The distilled water of the plant is effective for all the aforementioned diseases, for washing external wounds and sores, and for applying tents <note>medicinal plugs or dressings</note> or cloths soaked in it.

# Mugwort.

Deſcript.] **Common** Mugwort has various *leaves lying upon the ground, very much divided, or cut deeply in about the edges, somewhat like wormwood, but much larger, of a dark green color on the upper side, and very hoary white underneath. The stalks rise to be four or five feet high, having on them such leaves as those below, but somewhat smaller, branching forth very much toward the top, whereon are set very small pale yellowish flowers like buttons, which fall away; and after them come small seed enclosed in round heads: The root is long and hard with many small fibers growing from it, by which it takes strong hold in the ground, but both stalk and leaf die down every year, and the root shoots anew in the spring. The whole plant is of a reasonably good scent, and is more easily propagated by the slips than by the seed.*

Place.] *It grows plentifully in many places of this land, by the way sides, as also by small water-courses, and in various other places.*

Time.] *It flowers and seeds in the end of summer.*

<margin>

Womb inflamed,

Sciatica,

Cramp.
</margin>
Government and Virtues.] This is an herb of *Venus*, therefore it maintains the parts of the body she rules and remedies the diseases of the parts that are under her signs, *Taurus* and *Libra*. Mugwort is with good success put among other herbs that are boiled for women to sit over the hot decoction to draw down their menstrual courses, to help the delivery of the birth, and expel the afterbirth, as also for the obstructions and inflammations of the womb <note>the "mother"</note>. It breaks the stone and causes one to urinate where it is stopped. The juice thereof made up with myrrh and used as a pessary works the same effect, and so does the root also; being made up with hog's grease into an ointment, it takes away wens and hard knots and kernels that grow about the neck and throat, and eases the pains about the neck more effectually if some field daisies be put with it. The herb itself being fresh, or the juice thereof taken, is a special remedy for the overmuch taking of opium. Three drams of the powder of the dried leaves taken in wine is a speedy and the best certain help for sciatica. A decoction thereof made with chamomile and agrimony, and the place bathed therewith while it is warm, takes away the pains of the sinews and the cramp.

## Mullein.

<margin>Description]</margin> Common white Mullein has many fair, large, woolly white leaves lying next to the ground, somewhat longer than broad, pointed at the ends, and as it were toothed around the edges. The stalk rises up to be four or five feet high, covered over with such leaves, but smaller, so that no stalk can be seen for the multitude of leaves on it up to the flowers, which come forth on all sides of the stalk, without any branches for the most part; they are many set together in a long spike, in some of a gold-yellow color, in others more pale, consisting of five round-pointed petals <note>Culpeper calls these "leaves"</note>, which afterward produce small round heads, wherein small brownish seed is contained. The root is long, white, and woody, perishing after it has produced seed.

<margin>Place]</margin>
It grows by waysides and lanes in many places of this land.

<margin>Time]</margin>
It flowers in July, or thereabouts.

<margin>Government and Virtues]</margin>
<margin>Flux, Ruptures, Cramp, Convulsion, Cough, Toothache, Hemorrhoids, Bloody Flux</margin>
It is under the dominion of *Saturn*. A small quantity of the root given in wine is commended by *Dioscorides* against lasks <note>diarrhea</note> and fluxes of the bowels. The decoction thereof drunk is profitable for those that are ruptured, and for cramps and convulsions, and for those that are troubled with an old cough. The decoction thereof gargled eases the pains of the toothache. An oil made by the repeated infusion of the flowers is of very good effect for the piles. The decoction of the root in red wine, or in water (if there is a fever) wherein red-hot steel has been often quenched, stops the bloody flux <note>dysentery</note>. The powder of the dried flowers is a special remedy for those who are troubled with belly-aches or the pains of the colic. A decoction of the root, as well as the leaves, is very effective at dissolving tumors, swellings, or inflammation of the throat. The seeds and leaves boiled in wine and applied quickly draw out thorns or splinters that have entered the flesh, easing the pain and healing them as well. The leaves, bruised and wrapped in double papers, then covered with hot ashes and embers to bake for a while, and then taken out and laid warm on any botch <note>a skin sore</note> or boil occurring in the groin or share <note>the pubic area</note>, dissolve and heal them. The seeds, bruised and boiled in wine and applied to any limb that has been out of joint and is newly reset, take away all swelling and pain.

### Mustard.

<margin>Description]</margin>
Our common mustard has large, broad, rough leaves, very much jagged with uneven and irregular gashes, somewhat like turnip leaves but smaller and rougher. The stalk rises to be more than a foot high, and sometimes two feet high, being round, rough, and branched at the top, bearing similar leaves to those below, but smaller and less divided; it has various yellow flowers one above another at the tops; after these come small rough pods with small, thin, flat ends, which contain round yellowish seeds that are sharp, hot, and biting to the tongue. The root is small, long, and woody when it bears stalks, and it perishes every year.

<margin>Place]</margin>
This grows among us in gardens only, and other cultivated places.

<margin>Time]</margin>
It is an annual plant, flowering in *July*, and its seed is ripe in *August*.

<margin>Government and Virtues]</margin>
It is an excellent sauce for those whose blood needs clarifying and for weak stomachs; it is an herb of *Mars*, but it is no good for choleric <note>easily angered or having an excess of yellow bile</note> people, though it is as good for those who are elderly or troubled with cold diseases. *Aries* also has a claim to it; therefore, it strengthens the heart and resists poison. Let those whose stomachs are so weak they cannot digest their food or have no appetite for it, take a dram of mustard seed and as much cinnamon; having beaten them into powder, add half as much powdered mastic <note>a resin from the mastic tree</note>. With gum arabic dissolved in rose water, make it into troches <note>medicinal lozenges</note>, of which they may take one of about half a dram

## Nail-wort, or Whitlow-grass.

*Descript.*] This very small and common herb has no roots except for a few strings, nor does it ever grow to be above a hand-breadth high. The leaves are very small and somewhat long, not much unlike those of chickweed; among which arise several slender stalks, bearing many white flowers one above another, which are exceedingly small. After these come small, flat pouches containing the seed, which is very small but has a sharp taste.

*Place.*] It grows commonly upon old stone and brick walls, and sometimes in dry, gravelly grounds, especially if there is grass or moss nearby to shade it.

*Time.*] They flower very early in the year, sometimes in *January* and in *February*, for before the end of *April* they are not to be found.

**Place.]** It grows in moist, shadowy, and grassy places in woods, in many parts of this land.

**Time.]** It flowers about *May*, and the berries are ripe in *June*, and then it quickly perishes until the following year, when it springs from the same root again.

**Government and Virtues.]** It is a precious herb of the *Sun*. Half a dram, or a dram at most, of the powder of its roots taken in wine and vinegar—using equal parts of each—after which the person is immediately laid to sweat, is held to be a sovereign remedy for those who are infected with the plague and have a sore upon them. It works by expelling the poison and infection and defending the heart and spirits from danger. It is an exceptionally good wound herb, and is therefore used with other similar ingredients in making compound balms for the curing of wounds, whether they are fresh and green, or old and malignant, and especially if the sinews are hurt.

## Orchis.

It has had almost as many different names attributed to its various kinds as would almost fill a sheet of paper; such as dogs-stones, goats-stones, fools-stones, fox-stones, satyrion, cullions, together with many others, too tedious to rehearse.

*Description.] To describe all the various kinds of it would be an endless task; therefore I shall only describe the roots because they are to be used with some discretion: They each have a double root within; some are round, in others like a hand. These roots change every year in turn: when one rises and grows full, the other becomes lank and perishes. Now, it is the one that is full which is to be used in medicine; the other is either of no use at all, or else, according to the opinion of some, it destroys and cancels the virtue of the other, completely undoing what that one does.*

**Time.]** One or another of them may be found in flower from the beginning of *April* to the end of *August*.

<margin>Lust provoked, worms, King's evil.</margin>
**Government and Virtues.]** They are hot and moist in operation, under the dominion of Dame *Venus*, and provoke lust exceedingly, which they say the dry or withered root restrains again. They are held to kill worms in children; also, being bruised and applied to the area, they help the King's evil <note>Scrofula, a swelling of the lymph nodes in the neck caused by tuberculosis</note>.

## Onions.

These are so well known that I need not spend time writing a description of them.

**Government and virtues.]** *Mars* owns them, and they have acquired this quality: to draw any corruption to them. For if you peel one and lay it upon a dunghill, you shall find it rotten in half a day by drawing putrefaction to itself; therefore, being bruised and applied to a plague sore, it is very probable it will do the same.

Being roasted under the embers and eaten with honey, or sugar and oil, they much help a persistent cough and expectorate tough phlegm. The juice, being snuffed up into the nostrils, purges the head and helps lethargy (yet frequent eating of them is said to cause pains in the head). It has been held by various country people to be a good preservative against infection to eat onions while fasting with bread and salt; also to make a large onion hollow, filling the space with good treacle, and then to roast it well under the embers. After taking away the outermost skin and beating it together, it is a sovereign salve for either a plague-sore or any other putrid ulcer. The juice of onions is good for either scalding or burning by fire, water, or gunpowder, and used with vinegar, it takes away all blemishes, spots, and marks in the skin; dropped into the ears, it eases the pains and noise in them. Applied also with beaten figs, it helps to ripen and break abscesses and other sores.

Leeks are as like onions in quality as a pomewater apple is like an apple. They are a remedy against an overindulgence of mushrooms when baked under the embers and taken; and being boiled and applied warm, they help the piles. In other things, they have the same properties as onions, although they are not as effective.

# Orpine.

<margin>Description.]</margin> Common Orpine *rises up with various round, brittle stalks, set thickly with thick and fleshy leaves without any order, and little or nothing notched about the edges, of a pale green color. The flowers are white or whitish, growing in tufts, after which come small chaffy husks with seed like dust in them. The roots are various thick, round, white, tuberous clogs; and the plant does not grow as large in some places as in others where it is found.*

<margin>Place.]</margin> It is frequent in almost every county of this land, and is cultivated in gardens among us, where it grows larger than the wild variety, which grows in the shadowy sides of fields and woods.

<margin>Time.]</margin> It flowers about *July*, and the seed is ripe in *August*.

<margin>Government and Virtues.]</margin> The *Moon* owns the herb, and he who knows but her exaltation knows what I say is true. Orpine is seldom used in internal medicines among us, although *Tragus* says from experience in *Germany* that the distilled water

## Parsley-Piert, or Parsley Break-Stone.

<margin>Description</margin>
The root, although it is very small and thready, yet it continues for many years. From it arise many leaves lying along the ground, each standing upon a long, small footstalk. The leaves are as broad as a man's nail, very deeply indented on the edges, somewhat like a parsley leaf, but of a very dusky green color. The stalks are very weak and slender, about three or four fingers in length, and set so full of leaves that they can hardly be seen, having either no footstalk at all or only a very short one. The flowers are so small they can hardly be seen, and the seed is as small as can be.

<margin>Place</margin>
It is a common herb throughout the nation and thrives in barren, sandy, moist places. It may be found plentifully about Hampstead Heath, in Hyde Park, and in Tothill Fields.

<margin>Time</margin>
It may be found all summer long, even from the beginning of April to the end of October.

<margin>Government and Virtues. Provokes urine; stone.</margin>
Its operation is very effective in provoking urine and breaking the stone; it is a very good salad herb. It would be good if the gentry would pick it as they pick samphire for their use all winter. I cannot teach them how to do it <note>likely referring to pickling or preserving</note>, yet this I can tell them: it is a very wholesome herb. They may also keep the herb dry or in a syrup if <margin>Gravel in the kidneys; strangury.</margin> they please. You may take a dram of the powder of it in white wine; it will bring away gravel from the kidneys imperceptibly and without pain. It also helps the strangury <note>painful or difficult urination</note>.

## Parsnip.

The garden kind is so well known (the root being commonly eaten) that I shall not trouble you with any description of it. But since the wild kind is of more medicinal use, I shall describe it to you here.

<margin>Description</margin>
The wild parsnip differs little from the garden kind, but does not grow as fair and large, nor has it as many leaves. The root is shorter, more woody, and not so fit to be eaten, and therefore it is the more medicinal.

<margin>Place</margin>
The name of the first shows where it grows. The other grows wild in various places, such as in the marshes by Rochester and elsewhere, and flowers in July. The seed is ripe about the beginning of August, the second year after sowing; for if they flower the first year, the country people call them <term>Madneps</term>.

## Cow-Parsnip.

*Description.*] **T**his grows with three or four large, spread, winged, rough leaves, often lying on the ground, or else raised a little from it, with long, round, hairy footstalks under them, usually divided into five parts, the two pairs standing opposite each other and one at the end; each leaf being almost round, yet somewhat deeply cut on the edges in some leaves, and not so deep in others, of a whitish green color, smelling somewhat strongly. Among these arises a round, ridged, hairy stalk two or three feet high with a few joints and leaves on it, and branched at the top, where stand large umbels of white and sometimes reddish flowers, and after them, flat, whitish, thin-winged seed, two always joined together. The root is long and white with two or three long strings growing down into the ground, likewise smelling strongly and unpleasantly.

*Place.*] It grows in moist meadows, and the borders and corners of fields, and near ditches, generally throughout this land.

*Time.*] It flowers in *July*, and seeds in *August*.

<margin>*Cough, difficulty of breath, falling-sickness, jaundice, fistula, phlegm, liver, mother, lethargy, frenzy, headache, scabs, shingles.*</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] *Mercury* has the dominion over them. The seed of this, as *Galen* says, is of a sharp and cutting quality, and is therefore a fit medicine for the cough and shortness of breath, the falling-sickness, and the jaundice. The root is available for all the purposes aforesaid, and is also of great use to take away the hard skin that grows on a fistula, if it is simply scraped upon it. The seed of this being drunk cleanses the belly from tough phlegmatic matter within it, eases those that are liver-grown, and women's passions of the mother, both when drunk and when the smoke of it is received from below; and likewise raises such as have fallen into a deep sleep or have the lethargy by burning it under their nose. The seed and root boiled in oil, and the head rubbed with it, helps not only those who have fallen into a frenzy, but also the lethargy or drowsy evil, and those who have been long troubled with the headache, if it is likewise used with rue. It helps also the running scab and the shingles. The juice of the flowers dropped into ears that run and are full of matter cleanses and heals them.

# The Peach-tree.

<margin>Description.]</margin> A peach tree does not grow as large as the apricot tree, yet its branches spread reasonably well, from which spring smaller reddish twigs, where long and narrow green leaves are set, which are jagged around the edges. The blossoms are larger than the plum and of a light purple color. The fruit is round, and sometimes as big as a decent Pippin apple; others are smaller, and they also differ in colors and tastes, such as russet, red, or yellow, watery or firm, with a fuzz or down all over, with a cleft in it like an apricot, and a rugged, furrowed, large stone within it, and a bitter kernel within the stone. It grows old and decays much sooner than the apricot.

<margin>Place.]</margin> They are cultivated in gardens and orchards throughout this land.

<margin>Time.]</margin> They flower in the *Spring* and bear fruit in *Autumn*.

<margin>Government and Virtues.]</margin> Lady Venus owns this tree, and by it she opposes the ill effects of Mars. Indeed, for children and young people, nothing is better to purge choler and the jaundice than the leaves and flowers of this tree, made into a syrup or conserve. Let those who delight to please their lust regard the fruit, but those who love their health and their children's, let them regard what I say: they may safely give two spoonfuls of the syrup at a time; it is as gentle as *Venus* herself. # The Pear-tree.

Pear trees are so well known that they need no description.

*Government and Virtues.*] The tree belongs to *Venus*, and so does the apple tree. For their medicinal use, they are best distinguished by their tastes. All the sweet or luscious types, whether cultivated or wild, help to move the bowels more or less. Those that are harsh and sour, on the contrary, bind the bowels just as much; and the leaves do so also. And wild pears close up the lips of fresh wounds sooner than the others.
The *Schola Salerni* advises one to drink plenty of wine after eating pears, or else (they say) they are as bad as poison—indeed, they even curse the tree for it. But if a poor man finds his stomach oppressed by eating pears, it is only necessary to work hard, and it will serve just as well as drinking wine.

# Pellitory of the Wall.

*Description.*] It rises up with many brownish, red, tender, and weak, clear, and almost transparent stalks about two feet high, upon which grow at the various joints two leaves, somewhat broad and long, of a dark green color, which afterwards turn brownish; they are smooth on the edges, but rough and hairy, as the stalks are also. At the joints with the leaves, from the middle of the stalks upward where it spreads into branches, stand many small, pale, purplish flowers in hairy, rough heads or husks; after which come small, black, and rough seeds, which will stick to any cloth or garment that touches them. The root is somewhat long, with many small fibers, of a dark reddish color; it survives the winter, although the stalks and leaves perish and spring fresh every year.

*Place.*] It grows wild generally throughout this land, around the borders of fields, by the sides of walls, and among rubbish. It will endure well being brought into gardens and planted on the shady side, where it will spring up from its own sowing.

## Pennyroyal.

Pennyroyal is so well known to everyone (I mean the common kind) that it needs no description.

*There is a larger kind than the ordinary sort found growing wild among us, which remains so even when brought into gardens; it does not differ from the common kind except for the size of the leaves and stalks, rising higher and not creeping along the ground as much. Its flowers are purple, growing in whorls around the stalk like the other.*

Place.] The first, which is common in gardens, also grows in many moist and watery places in this country.

Time.] They flower in the latter end of summer, around *August*.

## Peony, Male & Female.

<margin>Description.]</margin>
*Male Peony rises up with many brownish stalks, on which grow many fair green, and sometimes reddish leaves, set opposite one another upon a stalk without any particular division in the leaf at all. The flowers stand at the tops of the stalks, consisting of five or six broad leaves of a fair purplish red color, with many yellow threads in the middle standing around the head, which afterward rises to be the seed vessels, divided into two, three, or four rough, crooked pods like horns; which, being fully ripe, open and turn themselves downward from one edge to another, showing within them several round, black, shining seeds, also having many red or crimson grains intermixed with the black, which makes a very pretty show. The roots are large, thick, and long, spreading and running reasonably deep into the ground.*

*The ordinary female peony has many stalks, and more leaves on them than the male; the leaves are not as large, but notched diversely on the edges, some with large and deep cuts, others with smaller divisions, and of a dark or dull green color. The flowers have a strong, heady scent, and are usually smaller and of a more purple color than the male, with yellow threads around the head as the male has. The seed vessels are like horns as in the male, but smaller; the seed is also black, but less shining. The roots consist of many thick and short tuberous clumps, fastened at the ends of long strings, all coming from the head of the root, which is thick and short, and of a similar scent to the male.*

<margin>Place and Time.]</margin>
They grow in gardens and flower usually around May.

</margin>

## Periwinkle.

Descript.] *The common sort of this has many branches trailing or running upon the ground, shooting out small fibers at the joints as it runs, taking hold thereby in the ground, and rooting in various places. At the joints of these branches stand two small, dark green, shining leaves, somewhat like bay leaves, but smaller; and with them come forth also the flowers (one at a joint standing upon a tender footstalk), being somewhat long and hollow, parted at the rims, sometimes into four, sometimes into five leaves; the most ordinary sort are of a pale blue color, some are pure white, and some of a dark reddish purple color. The root is little larger than a rush, bushing in the ground, and creeping with its branches far about, whereby it quickly occupies a great area, and is therefore most usually planted under hedges, where it may have room to run.*

Place.] Those with the pale blue and those with the white flowers grow in woods and orchards, by the hedge-sides, in various places of this land. But those with the purple flowers grow in gardens only.

Time.] They flower in *March* and *April*.

<margin>Stopping bleeding, women's courses, and flux of the belly.</margin>
Government and Vertues.] *Venus* owns this herb, and says that the leaves eaten by husband and wife together cause love between them. The *Periwinkle* is a great binder, stopping bleeding both at the mouth and nose if some of the leaves are chewed. The *French* use it to stop women's courses <note>menstrual flow</note>. *Dioscorides*, *Galen*, and *Aegineta* commend it against the lask <note>diarrhea</note> and fluxes of the belly, to be drunk in wine.

## St. Peter’s-wort.

If superstition had not been the father of tradition, as well as ignorance the mother of devotion, this herb (as well as St. John’s-wort) would have found some other name to be known by; but we may say of our forefathers, as *St. Paul* said of the *Athenians*, I perceive that in many things you are too superstitious. Yet seeing it has come to pass that custom, having gained possession, pleads prescription for the name, I shall let it pass and come to the description of the herb, which is as follows:

Descript.] *It rises up with square upright stalks for the most part, somewhat larger and higher than St. John’s-wort (and for good reason too, St. Peter being the greater Apostle—ask the Pope else!); for though God would have the*

# Pimpernel.

<margin>
*Thorns or splinters, purges the head, wounds and ulcers, cleanses the face, plague and pestilential fevers.*
</margin>
• *Descript.*] Common pimpernel has several weak square stalks lying on the ground, beset all along with two small and almost round leaves at every joint, one against another, very like chickweed, but has no footstalks, for the leaves do as it were compass the stalk: The flowers stand singly each by themselves at the leaves and the stalks, consisting of five round small pointed leaves of a fine pale red color, tending to an orange, with as many threads in the middle, in whose places succeed smooth round heads, wherein is contained small seed. The root is small and fibrous, perishing every year.

*Place.*] It grows almost everywhere, as well in the meadows and cornfields as by the waysides and in gardens, arising of itself.

*Time.*] It flowers from *May* until *August*, and the seed ripens in the meantime and falls.

*Government and Virtues.*] It is a gallant solar herb. ## Ground Pine, or Chamepitys.

<margin>Descript.]</margin> **O**ur common ground-pine grows low, seldom rising above a hand-breadth high, shooting forth various small branches set with slender, small, long, narrow grayish or whitish leaves that are somewhat hairy. They are often divided into three parts, many clustering together at a joint, and sometimes some growing scattered upon the stalks, smelling somewhat strongly like resin. The flowers are small and of a pale yellow color, growing from the joints of the stalks all along among the leaves, after which come small, long, and round husks. The root is small and woody, perishing every year.

<margin>Place.]</margin> It grows more plentifully in *Kent* than in any other county of this land; namely, in many places on this side of *Dartford*, along to *Southfleet*, *Cotham*, and *Rochester*, and upon *Chatham* Down right by the beacon, and half a mile from *Rochester* in a field near a house called *Selsey*.

<margin>Time.]</margin> It flowers and produces seed in the summer months.

<margin>Government and Virtues.]</margin> *Mars* owns the herb. ## Plantain.

This grows so commonly in meadows and fields, and by pathways, and is so well known that it needs no description.

*Time.]* It is in its beauty about *June*, and the seed ripens shortly after.

*Government and Virtues.]* It is true *Myzaldus* and others, yes, almost all astro-physicians, hold this to be an herb of *Mars*, and they give a semblance of truth for it too, *namely:* Because it cures diseases of the head and private parts, which are under the houses of *Mars*, *Aries*, and *Scorpio*: All diseases of the head coming from heat are caused by *Mars*, for *Venus* is made of no such hot metal, or at least deals in lower parts. The truth is it is under the command of *Venus*, and cures the head by antipathy to *Mars*, and the private parts by sympathy to *Venus*; neither is there hardly a Martial disease but it cures. If I were to fortify my body against a Martial disease, I would do it by this herb as soon as by any, and may do it (perhaps) when time shall serve.

# Plums.

<margin>

<margin>Government and Virtues.]</margin> These are so well known that they need no description.
All plums are under *Venus*, and are like women: some better, some worse. As there is great diversity in the kinds, so is there in the operation of plums; for some that are sweet moisten the stomach and make the bowels loose; those that are sour quench thirst more and bind the bowels; the moist and watery ones soonest corrupt in the stomach, but the firm ones nourish and bind more and offend less. The dried fruit sold by the grocers under the name of *Damask prunes* does somewhat loosen the bowels, procure appetite, allay the choler, and being stewed, they are often used both in health and sickness to relish the mouth and stomach, to procure appetite, and a little to open the body, allay choler, and cool the stomach. *Plum-tree leaves* boiled in wine are good to wash and gargle the mouth and throat, to dry the flux of rheum coming to the palate, gums, or tonsils <note>The original text refers to tonsils as "almonds of the ears"</note>. The gum of the trees is good to break the stone. The gum or leaves boiled in vinegar and applied kills tetters and ringworms. *Mathiolus* <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a 16th-century physician</note> says the oil pressed out of the kernels of the stones, made as oil of almonds is made, is good against inflamed piles, the tumors or swellings of ulcers, hoarseness of the voice, roughness of the tongue and throat, and likewise the pains in the ears. And that five ounces of the said oil taken with one ounce of *Muscadine* <note>A sweet wine</note> drives forth the stone and helps the colic.

# Polypody of the Oak.

<margin>Description.]</margin> This is a *small herb, consisting of nothing but roots and leaves: bearing neither stalk, flower, nor seed, as it is thought. It has three or four leaves rising from the root, every one singly by itself, of about a hand's length, which are winged, consisting of many small narrow leaves cut into the middle rib standing on each side of the stalk, large below and smaller up to the top, not dented or notched on the edges at all, as the male fern has; of a dark green color and smooth on the upper side, but on the under side somewhat rough by reason of some yellowish spots set thereon. The root is smaller than one's little finger, lying aslope or creeping along under the upper crust of the earth, brownish on the outside and greenish within, of a sweetish harshness in taste, set with certain rough knags on each side thereof, having also much mossiness or yellow hairiness upon it, and some fibers underneath it by which it is nourished.*

<summary>This page concludes the medicinal uses of plantain for skin conditions and details the astrological government and healing properties of various plums and polypody of the oak.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the botanical and medicinal descriptions in "The English Physician Enlarged," specifically detailing the locations and virtues of Polypodium (Polypody of the Oak).</meta>

*Place.*] It grows as well upon old rotten stumps or trunks of trees—such as oak, beech, hazel, willow, or any other—as in the woods under them, and upon old mud walls, as also in mossy, stony, and gravelly places near woods. That which grows upon oaks is accounted the best, but the quantity of it is scarcely sufficient for common use.

*Time.*] Being always green, it may be gathered for use at any time.

<margin>Dries humors, purges burnt choler, phlegm, melancholy, quartan agues, spleen, colic, troublesome sleep, cough, shortness of breath, lungs, phthisis, dislocated joints, polypus or disease in the nose, cracks in the fingers or toes.</margin>

*Government and Virtues.*] And why, I pray, must *Polypodium* of the oak only be used, gentle College of Physicians? Can you give me but a glimpse of a reason for it? Is it only because it is dearest? Will you never leave your covetousness until your lives leave you? The truth is, that which grows upon the earth is best (it is an herb of *Saturn*, and he seldom climbs trees) to purge melancholy; if the humor be otherwise, choose your *Polypodium* accordingly. *Mesue* <note>A 9th-century Persian physician, often cited in early modern herbals</note> (who is called the physicians' evangelist for the certainty of his medicines and the truth of his opinions) says that it dries up thin humors, digests thick and tough ones, and purges burnt choler, and especially tough and thick phlegm—and thin phlegm also—even from the joints. It is therefore good for those who are troubled with melancholy or quartan agues, especially if it be taken in whey, honeyed water, barley water, or the broth of a chicken with *epithymum* <note>Dodder of thyme</note>, or with beets and mallows. It is also good for the hardness of the spleen and for prickings or stitches in the sides, as also for the colic. Some choose to add to it some fennel seeds, anise seeds, or ginger to correct the nausea it brings to the stomach, which is more than is necessary, as it is a safe and gentle medicine fit for all persons at all seasons, which daily experience confirms; an ounce of it may be given at a time in a decoction, provided there is no senna or some other strong purger added to it. A dram or two of the powder of the dried roots, taken fasting in a cup of honeyed water, works gently and for the purposes aforesaid. The distilled water of both roots and leaves is much commended for the quartan ague, to be taken for many days together; it is also useful against melancholy or fearful or troublesome sleep or dreams. With some sugar-candy dissolved in it, it is good against the cough, shortness of breath, wheezing, and those distillations of thin rheum upon the lungs which cause phthisis <note>A term for pulmonary tuberculosis or similar wasting diseases</note> and often consumption. The fresh roots beaten small, or the powder of the dried roots mixed with honey and applied to any limb that is out of joint, helps it much. Applied also to the nose, it cures the disease called *polypus*, which is a piece of flesh growing therein that in time stops the passage of breath through that nostril; it also helps those clefts or cracks that occur between the fingers or toes.

# The Poplar-Tree.

Descript.] **T**here *are two types of Poplars that are most familiar to us, namely the Black and the White, both of which I shall describe for you here.*

*The white Poplar grows large and reasonably high, covered with a thick, smooth, white bark, especially the branches, having large leaves cut into several divisions almost like a vine leaf, but not of such a deep green on the upper side, and hoary white underneath, of a reasonably good scent, the whole form representing the leaf of Coltsfoot. The catkins which it brings forth before the leaves are long and of a faint reddish color; these fall away, seldom bearing good seed with them. The wood of it is smooth, soft, and white, very finely waved, for which it is much esteemed.*

*The black Poplar grows higher and straighter than the white, with a grayish bark bearing broad and green leaves somewhat like ivy leaves, not cut in on the edges like the white, but whole and dented, ending in a point, and not white underneath, hanging by slender long footstalks which are continually shaken by the air just like Aspen leaves are. The catkins of it are larger than those of the white, composed of many round green berries, as if set together in a long cluster, containing much downy matter which, when ripe, is blown away with the wind. The clammy buds of it, before they spread into leaves, are gathered to make the Unguentum Populeon <note>A cooling ointment made from poplar buds</note>, and are of a yellowish-green color and small, somewhat sweet but strong. The wood is smooth, tough, and white, and easy to be split. On both these trees grows a sweet kind of musk, which in former times was used to be put into sweet ointments.*

Place.] They grow in moist woods and by watersides in various places of the land, yet the white is not as frequent as the other.

Time.] Their time is likewise expressed before. The catkins come forth before the leaves and ripen at the end of summer.

<margin>Sciatica, strangury <note>difficulty in passing urine</note>, pain in the ears, dull sight, gout, falling sickness <note>epilepsy</note>, warts, pustules and wheals, heat and inflammations, dries women's milk.</margin>
Government and Virtues.] Saturn has dominion over both. The White Poplar, says *Galen*, is of a cleansing property: the weight of one ounce of the powdered bark being drunk, says *Dioscorides*, is a remedy for those who are troubled with sciatica or strangury. The juice of the leaves dropped warm into the ears eases the pains in them. The young clammy buds or eyes before they break out into leaves, bruised and mixed with a little honey, is a good medicine for a dull sight. The black Poplar is held to be more cooling than the white, and therefore the leaves bruised with vinegar and applied help the gout. The seed drunk in vinegar is held good against the falling sickness. The water that drops from the hollow places of this tree takes away warts, pustules, wheals, and other such breakouts on the body. The young black poplar buds, says *Mathiolus*, are much used by women to beautify their hair, bruising

# Poppy.

Of this I shall describe three kinds, namely: the white and black of the garden, and the erratic wild poppy or corn rose.

*Descript.*] *The white poppy has at first four or five whitish-green leaves lying upon the ground, which rise with the stalk, encompassing it at the bottom. They are very large, much cut or torn on the edges, and also dented. The stalk, which is usually four or five feet high, sometimes has no branches at the top, and usually but two or three at most, each bearing one head wrapped in a thin skin, which bows down before it is ready to bloom. Then, rising and breaking, the flower within it spreads itself open and consists of four very large, white, round leaves, with many whitish round threads in the middle, set around a small, round, green head having a crown or star-like cover at the top. When it grows ripe, it becomes as large as a great apple, containing a great number of small round seeds in several partitions or divisions next to the shell, the middle remaining hollow and empty. The whole plant—leaves, stalks, and heads—while they are fresh, young, and green, yields a milk when broken. This milk has an unpleasant bitter taste, almost enough to provoke vomiting, and a strong, heady smell; when condensed, it is called opium. The root is white and woody, perishing as soon as it has produced ripe seed.*

*The black poppy differs little from the former until it bears its flower, which is somewhat smaller and of a blackish-purplish color, but without any purple spots at the bottom of the leaf. The head of seed is much smaller than the former and opens itself a little all around the top under the crown, so that the seed, which is very black, will fall out if one turns the head downward.*

*The wild poppy, or corn rose, has long and narrow leaves, very much cut on the edges into many divisions, of a light green color and sometimes hairy. The stalk is blackish and hairy also, but not as tall as the garden kinds, having some leaves on it like those growing below. It is sometimes parted into three or four branches, on which grow small hairy heads that bow down before the skin breaks to reveal the flower. When it is fully blown open, the flower is of a fair yellowish-red or crimson color (and in some, much paler), without any spot at the bottom of the leaves, having many black soft threads in the middle surrounding a small green head. When ripe, this head is no bigger than one's little finger end, containing much black seed, smaller by half than that of the garden. The root perishes every year and springs again from its own sowing. Of this kind, there is one smaller in all its parts, but differing in nothing else.*

*Place.]* The garden kinds do not naturally grow wild in any place, but are all sown in gardens where they grow.

The *wild poppy*, or *corn rose*, is plentiful enough—and often too much so—in the cornfields of all countries throughout this land, and also upon ditch banks and by hedge sides. The smaller *wild kind* is also found in cornfields, and also in some other places, but not as plentifully as the former.

*Time.]* The *garden kinds* are usually sown in the spring, and then flower about the end of *May*, or somewhat earlier if they grow from their own seeding.

The *wild kinds* flower usually from *May* until *July*, and their seed is ripe soon after the flowering.

<margin>
Procures sleep, treats catarrhs and flows of rheum, stops hoarseness, flux of the belly and women's courses, inflammations, St. Anthony's fire, pains in the head, frenzies, and toothache.
</margin>
*Government and Virtues.]* The herb is *lunar*, and from its juice *opium* is made; only for the sake of money do they cheat you and tell you it is a kind of tear, or some such thing that drops from poppies when they weep, and that it is somewhere beyond the seas—I know not where, beyond the moon. The *garden poppy* heads, with the seeds made into a syrup, are frequently and effectively used to procure rest and sleep in the sick and weak, and to stop catarrhs and flows of hot, thin rheums from the head into the stomach and upon the lungs, causing a continual cough, which is the forerunner of a consumption. It also helps hoarseness of the throat, and when one has lost their voice, which the oil of the seed does likewise. The black seed boiled in wine and drunk is also said to stop the flux of the belly and women’s courses. The empty shells of the poppy heads are usually boiled in water and given to procure rest and sleep; the leaves do the same in the same manner. Also, if the head and temples are bathed with the warm decoction, or with the oil of poppies, or if the green leaves or heads are bruised and applied with a little vinegar, or made into a poultice with barley meal or hog’s grease, it cools the head and tempers all inflammations, as well as the disease called *St. Anthony's Fire*. It is generally used in treacle and mithridate, and in all other medicines that are made to procure rest and sleep and to ease pains in the head as well as in other parts. It is also used to cool inflammations, agues, or frenzies, and to stop the flows which cause a cough or consumption, and also other fluxes of the belly or women's courses. It is also put into hollow teeth to ease the pain, and has been found by experience to ease the pain of the gout.

## Purslane.

Garden purslane (being used as a salad herb) is so well known that it needs no description; I shall therefore only speak of its virtues as follows.

<margin>
Cools heat of the blood in hot agues, choleric fluxes, women's courses, the whites and gonorrhea, distillations, frenzy, heat of urine, lust and venereal dreams, worms, vomiting, old dry cough, short breath, phthisic, ulcers in the private parts, redness of the eyes and inflammations, cricks or pain in the neck, blastings by lightning, burning by gunpowder, sore breasts, children's navels, sore mouths, swollen gums, fastens teeth, toothache, bloody flux.
</margin>

*Government and Virtues.*] It is an herb of the **Moon**. It is good for cooling any heat in the liver, blood, reins <note>kidneys</note>, and stomach, and in hot agues <note>fevers</note>, nothing is better. It stops hot and choleric fluxes of the belly, women's courses, the whites <note>leukorrhea</note>, and gonorrhea (or running of the reins), distillations <note>catarrh</note> from the head, and pains therein proceeding from heat, lack of sleep, or frenzy. The seed is more effective than the herb and is of singular good use for cooling the heat and sharpness of urine, and the outrageous lust of the body, venereal dreams, and the like—so much so that the over-frequent use of it extinguishes the heat and power of natural procreation. The seed, bruised and boiled in wine and given to children, expels worms. The juice of the herb is held to be as effective for all the purposes mentioned above, as well as for stopping vomiting; and taken with some sugar or honey, it helps an old and dry cough, shortness of breath, and phthisic <note>consumption or tuberculosis</note>, and stops immoderate thirst. The distilled water of the herb is used by many (being more pleasant) with a little sugar, to achieve the same effects. The juice is also singularly good for inflammations and ulcers of the private parts in man or woman, as also of the bowels and hemorrhoids when they are ulcerous or have excoriations <note>skin abrasions</note> in them. The herb, bruised and applied to the forehead and temples, allays excessive heat there which hinders rest and sleep; and applied to the eyes, it takes away the redness and inflammation in them, and in those other parts where pushes <note>pustules</note>, wheals, pimples, St. Anthony's fire <note>erysipelas</note>, and the like break out, especially if a little vinegar is added to it. When laid to the neck with an equal amount of galls and linseed together, it takes away the pains there and the crick in the neck. The juice is used with oil of roses for the said causes, or for blastings by lightning, burns from gunpowder, or for women's sore breasts, and to allay the heat in all other sores or hurts. It is also applied to the navels
