### Primroses.

These are so well known that they need no description. From the leaves of primroses is made as fine a salve to heal fresh wounds as any that I know; you shall be taught to make salves from any herb at the end of the book. Make this as you are taught there, and do not (those of you who have any ingenuity) see your poor neighbors go with wounded limbs when a half-penny’s cost will heal them.

### Privet.

<margin>Description.]</margin> Our common privet is raised with many slender branches to a reasonable height and breadth to cover arbors, bowers, and banqueting houses, and is shaped, worked, and cut into many forms—of men, horses, birds, etc.—which, though supported at first, grows strong on its own afterward. It bears long and narrow green leaves in pairs, and sweet-smelling white flowers in tufts at the ends of the branches, which turn into small black berries that have a purplish juice within them and some seeds that are flat on one side with a hole or dent in them.

<margin>Place.]</margin> It grows in this land in various woods.

<margin>Time.]</margin> Our privet flowers in June and July; the berries are ripe in August and September.

<margin>Government and Virtues.]</margin>
<margin>Lotions to wash sore mouths, throats, cool inflammations, dry up fluxes, inflammation in wounds, headache, fluxes, and women's courses, voiding blood, rheum in the eyes.</margin>
The Moon is Lady of this. It is little used in medicine with us in these times, other than in lotions to wash sores and sore mouths, and to cool inflammations and dry up fluxes. Yet *Matthiolus* says it serves all the uses for which *Cyprus*, or the East privet, is appointed by *Dioscorides* and *Galen*. He further says that the oil made of the flowers of privet infused in it and set in the sun is exceptionally good for the inflammations of wounds and for headaches coming from a hot cause. There is also a sweet water distilled from the flowers that is good for all those diseases that need cooling and drying, and therefore helps all fluxes of the belly or stomach, bloody fluxes, and women's courses, whether drunk or applied; it is also for those who void blood at their mouth or at any other place, and for the distillation of rheums in the eyes, especially if it is used with Tutia <note>A medicinal powder, usually zinc oxide</note>.

# Queen of the Meadows, Meadow-sweet,
->Or, Mead-sweet.<-

*Descript.*] The stalks of this are reddish, rising to be three feet high, sometimes four or five feet, having at its joints large winged leaves, standing one above another at distances, consisting of many somewhat broad leaves, set on each side of a middle rib, being hard, rough, or rugged, crumpled much like elm leaves, having also some smaller leaves with them (as agrimony has) somewhat deeply dented about the edges, of a dark green color on the upper side, and grayish underneath, of a fairly sharp scent and taste, somewhat like burnet; a leaf of this put into a cup of claret wine also gives a fine relish to it. At the tops of the stalks and branches stand many tufts of small white flowers, thrust thick together, which smell much sweeter than the leaves; and in their places, once fallen, come crooked and cornered seeds. The root is somewhat woody, and blackish on the outside, and brownish within, with several greater strings and lesser fibers attached to it, of a strong scent, but nothing so pleasant as the flowers and leaves; it does not perish, but abides many years, shooting forth anew every spring.

*Place.*] It grows in moist meadows that lie very wet, or near the courses of water.

*Time.*] It flowers in some place or other all the three summer months, that is, June, July, and August, and its seed is ripe quickly after.

<margin>Bleedings, Fluxes, Vomitings, women's periods & the whites, Quartan Ague, Colic, opens the bowels, Old Ulcers, heals sore Mouths, or Private Parts, raises Blisters, inflammation in the Eyes.</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] Venus claims dominion over the herb. It is used to stop all manner of bleedings, fluxes, vomitings, and women's periods, as also their whites. It is said to alter and take away the fits of quartan agues, and to make a merry heart, for which purpose some use the flowers, and some the leaves. It helps speedily those that are troubled with the colic, being boiled in wine; and with a little honey taken warm, it opens the bowels; but boiled in red wine and drunk, it stops the flux of the belly. Being outwardly applied, it heals old ulcers that are cancerous or eaten, or hollow and fistulous, for which it is much commended by many, as also for sores in the mouth or private parts. The leaves, when they are full grown, if laid upon the skin, will in a short time raise blisters thereon, as Tragus says. The water thereof helps the heat and inflammation in the eyes.

# The Quince-Tree.

*Descript.*] The ordinary quince tree grows often to the height and size of a moderate apple tree, but more usually lower and crooked with a rough bark, spreading arms and branches far abroad. The leaves are somewhat like those of the apple tree, but thicker, harder, and fuller of veins, and white on the underside, not dented at all about the edges.

edges. *The flowers are large and white, sometimes dashed over with a blush. The fruit that follows is yellow when near ripe, and covered with a white fuzz or cotton, thick-set on the younger ones, and growing less as they grow to be thoroughly ripe; it is often bunched out in some places, some being more like an apple and some like a pear, of a strong, heady scent, and not durable to keep, and is sour, harsh, and of an unpleasant taste to eat fresh; but being scalded, roasted, baked, or preserved, it becomes more pleasant.*

*Place and Time.*] It likes best to grow near ponds and water sides, and is frequent throughout this land; it flowers not until the leaves have come forth. The fruit is ripe in September or October.

<margin>*Fluxes, Diarrhea, etc.*</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] Old Saturn owns the tree. Quinces, when they are green, help all sorts of fluxes in man or woman, and choleric diarrhea, vomitings, and whatever needs binding more than any way prepared by fire; yet the syrup of the juice, or the conserve, are very helpful, much of the binding quality being consumed by the fire. <margin>*Provokes appetite, stops vomiting,*</margin> If a little vinegar be added, it stirs up the languishing appetite and the stomach given to vomiting. <margin>*Fainting spirits,*</margin> Some spices being added, it comforts and strengthens the decayed and fainting spirits, and helps the liver when it is so oppressed that it cannot perfect the digestion; and <margin>*Choler, Phlegm,*</margin> it corrects choler and phlegm. If you would have them purging, put honey to them instead of sugar; and if you want them more laxative, for choler, use rhubarb; for phlegm, <term>turbith</term>; for watery humors, <term>scammony</term>; but if you want them to bind more forcibly, use the unripe quinces with roses, and <term>acacia</term>, or <term>hypocistis</term>, and some toasted rhubarb. <margin>*poison,*</margin> To take the crude juice of quinces is held to be a preservative against the force of deadly poison; for it has been found most certainly true that the very smell of a quince has taken away all the strength of the poison of white hellebore. If there be need of any outward binding and cooling of any hot fluxes: the oil of quinces, or other medicines that may be made from them, are very available to anoint the belly or other parts with. It likewise strengthens the stomach and belly, and the sinews that are loosened by sharp humors falling on them, and restrains immoderate sweatings. <margin>*Women's breasts,*</margin> The mucilage taken from the seeds of quinces, boiled a little in water, is very good to cool the heat and heal the sore breasts of women. The same with a little sugar is good to soften the harshness and hoarseness of the throat and the roughness of the tongue. <margin>*plague sores,*</margin> The cotton or down of quinces boiled and applied to plague sores heals them up; and <margin>*preserves hair.*</margin> laid as a plaster made up with wax, it brings hair to those who are bald and keeps it from falling if it be ready to shed.

## Radish and Horse-Radish.

The garden radish is so well known that it needs no description.

## Ragwort.

**I**t is called also St. James-wort, Stagger-wort, Stammer-wort, and Seggrum.

*Descript.*] The greater common ragwort has many large and long dark green leaves lying on the ground, very much rent and torn on the sides into many pieces; from among which rise up sometimes but one, and sometimes two or three square or crested blackish or brownish stalks three or four feet high, sometimes branched, bearing various such leaves upon them at several distances unto the tops, where it branches forth into many stalks bearing yellow flowers, consisting of various leaves set as a pale or border, with a dark yellow thrum in the middle, which remain a great while, but at last are turned into down, and with the small blackish gray seed are carried away with the wind. The root is made of many fibers, whereby it is firmly fastened into the ground, and lives for many years.

In *Sussex*, we call it Ragweed.

## Rattle-grass.

Of this, there are two kinds which I shall speak of, namely: the Red and the Yellow.

*Description.*] The common Red Rattle has several reddish hollow stalks, and sometimes green ones, rising from the root, lying for the most part on the ground, yet some growing more upright, with many small reddish or greenish leaves set on both sides of a middle rib, finely dented around the edges. The flowers stand at the tops of the stalks and branches, of a fine purplish-red color, like small gaping hoods; after which come flat blackish seeds in small husks, which, lying loose inside, will rattle when shaken. The root consists of two or three small whitish strings with some fibers on them.

The common Yellow Rattle seldom has more than one round green stalk rising from the root, about half a yard or two feet high, and but few branches on it, having two long and somewhat broad leaves set at a joint, deeply cut in on the edges, resembling the comb of a cock, broadest next to the stalk and smaller toward the end. The flowers grow at the tops of the stalks with some shorter leaves with them, hooded in the same manner as the others, but of a beautiful yellow color in most, or in some paler, and in

# Rest-Harrow, or Cammock.

*Description.*] Common *rest-harrow* rises up with various rough, woody twigs, half a yard or a yard high, set at the joints without order, with little roundish leaves—sometimes more than two or three at a place—of a dark green color; it is without thorns while young, but afterwards armed in several places with short and sharp thorns. The flowers come forth at the tops of the twigs and branches, of which it is full; they are shaped like peas or pea blossoms, but smaller, flatter, and somewhat closer, of a faint purplish color. Afterwards come small pods containing small, flat, and round seed. The root is blackish on the outside and whitish within, very tough and hard to break when it is fresh and green, and as hard as horn when it is dried, pushing down deep into the ground and spreading likewise; every piece is likely to grow again if it is left in the ground.

*Place.*] It grows in many places in this land, as well in arable as waste ground.

*Time.*] It flowers about the beginning or middle of *July*, and the seed is ripe in *August*.

# Rocket.

Since the garden rocket is used more as a salad herb than for any medicinal purposes, I shall omit it and only speak of the common wild rocket. The description of it follows:

*Description.*] *The common wild rocket has longer and narrower leaves, much more divided into slender cuts and jags on both sides of the middle rib than the garden kinds have, of a dull, faded green color. From among these rise several stiff stalks two or three feet high, sometimes set with similar leaves, but becoming smaller toward the top, branched from the middle into various stiff stalks, bearing several yellow flowers made of four leaves each, as the others are, which afterwards yield small reddish seed in small long pods, of a more bitter and hot, biting taste than the garden kinds, as the leaves are also.*

*Place.*] It is found wild in various places in this land.

*Time.*] It flowers about *June* and *July*, and the seed is ripe in *August*.

# Winter Rocket, or Cresses.

<margin>Description.]</margin> Winter Rocket, or Winter Cresses, has several somewhat large, dull green leaves lying upon the ground, torn or cut into various parts, somewhat like those of *Rocket* or turnip leaves, with smaller pieces next to the bottom and broad at the ends. These remain all winter (if they spring up in *autumn*, when they are commonly eaten). From among these rise several small round stalks full of branches, bearing many small yellow flowers with four petals each, after which come small long pods with reddish seed in them. The root is somewhat stringy and dies every year after the seed is ripe.

<margin>Place.]</margin> It grows of its own accord in gardens and fields, by the roadsides in various places, and particularly in the pasture next to the Conduit-Head behind *Gray's Inn* that brings water to *Mr. Lamb's* conduit in *Holborn*.

<margin>Time.]</margin> It flowers in *May* and seeds in *June*, and then dies.

<margin>Government and Virtues.]</margin> This is beneficial for promoting urine and helping the strangury <note>painful or difficult urination</note>, and for expelling gravel and the stone; it is also effective against the scurvy. It is found by experience to be an exceptionally good wound herb for cleansing inward wounds; the juice or decoction being drunk, or outwardly applied to wash foul ulcers and sores, cleanses them by its sharpness, <margin>Strangury, gravel, and stone; scurvy; wounds, ulcers, and sores.</margin> hindering or reducing the growth of proud flesh within them, and healing them by its drying quality.

In the middle of these balls are often found certain white worms, which, being dried and made into powder and some of it drunk, is found by the experience of many to kill and drive forth worms from the belly.

# Rosa Solis, or Sun-dew.

<margin>*Description.*]</margin>
This has several small, round, hollow leaves, somewhat greenish, but full of certain red hairs which make them seem red, every one standing upon its own footstalk, which is similarly reddish and hairy. The leaves are continually moist even on the hottest day; indeed, the hotter the sun shines on them, the moister they are, with a certain sliminess that will "rope" (as we say), the small hairs always holding this moisture. Among these leaves rise up small slender stalks, also reddish, three or four fingers high, bearing several small white knobs one above another, which are the flowers; after which, in the heads, are certain small seeds. The root consists of a few small hairs.

<margin>*Place.*]</margin>
It grows usually on bogs, and in wet places, and sometimes in moist woods.

<margin>*Time.*]</margin>
It flowers in June, and then the leaves are fittest to be gathered.

<margin>*Government and Virtues.*] *Distillations of rheum, phthisic, wheezing, shortness of breath, cough, ulcers in the lungs, comfort the heart, raise blisters, passions of the heart.*</margin>
The Sun rules it, and it is under the sign Cancer. *Rosa Solis* is accounted good to help those that have salt rheum <note>a watery discharge from the mucous membranes</note> distilling on their lungs, which breeds a consumption; and therefore the distilled water of it in wine is held fit and profitable for such people to drink, which water will be of a golden yellow color. The same water is held to be good for all other diseases of the lungs, such as phthisics <note>wasting diseases or pulmonary consumption</note>, wheezing, shortness of breath, or the cough, as also to heal the ulcers that happen in the lungs; and it comforts the heart and fainting spirits. The leaves outwardly applied to the skin will raise blisters, which has caused some to think it dangerous to be taken internally; but there are other things which will also draw blisters, yet are not at all dangerous to be taken internally. There is a common drink made of this with *aqua vitae* <note>strong distilled spirits</note> and spices, used frequently and without any offense or danger, but to good purpose in qualms and palpitations <note>passions</note> of the heart.

The Sun claims privilege in it, and it is under the celestial Ram <note>Aries</note>. It is an herb of as great use with us in these days as any whatsoever, not only for medicinal but civil purposes. The medicinal...

# Rhubarb, or Rhapontic.

Do not be startled and say this grows you know not how far away, and then ask me how it comes to pass that I bring it among our English simples <note>medicinal plants consisting of a single ingredient</note>? For though the name may suggest it is foreign, yet it grows with us in *England*, and quite frequently in our gardens. And when you have thoroughly read through its virtues, you will conclude it is in no way inferior to that which is brought to us from *China*; and by the time this has been as much used as that has been, the name which the other has gained will be eclipsed by the fame of this. Take, therefore, a description at large of it, as follows.

*Descrip.] At its first appearance out of the ground, when the winter is past, it has a great, round, brownish head, rising from the middle or sides of the root, which opens itself into several leaves one after another, very much crumpled or folded together at first, and brownish. But afterward it spreads itself and becomes smooth, very large, and almost round, each one standing on a brownish stalk the thickness of a man’s thumb when they are grown to their fullness, and most of them two feet and more in length—especially when they grow in any moist or good ground. And the stalk of the leaf also, from the bottom of it to the leaf itself, is also two feet; the breadth of it from edge to edge in the broadest place is also two feet; of a dull or dark green color, of a fine tart or sourish taste, much more pleasant than the garden or wood sorrel. From among these there rises up some years, but not every year, a strong thick stalk, not growing so high as the patience or garden dock, with such round leaves as grow below, but smaller at every joint up to the top. Among the flowers, which are white, it spreads forth into many branches, consisting of five or six small white leaves each, hardly to be distinguished from the white threads in the middle, and appearing to be all threads; after which come brownish three-cornered seeds like those of other docks, but larger, by which it may be plainly known to be a dock. The root grows in time to be very great, with various and several great spreading branches from it, of a dark, brownish, or reddish color on the outside, with a pale yellow skin under it which covers the inner substance or root. When this rind and skin are pared away, the root appears of so fresh and lively a color, with fresh-colored veins running through it, that the choicest rhubarb that is brought to us from beyond the seas cannot excel it. If this root is dried carefully and as it ought to be (which in our country must be done by the gentle heat of a fire, because the sun is not hot enough here to do it, and every piece must be kept from touching one another), it will hold its color almost as well as when it is fresh; and it has been approved of and commended by those who have often used them.*

Place.] It grows in gardens, and flowers about the beginning or middle of *June*, and the seed is ripe in *July*.

Time.] The roots that are to be dried and kept all the year following,

## Garden Patience, or Monk’s Rhubarb.

<margin>*Description*</margin> This is a dock bearing the name of rhubarb because of its purging quality. It grows with large, tall stalks set with somewhat broad and long, beautiful green leaves that are not serrated at all. The tops of the stalks, being divided into many small branches, bear reddish or purplish flowers and three-sided seeds like other docks. The root is long, large, and yellow like the wild dock's, but a little redder; and if it is slightly dried, it shows fewer discolored veins than the next one does when it is dry.

## Great Round-leaved Dock, or Bastard Rhubarb.

<margin>*Description*</margin> This has several large, round, thin, yellowish-green leaves rising from the root, a little wavy around the edges, each standing on a reasonably thick and long brownish footstalk. From among these rises up a fairly large stalk about two feet high, with some similar leaves growing on it, but smaller. At the top of it, many small brownish flowers stand in a long spike; these turn into hard, three-sided, shining brown seeds, like the Garden Patience described before. This root grows larger than that one, with many branches of large fibers. It is yellow on the outside and somewhat pale yellow within, with some discolored veins like the rhubarb first described, but much less so, especially when it is dry.

<margin>*Place and Time*</margin> These also grow in gardens, and flower and seed at or near the same time that our true rhubarb does; namely, they flower in *June*, and the seed is ripe in *July*.

<margin>*Government and Virtues*</margin> <margin>Purges choler and phlegm, stays diarrhea and blood</margin> *Mars* claims predominance over all these wholesome herbs. You cry out against him as an ill fortune, when God created him for your good (he is only angry with fools). What dishonor is this, not to *Mars*, but to God himself? ## Meadow Rue.

**Description.**] Meadow Rue rises up with a yellow stringy root, spreading extensively in the ground and shooting forth new sprouts all around, with many herbaceous green stalks two feet high, ridged along their entire length, set with joints here and there. It has many large leaves on the stalks as well as below, which are divided into smaller leaves, notched or indented at their front part, of a dull green color on the upper side and pale green underneath. Toward the top of the stalk, several short branches shoot forth; on every one of these stand two, three, or four small round heads or buttons which, when they break the skin that encloses them, show a tuft of pale greenish-yellow threads. When these fall away, small three-cornered pods take their place, containing small, long, and round seed. The whole plant has a strong, unpleasant scent.

**Place.**] It grows in many places of this land, in the borders of moist meadows and by the sides of ditches.

**Time.**] It flowers about *July* or the beginning of *August*.

**Government and Virtues.**] Dioscorides says that this herb, when bruised and applied, perfectly heals old sores; the distilled water of the herb and flowers does the same. In *Italy*, it is used against the plague, and in *Saxony* against the jaundice, as *Camerarius* says.

# Rupture wort.

**Descript.]** This *spreads very many thread-like branches all around upon the ground, about a span long, divided into many other smaller parts, full of small joints set very thick together, where there come forth two very small leaves of a French yellow-green color; along the branches also grow a number of exceedingly small yellowish flowers, scarcely to be discerned from the stalks and leaves, which turn into seeds as small as dust. The root is very long and small, pushing down deep into the ground. This has neither smell nor taste at first, but afterward has a little astringent taste, without any manifest heat, yet a little bitter and sharp withal.*

**Place.]** It grows in dry, sandy, and rocky places.

**Time.]** It is fresh and green all the summer.

Being outwardly applied, it joins wounds together notably and helps much to stop defluxions <note>flows</note> of rheum from the head to the eyes, nose, and teeth, being bruised green and bound to them; or the decoction of the dried herb may be used to bathe the forehead and temples, or the nape of the neck behind. It also dries up the moisture of fistulous ulcers, or any others that are foul and spreading.

## Rushes.

**A**lthough there are many kinds of rushes, yet I shall only here insist upon those which are best known and most medicinal, such as the bulrushes and others of the soft and smooth kinds; which grow so commonly in almost every place of this land and are so generally noted that I suppose it is needless to trouble you with any description of them. Briefly then, take their virtues as follows.

<margin>*Government and virtues.*</margin>
The seeds of these soft rushes, says *Dioscorides* and *Galen*, toasted (says *Pliny*) and drunk in wine and water, stops the lask <note>diarrhea</note> and women's menstrual courses when they come down too abundantly; but it causes headache. It provokes sleep likewise, but must be given with caution, lest the person who takes it does not wake until the Resurrection. *Pliny* says the root boiled in water until one-third has evaporated helps the cough.

Thus you see that conveniences have their inconveniences, and virtue is seldom unaccompanied by some vices. What I have written concerning rushes is to satisfy my countrymen's question, *Are our rushes good for nothing?* Yes, and they are as well left alone as taken; there are remedies enough without them for any disease, and therefore, as the proverb goes, I care not a rush for them, or rather they will do you as much good as if someone had given you a rush.

## Rye.

**T**his is so well known in all the counties of this land, and especially to the country people who feed much upon it, that if I should describe it, they would presently say I might well have spared that labor.

<margin>*Its virtues follow. Abscesses, boils, and swellings; pains of the head; chaps of the hands or feet.*</margin>
*Government and virtues.*] Rye is more digesting than wheat. The bread and the leaven thereof ripen and break abscesses, boils, and other swellings. The meal of rye put between a double cloth, moistened with a little vinegar, and heated in a pewter dish set over a chafing dish of coals, and bound fast to the head while it is hot, does much ease the continual pains of the head. *Mathiolus* says that the ashes of rye straw put into water and left there for a day and a night, and the chaps <note>cracks in the skin</note> of the hands or feet washed therewith, heals them.

# Saffron.

The herb needs no description, as it is generally known where it grows.

<margin>Strengthens the heart and brain.</margin>
*Place.*] It grows frequently at Walden in Essex, and in Cambridgeshire.

<margin>Consumption of the lungs, plague, smallpox, measles, yellow jaundice. Purges phlegm.</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] It is an herb of the Sun, and under the sign of Leo, and therefore you need not ask for a reason why it strengthens the heart so exceedingly. Let no more than ten grains be given at one time; for if the Sun, which is the fountain of life, may dazzle the eyes and make them blind, a cordial being taken in an immoderate quantity may hurt the heart instead of helping it. It quickens the brain, for the Sun is exalted in Aries just as he has his house in Leo. It helps consumption of the lungs and difficulty of breathing; it is an excellent thing for epidemic diseases, such as the plague, smallpox, and measles. It is a notable expulsive medicine, and a notable remedy for yellow jaundice. My own opinion is (though I have no author for it) that Hermodactyls are nothing else but the roots of saffron dried; and my reason is that the roots of all crocus, both white and yellow, purge phlegm as Hermodactyls do; and if you please to dry the roots of any crocus, neither your eyes nor your taste shall distinguish them from Hermodactyls.

# Sage.

Our ordinary garden sage needs no description.
*Time.*] It flowers in or about July.

<margin>Provokes urine and women's courses; expels the dead fetus and afterbirth; stops bleeding; cleanses ulcers and sores; relieves itching of the scrotum; helps conception and prevents miscarriage; stops spitting blood; helps consumption, pains of the head and joints, and falling sickness.</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] Jupiter claims this, and bids me tell you it is good for the liver and to produce good blood. A decoction of the leaves and branches of sage made and drunk, says Dioscorides, provokes urine, brings down women's courses, helps to expel the dead fetus, and causes the hair to become black; it stops the bleeding of wounds and cleanses foul ulcers or sores. The same decoction made in wine takes away the itching of the scrotum <note>cods</note> if it is bathed with it. It is much commended against the stitch or pains in the side coming from wind, if the place be warmed with the decoction thereof in wine, and the herb also after boiling be laid warm upon it.

## Wood-Sage.

<margin>Description.]</margin> *Wood-Sage rises up with square, hoary stalks at least two feet high, with two leaves set at every joint, somewhat like other Sage leaves, but smaller, softer, whiter, and rounder, and a little dented about the edges, and smelling somewhat stronger. At the tops of the stalks and branches stand the flowers on a slender long spike, turning themselves all one way when they bloom; they are of a pale and whitish color, smaller than Sage, but hooded and gaping like them. The seed is blackish and round, usually four set together in a husk. The root is long and stringy, with several fibers attached, and lasts for many years.*

The decoction of Wood-Sage provokes urine and women's courses; it also provokes sweat, digests humors, and disperses swellings and nodes <note>hard lumps</note> in the flesh, and is therefore thought to be good against the French Pox. ## Solomon's Seal.

Description.] The common Solomon’s Seal rises up with a round stalk about *half a yard high*, bowing or bending down at the top, set with single leaves one above another, somewhat large and like the leaves of the Lily of the Valley, or *May Lily*, with a hint of bluish upon the green, with some ribs within, and more yellowish underneath. At the base of almost every leaf from the bottom up to the top of the stalk come forth small, long, white, and hollow pendulous flowers, somewhat like the flowers of the *May Lily*, but ending in five long points, for the most part two together at the end of a long footstalk, and sometimes but one, and sometimes also two stalks with flowers at the base of a leaf; these are without any scent at all and stand all on one side of the stalk. After they are past, there come in their places small round berries, green at first and blackish-green, tending toward blueness when they are ripe, wherein lie small, white, hard, and stony seeds. The root is of the thickness of one's finger or thumb, white and knobbed in some places, with a flat round circle representing a seal—from which it took its name—lying along under the upper crust of the earth and not growing downward, but with many fibers underneath.

Place.] It is frequent in various places of this land, namely in a wood two miles from *Canterbury*, by *Fishpool Hill*; as also in a bushy close belonging to the parsonage of *Alderbury* near *Clarendon*, two miles from *Salisbury*; in *Chesson Wood*, on *Chesson Hill*, between *Newington* and *Sittingbourne* in *Kent*; and in various other places in *Essex* and other counties.

Time.] It flowers about *May*. The root remains and shoots anew every year.

**Government and Virtues.]** Saturn owns the plant, for he loves his bones well. It also serves to knit and join broken bones in any part of the body when the roots are bruised and applied to the place. Indeed, it has been found by recent experience that a decoction of the root in wine, or the bruised root put in wine or another drink and strained hard after a night’s infusion and then drunk, has helped both man and beast whose bones have been broken by any cause; this is the most reliable source of help for people in various parts of this land. It is no less effective for helping ruptures and burstings, whether the decoction in wine or the powder in broth or drink is taken internally and applied externally to the area. The same is also effective for internal or external bruises, falls, or blows, both to disperse congealed blood and to take away both the pain and the black and blue marks that remain after the injury. This plant, or the distilled water of the whole plant applied to the face or other parts of the skin, cleanses it from morphew <note>scurfy skin eruptions</note>, freckles, spots, or any marks whatsoever, leaving the place fresh, fair, and lovely; for this purpose, it is much used by the *Italian ladies*.

## Samphire.

<margin>Description.]</margin>
Rock Samphire grows up with a tender green stalk about half a yard or two feet high at the most, branching out almost from the very bottom, and is filled with various thick, almost round, and somewhat long leaves of a deep green color. These are sometimes three together and sometimes more on a stalk, and they are succulent and have a pleasant, hot, or spicy taste. At the tops of the stalk and branches stand umbels of white flowers, followed by large seeds bigger than fennel seeds, yet somewhat similar. The root is large, white, and long, living for many years, and also has a hot, spicy taste.

<margin>Place.]</margin>
It grows on the rocks that are at least frequently moistened, if not flooded, by seawater.

<margin>Time.]</margin>
It flowers and seeds at the end of *July* and *August*.

<margin>Government and Virtues.] Helps digestion, opens obstructions</margin>
**Government and Virtues.]** It is an herb of *Jupiter*, and in former times it was used more than it is now—which is a pity. # Sanicle.

**Description.]** *Ordinary Sanicle sends forth many large round leaves standing upon long brownish stalks, every one somewhat deeply cut or divided into five or six parts, and some of those also cut in, somewhat like the leaf of a crowfoot or dove's-foot, and finely dented around the edges, smooth, and of a dark green shining color, and sometimes reddish around the brims; from among these rise up small round green stalks, without any joint or leaf on them, except at the top, where it branches out into flowers, having a leaf divided into three or four parts at that joint with the flowers, which are small and white, starting out of small round greenish-yellow heads, many standing together in a tuft; in these the seeds are afterward contained, which are small round rough burs, somewhat like the seeds of cleavers, and they stick in the same manner upon anything that they touch. The root is composed of many black strings of fibers set together at a small long head, which remains with the green leaves all winter and does not perish.*

**Place.]** *It is found in many shady woods and other places of this land.*

**Time.]** *It flowers in June, and the seed is ripe shortly after.*

<margin>
Fresh wounds, ulcers, abscesses, internal bleedings, swellings, ulcers in the mouth, throat, and private parts, women's periods, flows of blood, diarrhea, ulcers in the kidneys, running of the reins, rupture.
</margin>
**Government and Virtues.]** *This is one of **Venus's** herbs to cure either **wounds**, or whatever other mischief **Mars** inflicts upon the body of man. It is exceedingly good to heal all **fresh wounds** speedily, or any **ulcers, abscesses**, or **internal bleedings**. It wonderfully helps those who have any **tumors** in any part of their bodies, for it represses and dissipates the humors if the decoction or juice is taken, or the powder in drink, and the juice used externally; for there is no herb found that can give such immediate help to either man or beast when the disease falls upon the **lungs** or **throat**, and to heal up all the **putrid malignant ulcers** in the **mouth, throat**, and **private parts**, by gargling or washing with the decoction of the leaves and root, made in water with a little honey added. ## Saracen's Confound, or Saracen's Woundwort.

<margin>Description.]</margin> *This grows very high, sometimes with brownish stalks, and at other times with green and hollow ones to a man's height, having many long and narrow green leaves snipped about the edges, somewhat like those of the peach tree or willow leaves, but not of such a white-green color. The tops of the stalks are furnished with many pale yellow star-like flowers standing in green heads, which, when they have fallen and the seed is ripe—which is somewhat long, small, and of a yellowish-brown color wrapped in down—is carried away with the wind. The root is composed of many strings or fibers, set together at a head, which do not perish in winter but remain, although the stalks dry away and no leaf appears in winter. The taste of it is strong and unpleasant, and so is the smell also.*

<margin>Place.]</margin> *It grows in moist and wet grounds by wood sides, and sometimes in the moist places of shady groves, as also by the waterside.*

<margin>Time.]</margin> *It flowers in July, and the seed is soon ripe and carried away with the wind.*

<margin>
Government and Virtues.]
Obstructions, yellow jaundice, dropsy, ulcers of the kidneys, inward wounds and bruises, pains in the body, the mother, agues, fresh wounds, old sores or ulcers, ulcers in the mouth or throat, sores in the private parts.
</margin>
Saturn owns this herb, and it is of a sober condition like him. Among the Germans, this wound-herb is preferred before all others of the same quality. Being boiled in wine and drunk, it helps the indisposition of the liver and frees the gall from obstructions, making it good for the yellow jaundice and for the dropsy in its beginning, for all inward ulcers of the kidneys or elsewhere, and inward wounds and bruises. And being steeped in wine and then distilled, the water from it, when drunk, is exceptionally good to ease all gnawings in the stomach or other pains of the body, as also the pains of the mother <note>pains associated with the uterus or hysteria</note>. And being boiled in water, it helps continual agues; and this said water, or the simple distilled water of the herb, or the juice, or decoction, are very effective to heal any fresh wound or old sore or ulcer whatsoever, cleansing them from corruption and quickly healing them up. It is no less effective for ulcers in the mouth or throat, be they ever so foul or stinking, by washing and gargling them with it; and likewise for such sores as happen in the private parts of man or woman. Briefly, whatever has been said of bugle or sanicle may be found herein.

## Sauce-alone, or Jack-by-the-Hedge.

*Descript.*] The lower leaves of this are rounder than those that grow towards the tops of the stalks, and are set singly at each joint, being somewhat round and broad, and pointed at the ends, and also dented about the edges, somewhat resembling nettle leaves in form, but of a fresher green color, and not rough or pricking. The flowers are very small and white, growing at the tops of the stalks one above another; after they are past, there follow small, long, and round pods, in which are contained small round seeds, somewhat blackish. The root is stringy and thready, dying every year after it has given seed, and raising itself again from its own sowing. The plant, or any part of it being bruised, smells of garlic, but more pleasantly, and tastes somewhat hot and sharp, almost like rocket.

*Place.*] It grows under walls, and by hedge-sides and pathways in fields, in many places.

*Time.*] It flowers in *June, July,* and *August.*

<margin>
Helps digestion, cough, tough phlegm, wind colic, stone, ulcers in the legs.
</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] It is an herb of *Mercury.* This is eaten by many country people as a sauce for their salt-fish, and helps well to digest the crudities and other corrupt humors engendered thereby; it also warms the stomach and causes digestion. The juice thereof boiled with honey is accounted to be as good as hedge-mustard for the cough, to cut and expectorate tough phlegm. The seed bruised and boiled in wine is a singularly good remedy for the wind colic or the stone, being drunk warm. It is also given to women troubled with the Mother, both to drink, and the seed put into a cloth and applied while it is warm is of singularly good use. The leaves or seed boiled are also good to be used in clysters to ease the pains of the stone. The green leaves are held to be good to heal ulcers in the legs.

To describe a plant so well known is unnecessary, as it is cultivated in almost every garden and stays green all winter.

## The common white Saxifrage.

<margin>
Description.
</margin>
*Description.*] This has a few small reddish kernels for roots, covered with some skins lying among various small blackish fibers, which send forth various round, pale, or yellowish-green leaves, grayish underneath, lying above the ground and unevenly dented about the edges and somewhat hairy, each on a little footstalk. From these rises a round, brownish, hairy green stalk, two or three feet high, with a few such round leaves as grow below but smaller, and somewhat branched at the top, where there stand fairly large white flowers of five leaves each, with some yellow threads in the middle, standing in long, crested, brownish-green husks. # Burnet Saxifrage.

*Description.*] The greater sort of our English Burnet Saxifrage grows up with various long stalks of winged leaves, set directly opposite one another on both sides, each being somewhat broad, and a little pointed and dented about the edges, of a dull green color. At the tops of the stalks stand umbels of white flowers, after which comes small and blackish seed. The root is long and whitish, abiding long. Our lesser Burnet Saxifrage has much finer leaves than the former, and very small, and set one against another, deeply jagged about the edges, and of the same color as the former. The umbels of flowers are white, and the seed very small, and so is the root, being also somewhat hot and sharp in taste.

*Place.*] These grow in most meadows of this land, and are easy to be found, being well sought for among the grass, wherein many times they lie hidden, scarcely to be discerned.

*Time.*] They flower about *July*, and their seed is ripe in *August*.

<margin>*Promotes urine, eases wind & colic, the Mother, women's courses, stone, tough phlegm, venom, cramps & convulsions, wounds in the head, freckles and spots.*</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] They are both of them herbs of the *Moon*. These Saxifrages are as hot as pepper; and *Tragus* says by his experience, they are more wholesome. They have the same properties that the parsleys have, but in promoting urine and easing the pains thereof, or of gas and colic, they are much more effectual. The roots or seed being used either in powder, or in decoction, or any other way; it likewise helps the windy pains of the Mother <note>the uterus or hysteria</note>, and helps to procure their courses, to break and avoid the stone in the kidneys, to digest cold, viscous, and tough phlegm in the stomach, and is a most special remedy against all kind of venom. *Castoreum* being boiled in the distilled water hereof, is singularly good to be given to those that are troubled

# Scabious, three sorts.

<margin>Description.]</margin> *The common field scabious grows up with many hairy, soft, whitish-green leaves, some of which are very small, if at all jagged on the edges; others are very much torn and shredded on the sides and have threads in them, which may be plainly seen upon breaking them. From among these rise various hairy green stalks three or four feet high, with similar hairy green leaves on them, but more deeply and finely divided, and branched out a little. At the tops of these, which are naked and bare of leaves for a long stretch, stand round heads of flowers of a pale bluish color, set together in a head; the outermost of these are larger than the inward ones, with many threads also in the middle, somewhat flat at the top, as the seed head is also. The root is large, white, and thick, growing deep in the ground and lasting many years.*

*There is another sort of field scabious, differing in nothing from the former, except that it is smaller in all respects.*

*The corn scabious differs little from the first, except that it is larger in all respects, and the flowers lean more toward purple. The root creeps under the upper crust of the earth and does not run deep into the ground as the first one does.*

<margin>Place.]</margin> The first grows most usually in meadows, especially everywhere around London.

The second grows in some of the dry fields about this city, but not as plentifully as the former.

The third grows in the standing corn, or fallow fields, and the borders of such fields.

<margin>Time.]</margin> They flower in *June* and *July*, and some continue flowering until late in *August*; the seed is ripe in the meantime.

There are many other sorts of scabious, but I take those which I have described here to be the most familiar to us. Since the virtues of these and the rest are much alike, understand them as follows.

<margin>Government and Virtues.]</margin> <margin>Cough and shortness of breath, cold phlegm, inward ulcers and abscesses <note>impostumes</note>, pleurisy, infection, carbuncles or plague sores.</margin> *Mercury* owns the plant. Scabious is very effective for all sorts of coughs, shortness of breath, and all other diseases of the chest and lungs, ripening and digesting cold phlegm and other tough humors, expelling them by coughing and spitting. It also ripens all sorts of inward ulcers and abscesses <note>impostumes</note>, and pleurisy also, if the decoction of the herb (dried or green) is made in wine and drunk for some time together. ## Scurvy-grass.

<margin>Description.]</margin> OUR ordinary English *Scurvy-grass* has many thick fat leaves, longer than they are broad, and sometimes longer and narrower, sometimes also smooth on the edges, and sometimes a little waved, sometimes plain, smooth, and pointed, sometimes a little hollow in the middle and round-pointed, of a dark green, and sometimes bluish color; every one standing by itself upon a long footstalk, which is brownish or greenish also. From among these rise small slender stalks, bearing a few leaves on them like the others, but for the most part longer and smaller. At the tops of these grow many whitish flowers, with yellow threads in the middle, standing about a green head which becomes the seed vessel, which will be somewhat flat when it is ripe, in which is contained reddish seed tasting somewhat hot.

**IT** is so well known in the places where it grows that it needs no *Description*.

# Shepherd’s Purse.

It is also called Whoreman's Spermaceti, Shepherd's Scrip, Shepherd's Pouch, Toy-wort, Pick-purse, and Case-weed.

*Description.*] The root is small, white, and perishes every year. The leaves are small and long, of a pale green color, and deeply cut on both sides. Among these springs up a stalk which is small and round, containing small leaves upon it even to the top. The flowers are white and very small, after which come the little cases which hold the seed, which are flat and almost in the shape of a heart.

*Place.*] They are frequent in this nation, by almost every path’s side.

*Time.*] They flower all summer long; indeed, some of them are so fruitful that they flower twice a year.

<margin>
Stops fluxes, flux of the belly, spitting and urinating blood, stops menstrual courses, yellow jaundice, pains, noise, and discharges in the ears, wounds.
</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] It is under the dominion of Saturn and is of a cold, dry, and binding nature like him. It stops all fluxes of blood, whether caused by inward or outward wounds, as well as flux of the belly and bloody flux <note>dysentery</note>, spitting and urinating of blood. It stops the menstrual courses in women when bound to the wrists of the hands and the soles of the feet. It helps with yellow jaundice. The herb, being made into a poultice, helps inflammations and St. Anthony's Fire <note>erysipelas</note>. The juice, being dropped into the ears, helps their pains, noises, and discharges. A good ointment may be made of it for all wounds, especially wounds in the head.

## Soapwort, or Bruise-wort.

*Description.*] *The root creeps underground far and wide, with many joints in it, of a brown color on the outside and yellowish within, shooting forth in various places many weak round stalks, full of joints, with two leaves at each joint on opposite sides; these are ribbed somewhat like Plantain and shaped like the common field white Campion leaves, seldom having any branches from the sides of the stalks, but set with various flowers at the top standing in long husks like the wild Campions. These are made of five leaves each, round at the ends and a little dented in the middle, of a pale rose color, almost white, sometimes deeper and sometimes paler, with a reasonably good scent.*

*Place.*] It grows wild in many low and wet grounds of this land, by the brooks and sides of running waters.

*Time.*] It usually flowers in July, and so continues all through August and part of September before they are quite finished.

<margin>
*Cut fingers, provokes urine, expels gravel and stone, dropsy, French pox <note>syphilis</note>.*
</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] *Venus* owns it. The country people in various places use the bruised leaves of Soapwort and apply them to their fingers, hands, or legs when they are cut, to heal them again. Some boast that it is a diuretic to provoke urine, and thereby to expel gravel and the stone in the kidneys; and they also consider it exceptionally good for removing dropsical waters <note>fluid from edema</note>, thereby to cure the disease of dropsy. And they no less praise it for performing an absolute cure for the French pox <note>syphilis</note>, more than either *Sarsaparilla*, *Guaiacum*, or *China* <note>China root</note> can do; how true this is, I leave to others to judge.

## Wood Sorrel.

After the flowers are past, small round heads follow, with small yellowish seed in them. The roots are nothing but small strings fastened to the end of a small long piece, all of them being of a yellowish color.

Sponges or linen cloths wet in the juice and applied outwardly to any hot swellings or inflammations, do much to cool and help them. The same juice taken and gargled in the mouth, and fresh juice taken after it is spit forth, wonderfully helps a foul, stinking canker or ulcer therein. It is singularly good for wounds, thrusts, and stabs in the body to stop bleeding and to cleanse and heal the wounds speedily; and it helps to stop any hot defluxions <note>discharges of fluid</note> into the throat or lungs.

## Sow-Thistles.

<margin>Pains and heat of the stomach, shortness of breath and wheezing, gravel and stone, stinking breath, speedy delivery, strangury, milk increased, deafness and ringing in the ears, inflamed eyes, wheals and blisters, hemorrhoids, clear the face.</margin>
Sow-thistles are generally so well known that they need no description.
**Place.**] They grow in our gardens and manured grounds, and sometimes by old walls, the pathsides of fields, and highways.
**Government and Vertues.**] This and the former are under the influence of *Venus*. Sow-thistles are cooling and somewhat binding, and are very fit to cool a hot stomach and to ease its gnawing pains. The herb boiled in wine is very helpful to stop the weakness <note>literally "dissolutions"</note> of the stomach; and the milk that is taken from the stalks when they are broken, given in drink, is beneficial to those who are short-winded and have a wheezing besides. *Pliny* says that it has caused gravel and stone to be passed by urine, and that eating it helps a stinking breath. Three spoonfuls of its juice taken in warmed white wine, with some oil added, causes women in labor to have such an easy and speedy delivery that they may be able to walk immediately afterward. The said juice taken in a warm drink helps the strangury <note>painful or difficult urination</note> and pains in passing water. The decoction of the leaves and stalks causes an abundance of milk in nurses and their children to be well-colored, and it is good for those whose milk curdles in their breasts. The juice boiled or thoroughly heated with a little oil of bitter almonds in the peel of a pomegranate, and dropped into the ears, is a sure remedy for deafness, ringing, and all other diseases in them. The bruised herb or the juice is profitably applied to all hot inflammations in the eyes or elsewhere, and for wheals, blisters, or other similar heat eruptions on the skin; as also for the heat and itching of hemorrhoids, and the heat and sharpness of humors in the private parts of man or woman. The distilled water of the herb is not only effective for all the diseases mentioned above when taken inwardly with a little sugar (which medicine the most delicate stomach will not refuse), but also outwardly, by applying cloths or sponges wetted with it. It is wonderfully good for women to wash their faces with to clear the skin and give it a luster.

# Southernwood.

Southernwood is so well known to be an ordinary inhabitant in our gardens that I shall not need to trouble you with any description of it.

<margin>*Time.*</margin>
*Time.*] It flowers for the most part in *July* and *August*.

<margin>
*Government and Virtues.*
*Ruptures, cramps and convulsions, sciatica, difficulty urinating, women’s monthly courses, poison, agues, inflamed eyes, pimples, pustules and welts, worms, splinters and thorns, old ulcers, sores in the private parts, baldness, the French disease, the stone, the spleen, and the Mother.*
</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] It is an excellent Mercurial plant, worthy of more esteem than it has. *Dioscorides* says that the seed crushed, heated in warm water and drunk, helps those who are ruptured <note>herniated</note>, or troubled with cramps, or convulsions of the sinews, sciatica, or difficulty in urinating, and brings down women’s monthly courses. The same taken in wine is an antidote or counter-poison against all deadly poison, and drives away serpents and other venomous creatures; the smell of the herb being burnt does the same. The oil of it, rubbed on the backbone before the fits of agues <note>fevers</note> come, takes them away. It takes away inflammations in the eyes if it is put with a portion of a roasted quince, boiled with a few crumbs of bread, and applied. Boiled with barley meal, it takes away pimples, pustules, or welts that rise in the face or other parts of the body. The seed as well as the dried herb is often given to kill the worms in children. The herb crushed and applied helps to draw forth splinters and thorns out of the flesh. The ashes of it dry up and heal old ulcers that are without inflammation, although by their sharpness they bite sorely and cause great pain; they also heal sores in the private parts of man or woman. The ashes mingled with old salad oil help those whose hair has fallen out and are bald, causing the hair to grow again either on the head or beard. *Durantes* says that the oil made of Southernwood and added to the ointments used against the French disease <note>syphilis</note> is very effective, and likewise kills lice in the head. The distilled water of the herb is said to help those much who are troubled with the stone, as also for diseases of the spleen and the Mother <note>an archaic term for hysteria or uterine disorders</note>. The Germans commend it as a singular wound herb and therefore call it *Stabwort*. It is held by all writers, ancient and modern, to be more offensive to the stomach than Wormwood.

From this head rise several long stalks of most finely cut leaves like hairs, smaller than *Dill*, set thick on both sides of the stalks and having a good scent. Among these leaves

## Spleenwort, or Ceterach.

*Descript.*] The smooth *Spleenwort* from a black, threadlike, and bushy root sends forth many long single leaves, cut in on both sides into round notches almost to the middle, which is not so hard as that of <term>Polypody</term>; each division is not always set opposite to the other, but between each; smooth and of a light green on the upper side, and a dark yellowish roughness on the back, folding or rolling itself inward at the first springing up.

*Place.*] It grows as well upon stone walls as in moist and shadowy places about *Bristol* and other western parts plentifully; as also on *Framingham* Castle, on *Beaconsfield* Church in *Berkshire*, at *Stroud* in *Kent* and elsewhere, and stays green all the winter.

*Government and Virtues.*] *Saturn* owns it. It is generally used against infirmities of the spleen; it helps the strangury and breaks down the stone in the bladder, and is good against the yellow jaundice and the hiccup; but the use of it in women hinders conception. *Mathiolus* says that if a dram of the dust that is on the back side of the leaves is mixed with half a dram of *Amber* in powder, and taken with the juice of Purslane or Plantain, it will help the running of the reins <note>a discharge from the kidneys or bladder, often referring to gonorrhea</note> speedily; and that the herb or root being boiled and taken, helps all melancholic diseases, and those especially that arise from the French Disease <note>syphilis</note>. *Camerarius* says that the distilled water of it, being drunk, is very effective against the stone in the reins <note>kidneys</note> and

# Star thistle.

<margin>Description.]</margin>
**A** *common Star-thistle has diverse long and narrow leaves lying next to the ground, cut or torn on the edges, somewhat deeply, into many almost even parts, soft or a little woolly all over the green; among which rise up diverse weak stalks parted into many branches, all lying or leaning down to the ground, so that it seems like a pretty bush, set with diverse similar divided leaves up to the tops, where severally stand long and small whitish green heads, set with sharp and long white pricks (no part of the plant being else prickly) which are somewhat yellowish; out of the middle of which rises the flower composed of many small reddish purple threads; and in the heads after the flowers are past, come small whitish round seeds lying down as others do. The root is small, long, and woody, perishing every year, and rising again from its own sowing.*

<margin>Place.]</margin>
It grows wild in the fields about *London* in many places, as at *Mile-end-green* in *Finsbury Fields* beyond the windmills, and many other places.

<margin>Time.]</margin>
It flowers early, and seeds in *July*, and sometimes in *August*.

<margin>Provokes urine, stone, plague, fistula, French pox, obstructions, agues.</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] This, as almost all thistles, is under *Mars*. The seed of this Star-thistle made into powder and drunk in wine, provokes urine, and helps to break the stone and drive it forth. The root in powder, given in wine and drunk, is good against the plague or pestilence, and drunk in the mornings fasting for some time together, is very profitable for a fistula in any part of the body. *Baptista Sardus* does much commend the distilled water hereof being drunk to help the French disease <note>syphilis</note>, to open obstructions of the liver, and cleanse the blood from corrupted humors; it is also profitably given against quotidian or tertian agues.

# Succory.

It also bears blue flowers like Endive, and the seed is difficult to distinguish from the seed of the smooth or ordinary Endive.*

*The wild Succory has various long leaves lying on the ground, very much indented or jagged on the edges on both sides, even to the midrib, ending in a point; sometimes it has a red rib down the middle of the leaves, from among which rises up a hard, round, woody stalk spreading into many branches, set with smaller and less divided leaves up to the tops where the flowers stand. These are like the garden kind, as is the seed also (only take notice that the flowers of the garden kind close up on a sunny day, they being so cold that they are not able to endure the beams of the sun, and therefore they most delight in the shadow). ## English Tobacco.

*Description.]* **T**his rises up with a thick round stalk, about two feet high, whereon grow thick, fat, green leaves, not nearly as large as the other Indian kinds, somewhat round-pointed also, and not at all dented about the edges. The stalk branches forth and bears at the tops various flowers set in green husks, like the other, but not nearly as large; scarcely standing above the rims of the husks, round-pointed also, and of a greenish-yellow color. The seed that follows is not as bright, but larger, contained in similar large heads. The roots are neither as great nor woody, and perish every year with the hard frosts in winter, but it generally rises from its own sowing.

*Place.]* This came from some parts of *Brazil*, it is thought, and is more familiar in our country than any of the other sorts, early giving ripe seed, which the others seldom do.

*Time.]* It flowers from *June* sometimes to the end of *August*, or later, and the seed ripens in the meantime.

</margin>

# The Tamarisk-Tree.

It is so well known in the places where it grows that it needs no description.

*Time.*] It flowers about the end of *May* or in *June*, and the seed is ripe and blown away in the beginning of *September*.

<margin>Spleen, hemorrhoids, spitting blood, women’s courses, jaundice, and colic, venomous serpents, toothache, pain in the ears, watering eyes, gangrenes and ulcers, nits and lice, spleen, burning and scalding, French pox, leprosy and scabs, dropsy, melancholy, black jaundice.</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] It is an excellent Saturnine herb. If the root, leaves, or young branches are boiled in wine or vinegar and drunk, and applied outwardly, it is very powerful against the hardness of the spleen. The leaves boiled in wine and drunk are good to stop the bleeding of the hemorrhoidal veins, the spitting of blood, and women's excessive courses; it also helps the jaundice, the colic, and the bites of all venomous serpents, except the asp. The bark is as effective, if not more so, for all the purposes mentioned above; and both it and the leaves boiled in wine, and the mouth and the teeth washed with it, helps the toothache; being dropped into the ears, it eases pains and is good for the redness and watering of the eyes. The said decoction with some honey added to it is good to stop gangrenes and fretting ulcers, and to wash those who are subject to nits and lice. The wood is very effective to consume the spleen, and therefore drinking out of cups and cans made from it is good for splenetic persons. The ashes of the wood are used for all the purposes mentioned above, and besides, they quickly help the blisters raised by burnings or scaldings, by fire or water. *Alpinus* and *Veslingius* affirm that the Egyptians use the wood of this tree to cure the French disease <note>syphilis</note> with as much success as others use *Lignum Vitae* or *Guaiacum*; they also give it to those afflicted with leprosy, scabs, pustules, ulcers, or the like; and it is also available to help the dropsy arising from the hardness and obstruction of the spleen, as well as for melancholy and the black jaundice that arises from it.

## Garden Tansy.

Garden Tansy is so well known that it needs no description.

*Time.*] It flowers in June and July.

*Government and Virtues.*] Lady Venus intended to please pregnant women with this herb; for there is no herb better suited for their use than this is; it is as if it were made for the purpose. The herb, bruised and applied to the navel, prevents miscarriages; I know of no herb like it for that purpose. Boiled in ordinary beer and the decoction drunk, it does the same; and if her womb is not as she would wish it to be, this decoction will make it as she desires, or at least, as it should be. Let those women who desire children love this herb; it is their best companion, except for their husbands. It also consumes the phlegmatic humors with which the cold and moist nature of winter usually infects the human body, and that was the original reason for eating tansies in the spring. Eventually, the world being overrun with Popery, a monster called Superstition reared its head and, as a just judgment from God, obscured the bright beams of knowledge with its dismal looks. (Physicians, seeing the Pope and his imps were selfish, began to be so too.) And now, forsooth, tansies must be eaten only on Palm and Easter Sundays and the days surrounding them. Finally, superstition becoming too much to bear, and the selfishness of physicians remaining obscure—after the friars and monks had made the people ignorant—the superstition of the time was exposed, but the virtue of the herb remained hidden; and now it is almost, if not entirely, abandoned. Surely our physicians are beholden to no one as much as they are to monks and friars; for the lack of eating this herb in spring makes people sickly in summer, and that creates work for the physician. If it is against any man's or woman's conscience to eat a tansy in the spring, I am as unwilling to burden their consciences as I am for them to burden mine; they may boil it in wine and drink the decoction, and it will have the same effect. <margin>Dysury, strangury, reins, kidneys, wind, womb, miscarriage, stone, stomach, worms, cramps</margin> The decoction of the common tansy, or the juice drunk in wine, is an extraordinary remedy for all the ailments caused by the suppression of urine; it helps with strangury and those who have weak reins <note>kidneys or lower back</note> and kidneys. It is also very beneficial for dissolving and expelling wind in the stomach, belly, or bowels, for provoking women's courses, and for expelling windiness in the matrix <note>womb</note>. If it is bruised and often smelled, as well as applied to the lower part of the belly, it is very beneficial for women prone to miscarry, helping them to carry to full term. It is also used against stones in the kidneys, especially for men. The herb fried with eggs (as is customary in the springtime), which is called a "tansy," helps to digest and carry downward those bad humors that trouble the stomach. The seed is very beneficial when given to children for worms, and the juice in a drink is just as effective. Being boiled in oil, it is good for sinews shrunk by cramps or pained by cold, if applied to the area.

# Wild Tansy, or Silver-weed.

This is also so well known that it needs no description.

*Place.*] It grows almost in every place.

*Time.*] It flowers in *June* and *July*.

<margin>*Diarrhea, menstrual periods, stops vomiting of blood, the whites, ruptures, belly-ache, sciatica, joint aches, toothache, loose teeth, gums, ulcers, wounds, sore legs, pimples, freckles, sun-burning.*</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] Now Dame *Venus* has provided women with two herbs of the same name, one to help conception and the other to maintain beauty; and what more can be expected of her? What remains for you now but to love your husbands and not to be lacking toward your poor neighbors? Wild Tansy stops the lask <note>diarrhea</note> and all the fluxes of blood in men or women; some say it will do this if the green herb is worn in the shoes, so long as it is next to the skin; and it is true enough that it will stop the menstrual periods if worn so, and the whites <note>leucorrhea</note> too, for all I know. It also stops the spitting or vomiting of blood. The powder of the dried herb taken in some of its distilled water helps the whites in women, but especially if a little coral and ivory in powder is added to it. It is also much commended for helping children who are burst and have a rupture <note>hernia</note>, being boiled in water and salt. Being boiled in wine and drunk, it eases the griping pains of the bowels and is good for sciatica and joint aches. The same boiled in vinegar with honey and alum, and gargled in the mouth, eases the pains of the toothache, fastens loose teeth, helps sore gums, and settles the palate of the mouth in its place when it has fallen down. It cleanses and heals ulcers in the mouth or secret parts and is very good for inward wounds and to close the lips of green <note>fresh</note> wounds, as also to heal old, moist, corrupt, running sores in the legs or elsewhere. Being bruised and applied to the soles of the feet and the wrists, it wonderfully cools the hot fits of agues <note>fevers</note>, no matter how violent they are. The distilled water cleanses the skin of all discolorations, such as morphew <note>scurfy eruptions</note>, sun-burning, etc., as well as pimples, freckles, and the like; and dropped into the eyes, or applied with cloths wet in it, it takes away the heat and inflammations in them.

## The Melancholy Thistle.

<margin>Description.</margin> *It rises up with a tender, single, hoary green stalk, bearing four or five long, hoary green leaves, dented about the edges; the points of these are little or nothing prickly. At the top there is usually but one head, yet sometimes from the bosom of the uppermost leaf there shoots forth another smaller head, scaly and somewhat prickly, with many reddish-purple thrums <note>fringe-like threads</note>, or threads in the middle. These, being gathered fresh, will keep their color for a long time, and do not fade from the stalk for a long while, even as the plant perfects the seed, which is of an average size lying in the down. The root has many long strings fastened to the head, or upper part, which is blackish and does not die.*

*There is another sort differing little from the former, except that the leaves are greener above and more hoary underneath; and the stalk, being about two feet high, bears but one large scaly head, with threads and seeds like the former.*

<margin>Place.</margin> *They grow in many moist meadows of this land, as well in the Southern as in the Northern parts.*

<margin>Time.</margin> *They flower about July or August, and their seed ripens quickly after.*

<margin>Government and Virtues.</margin> *It is under Capricorn, and therefore under both Saturn and Mars; one rids melancholy by sympathy, the other by antipathy. Their virtues are but few, but those are not to be despised; for* <margin>Melancholy.</margin> *the decoction of the thistle in wine, being drunk, expels superfluous melancholy out of the body and makes a man as merry as a cricket. Superfluous melancholy causes care, fear, sadness, despair, envy, and many other evils besides; but religion teaches us to wait upon God's Providence and cast our care upon Him, who cares for us. What a fine thing it would be if men and women could live so? And yet seven years of care and fear never makes a man any wiser, nor a farthing richer.* Dioscorides *says the root, when worn on one's person, does the same and removes all diseases of melancholy. Modern writers laugh at him; let those laugh who win. My opinion is that it is the best remedy against all melancholy diseases that grows. Those who please may use it.*

*Time.]* It flowers and bears seed about the end of summer, when other thistles do flower and seed.

# The Fuller's Thistle, or Teasel.

It is so well known that it needs no description, being used by the cloth-workers.
*The wild teasel is in all things like the former, except that the prickles are small, soft, and upright, not hooked or stiff; and the flowers of this are of a fine blush or pale carnation color, while those of the cultivated kind are whitish.*
*Place.*] The first grows being sown in gardens or fields for the use of cloth-workers; the other grows near ditches and rills of water in many places of this land.
*Time.*] They flower in July and are ripe at the end of August.
*Government and Virtues.*] It is an herb of Venus. *Dioscorides* says that the root, bruised and boiled in wine until it becomes thick and kept in a bronze vessel or pot, and afterward spread as a salve and applied to the fundament <note>the anus</note>, heals the clefts thereof, as al-

The distilled water of the leaves dropped into the eyes takes away redness and mists in them that hinder the sight; and it is often used by women to preserve their beauty and to take away redness and inflammations, and all other heat or discoloring.

# Treacle Mustard.

<margin>Description.]</margin>
*It rises up with a hard, round stalk about a foot high, divided into several branches, having various soft green leaves, somewhat long and narrow, set upon it; these are waved but not cut in at the edges, broadest towards the ends, and somewhat round-pointed. The flowers are white and grow at the tops of the branches in a spike fashion, one above another; after which come large, round pouches, divided in the middle with a furrow, having one blackish-brown seed on either side, which is somewhat sharp in taste and smells of garlic, especially in the fields where it grows naturally, though not as much in gardens. The roots are small and thready, perishing every year.*

## Mithridate Mustard.

*Description*] This grows higher than the former, spreading more and longer branches, whose leaves are smaller and narrower, sometimes unevenly dented about the edges: the flowers are small and white, growing on long branches, with much smaller and rounder seed vessels after them, and parted in the same manner, having smaller brown seeds than the former, and much sharper in taste: The root perishes after seed time, but abides the first winter after the springing.

*Place.*] They grow in various places of this land; as half a mile from *Hatfield* by the river side under a hedge as you go to *Hatfield*, and in the street of *Peckham* on the Surrey side.

*Time.*] They flower and seed from *May* to *August*.

<margin>Purges the body, provokes the courses <note>menstruation</note>, abscesses, sciatica, poison, venom, putrefaction.</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] Both of them are herbs of *Mars*. These mustards are said to purge the body both upwards and downwards, and provoke women's courses so abundantly that it suffocates the birth <note>causes miscarriage</note>: It breaks inward abscesses being taken inwardly, and used in enemas, helps the sciatica: the seed applied outwardly does the same. It is a special ingredient in Mithridate and Treacle <note>an apothecary's compound</note>, being of itself an antidote resisting poison, venom, and putrefaction: It is also available in many cases for which the common mustard is used, but is somewhat weaker.

## The Black-Thorn, or Sloe-Bush.

It is so well known that it needs no description.
*Place.*] It grows in every county, in the hedges and borders of fields.

*Time.*] It flowers in *April*, and sometimes in *March*, but ripens the fruit after all other plums whatsoever, and is not fit to be eaten until the autumn frost has mellowed it.

<margin>Binds, cools, dries, bleeding, flux, gnawing in the bowels and stomach, sore mouth and throat, headache.</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] All the parts of the sloe-bush are binding, cooling, and drying, and all are effectual to stay bleeding at the nose and mouth, or any other place; the diarrhea of the belly or stomach, or the bloody flux <note>dysentery</note>, the too much abounding of women's courses, and helps to ease the pains in the sides, bowels, and guts that come by over-much scouring <note>purging</note>, by drinking the decoction of the bark of the roots, or more usually the decoction of the berries, either fresh or dried. The conserve is also of very much use, and most familiarly taken for the purposes aforesaid: But the distilled water of the flowers first steeped in sack <note>a fortified wine</note> for a night, and drawn therefrom by the heat of *Balneum*, in English a bath, is a most certain remedy, tried and approved to ease all manner of gnawings in the stomach, the sides and bowels, or any griping pains in any of them, by drinking a small quantity when the extremity of pain is upon them: The leaves also

# Thorough-wax, or Thorough-leaf.

*Descript.*] Common Thorough-wax sends forth one straight round stalk, and sometimes more, two feet high or more, whose lower leaves, being of a bluish-green color, are smaller and narrower than those higher up and stand close to it, not encompassing it. But as they grow higher, they do more and more encompass the stalk until it wholly (as it were) passes through them, branching toward the top into many parts where the leaves grow smaller again, every one standing singly, and never two at any joint. The flowers are very small and yellow, standing in tufts at the heads of the branches, where afterwards the seed grows—blackish and many thick ones thrust together. The root is small, long, and woody, perishing every year after seed time, and rising again plentifully from its own sowing.

*Place.*] It is found growing in many cornfields and pasture grounds in this land.

*Time.*] It flowers in *July*, and the seed is ripe in *August*.
