# Wild Thyme, or Mother of Thyme.

Wild Thyme also is so well known, it needs no description.
<margin>*Place.]*</margin> It may be found commonly in commons and other barren places throughout the nation.

<margin>provokes urine, provokes terms, pain and gripings of the belly, Cramp, Ruptures, inflammations of Liver, pains of the Head, Frenzies, Lethargies, spitting and urinating blood, Coughing, Vomiting, strengthens the Head, Stomach, Kidneys, Womb, wind, Stone.</margin>
<margin>*Government and Virtues.]*</margin> This also is under the dominion of *Venus*, though under the sign *Aries*, and therefore chiefly appropriated to the head. It provokes urine and the terms <note>menstrual periods</note>, and eases the gripping pains of the belly, cramps, ruptures, and inflammations of the liver. If you make a vinegar of the herb as vinegar of roses is made (you may find out the way in my translation of the *London Dispensatory*) and anoint the head with it, it presently stops the pains thereof. It is excellently good to be given either in a frenzy or lethargy, although they are two contrary diseases. It helps spitting and urinating <note>pissing</note> of blood, coughing, and vomiting; it comforts and strengthens the head, stomach, kidneys <note>reins</note>, and womb, expels wind, and breaks the stone.

# Tormentil, or Septfoil.

<margin>*Descript.]*</margin> This has many reddish, slender, weak branches rising from the root, lying upon the ground, or rather leaning than standing upright, with many short leaves that stand closer to the stalks than cinquefoil does (which this is very like) with the footstalk encompassing the branches in several places; but those that grow next to the ground are set upon long footstalks, each of which is like the leaves of cinquefoil, but somewhat longer and smaller, and notched <note>dented</note> about the edges. Many of them are divided into only five leaves, but most of them into seven, which is why it is also called septfoil <note>setfoyl</note>; yet some may have six and some eight, according to the fertility of the soil. At the tops of the branches stand several small yellow flowers consisting of five leaves, like those of cinquefoil, but smaller. The root is smaller than bistort, somewhat thick, but blacker on the outside and not so red within, yet sometimes a little crooked, having many blackish fibers attached to it.

<margin>*Place.]*</margin> It grows as well in woods and shadowy places as in the open 
champion <note>open fields or country</note>

***Government and Virtues.***] This is an excellent herb of the Sun. **Tormentil** is most excellent to stop all kinds of fluxes of blood or humors in man or woman, whether from the nose, mouth, belly, or any wound in the veins or elsewhere: The juice of the herb or root taken in a drink not only resists all poison and venom of any creature, but even the plague itself, as well as pestilential fevers and contagious diseases like the pox <note>smallpox</note>, measles, purples, etc., expelling the venom and infection from the heart by sweating. If the green root is not available, the powder of the dry root is just as effective, a dram of it being taken every morning. Likewise, the decoction of the herbs and roots made in wine and drunk works to the same effect; and so does the distilled water of the herb and root after being steeped in wine for a night and then distilled in a *Balneo Maria* <note>a water bath</note>. This distilled water, taken with some Venice Treacle and the person immediately laid down to sweat, will certainly (with God's help) expel any venom or poison, or the plague, fever, etc., for it is an ingredient of special regard in all antidotes or counter-poisons. There is no root found more effective than this to help any flux of the belly, stomach, spleen, or blood, whether it is taken internally or applied externally. The juice, when taken, wonderfully opens obstructions of the liver and lungs, and thereby helps the yellow jaundice in a short time. Some use it to make cakes, both to stop all fluxes and to restrain all choleric belchings and excessive vomiting with loathing in the stomach. The powder of the dried root, made up with the white of an egg and baked upon a hot tile, will do this. *Andreas Valesius* is of the opinion that the decoction of this root is no less effective to cure the French Pox <note>syphilis</note> than *Guaiacum* or *China* <note>China root</note>; and it is not unlikely, because it so mightily resists putrefaction. *Lobel* says that *Rondeletius* used it like *Hermodactils* <note>meadow saffron</note> for joint aches. The powder or decoction to be drunk, or to sit in as a bath, is a guaranteed remedy against miscarriage in women, if it proceeds from the excessive looseness or weakness of the inward retentive faculty; also, a plaster made with it and vinegar applied to the kidneys of the back much helps not only this, but also those who cannot hold their water, the powder being taken in the juice of plantain. It is also recommended against worms in children. It is very powerful in ruptures and burstings, as well as for bruises and falls, to be used both outwardly and inwardly. The root made up with Pellitory of Spain and alum, and put into a hollow tooth, not only eases the pain but stops the flux of humors which caused it. Tormentil is no less effective and powerful a remedy for outward wounds, sores, and hurts, than

# Turnsole, *or* Heliotropium

<margin>Description</margin>
The greater *Turnsole* rises up with one upright stalk about a foot high or more, dividing itself almost from the bottom into various smaller branches of a grayish color. At each joint of the stalk and branches grow two small broad leaves, somewhat white or grayish also. At the tops of the stalks and branches stand many small white flowers consisting of four and sometimes five very small leaves, set in order one above another upon a small crooked spike, which turns inwards like a bowed finger, opening by degrees as the flowers bloom. After these, in their places, come forth small cornered seeds, for the most part standing four together. The root is small and thread-like, perishing every year; and the seed, shedding every year, raises it again the next spring.

<margin>Place</margin>
It grows in gardens, and flowers and seeds with us in England; however, it is not natural to this land, but to *Italy*, *Spain*, and *France*, where it grows plentifully.

<margin>
Choler, Phlegm, Stones, Dysury, Provokes periods, Gout, Warts, Wens, Dislocations.
</margin>
**Government and Virtues.**] It is an herb of the *Sun*, and a good one too. *Dioscorides* says that a good handful of this, which is called the greater Turnsole, boiled in water and drunk, purges both <term>choler</term> and <term>phlegm</term>. And boiled with cumin and drunk, it helps the <term>stone</term> in the reins <note>kidneys</note>, kidneys, or bladder; provokes urine and women's courses <note>menstruation</note>; and causes an easy and speedy delivery in childbirth. The leaves, bruised and applied to places pained with the <term>gout</term>, or those that have been out of joint and newly set and are full of pain

## Meadow Trefoil, or Honeysuckles.

It is so well known, especially by the name of Honeysuckles—white and red—that I do not need to describe them.

*Place.*] They grow almost everywhere in this land.

<margin>
Bellyache,
Inflammations,
Pin and web,
Eyes.
</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] Mercury has dominion over the common sorts. *Dodoneus* says the leaves and flowers are good for easing the gripping pains of the guts if the herb is boiled and used in a clyster <note>enema</note>. If the herb is made into a poultice and applied to inflammations, it will ease them. The juice dropped into the eyes is a common medicine among many country people to take away the "pin and web" <note>a film or cataract</note> (as they call it) in the eyes; it also allays their heat and bloodshot appearance. In many places, country people also drink the juice of this herb against the bite of an adder; after boiling the herb in water, they first wash the area with the decoction and then lay some of the herb itself on the injured spot. The herb boiled in pig's grease and made into an ointment is also good to apply to the bite of any venomous creature.

<margin>
Venomous beast, Dysuria, Wounds, Scars, whites, Swellings, Abscesses
</margin>
The herb, bruised and heated between two tiles and applied hot to the share <note>the groin or pubic area</note>, helps those who had their urine blocked to pass water. It is also held to be good for wounds and for removing scars. The decoction of the herb and flowers, along with the seed and root, taken for some time, helps women who are troubled with the whites <note>leukorrhea</note>. The seed and flowers, boiled in water and then made into a poultice with some oil and applied, help hard swellings and abscesses.

## Heart-trefoil.

Besides the ordinary sorts of trefoil, here are two more remarkable kinds, one of which may probably be called Heart-trefoil, not only because the leaf is triangular like the heart of a man, but also because each leaf contains the perfect image of a heart, and that in its proper color—namely, a flesh color.

*Place.*] It grows in a field between Longford and Bow, as well as beyond Southwark toward Croydon, both on the main road and in adjacent areas.

<margin>
Heart strengthens vital spirit, fainting, swoonings, Poison, Pestilence, evil vapors
</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] It is under the dominion of the Sun, and if it were used, it would be found to be as great a strengthener of the heart and cherisher of the vital spirit as any plant that grows. It relieves the body of fainting and swooning, fortifies it against poisons and pestilence, and defends the heart against the noxious vapors of the spleen.

## Pearl-trefoil.

<margin>Pin and web in the eye.</margin>
It differs not from the common sort, except only in this one particular: that it has a white spot in the leaf like a pearl. It is particularly under the dominion of the Moon; and its appearance shows that it is of singular virtue against the "pearl," or pin and web <note>a film or cataract</note> in the eye.

## Tutsan, or Park Leaves.

<margin>Description.</margin>
It has many brownish, shining, round stalks, crested along their entire length, rising to be two and sometimes three feet high, branching out even from the bottom, having various joints, and at each of them two fair, large leaves standing, of a dark bluish-green color on the upper side and of a yellowish-green underneath, turning reddish toward autumn, but remaining on the branches all winter. At the tops of the stalks and branches stand large yellow flowers and heads with seed, which, being greenish at first and afterward reddish, turn to a blackish-purple color when they are thoroughly ripe, with small brownish seeds within them. They then yield a reddish juice or liquor of a reasonably good scent, somewhat resinous, and of a harsh and styptic <note>astringent</note> taste, as the leaves and the flowers also are, although much less so; but they do not yield such a clear claret-colored liquor as some say they do. The root is brownish, somewhat large, hard, and woody, spreading well in the ground.

*Place.*] It grows in many woods, groves, and woody grounds, such as parks and forests, and by hedge sides in many places of this land, such as in Hampstead Wood, by Ratley in Essex, in the Weald <note>Wild</note> of Kent, and in many other places unnecessary to list.

*Time.*] It flowers later than St. John’s or St. Peter’s wort.

<margin>Antevenerian.</margin>
<margin>Choler, Sciatica, Gout, Burns, Bleeding, wounds, Ulcers.</margin>
*Government and Virtues.*] It is an herb of Saturn and a most noble Antevenerian <note>a substance that counteracts the influence of Venus, often used to cool lust or treat venereal disease</note>. Tutsan purges choleric humors as St. Peter’s wort is said to do, for therein it works the same effects, both to help the sciatica and gout, and to heal burns from fire. It also stops the bleeding of wounds if either the green herb is bruised or the powder of the dried herb is applied to them. It has been accounted, and certainly is, a sovereign herb to heal any wound or sore either outwardly or inwardly, and therefore it is always used in drinks, lotions, balms, oils, and ointments for any sort of fresh wound or old ulcers and sores. In all of these, the continual experience of former ages has confirmed its use to be admirably good, though it is not so much in use now as when physicians and surgeons were so wise as to use herbs more than they do now.

It has excellent properties to heal any inward sores or wounds, as well as outward hurts or wounds, and draws any splinter or thorn out of the flesh.

The distilled water of the herb when it is at its full strength, dropped into the eyes, cleanses them from films, clouds, or mist that darken the sight, and wonderfully strengthens the optic nerves. The said water is very powerful in all the diseases aforesaid either inward or outward, whether they be old corroding sores or fresh wounds.

## The Vine.

<margin>Sore Mouths, Inflammations, Women's Longing, Stone, Black Teeth.</margin>
The leaves of the English Vine (I do not intend to send you to the Canary Islands for a medicine) being boiled make a good lotion for sore mouths; being boiled with barley meal into a poultice, it cools inflammations of wounds. The droppings of the vine when it is cut in the spring, which country people call "Tars," being boiled into a syrup with sugar and taken inwardly, is excellent to stop women’s longings after everything they see, which is a disease many women with child are subject to. The decoction of vine leaves in white wine does the like. Also, the tears of the vine drunk, two or three spoonfuls at a time, breaks the stone in the bladder. This is a very good remedy, and it is wisely done to kill a vine to cure a man, but the salt of the leaves is held to be better.

The ashes of the burnt branches will make teeth that are as black as a coal to be as white as snow, if you do but every morning rub them with it.

It is a most gallant tree of the Sun, very sympathetic with the body of man; and that is the reason spirit of wine is the greatest cordial among all vegetables.

## Violets.

These, both tame and wild, are so well known that they need no description.

*Time.*] They flower until the end of *July*, but are best in *March* and the beginning of *April*.

Drink the decoction of the leaves or flowers made with water or wine, or apply them poultice-wise to the afflicted place. It likewise eases pains in the head caused by lack of sleep, or in any other place arising from heat, being applied in the same manner or with oil of roses. A dram weight of the dried leaves or the flowers of violets (but the leaves more strongly) purges the body of choleric humors, and assuages the heat when taken in a draft of wine or any other drink. The powder of the purple leaves of the flowers only, picked and dried and drunk in water, is said to help the quinsy <note>inflammation of the throat</note> and the falling sickness <note>epilepsy</note> in children, especially in the beginning of the disease. ### Viper’s Bugloss.

<margin>Description.]</margin> This has many long, rough leaves lying on the ground, from among which rise several hard, round stalks, very rough as if they were thickly set with prickles or hairs. On these are set similar long, rough, hairy, or prickly dark green leaves, which are somewhat narrow; the middle rib is for the most part white. The flowers stand at the top of the stalks, branched out into many long spiked leaves of flowers, bowing or turning like the turnsole, with most of them opening on one side. These are long and hollow, turning up the rims a little, and are of a purplish-violet color in those that are fully blown, but more reddish while they are in the bud, as well as during their decay and withering. In some places, they are of a paler purple color, with a long pistil in the middle, feathered or parted at the top. After the flowers have fallen and the seeds grow ripe, they are blackish, cornered, and pointed somewhat like the head of a viper. The root is somewhat large, blackish, and woolly when it grows toward seed time; it perishes in the winter.

There is another sort differing little from the former, except that it bears white flowers.

<margin>Place.]</margin> The first grows wild almost everywhere. That with white flowers grows about the castle walls in Lewes in Sussex.

<margin>Time.]</margin> They flower in summer, and their seed is ripe quickly after.

When the flowers are dry, they are effective for pleurisy and all diseases of the lungs, to soothe the sharpness of hot rheums and the hoarseness of the throat, as well as the heat and sharpness of urine, and all pains of the back, kidneys, and bladder. It is also good for the liver and jaundice, and in all hot fevers to cool the heat and quench thirst. However, the syrup of violets is of most use and has a better effect when taken in some suitable liquid; and if a little of the juice or syrup of lemons is added to it, or a few drops of the oil of vitriol <note>sulfuric acid, used historically in very small diluted quantities</note>, it is made even more powerful to cool the heat and quench thirst, giving the drink a claret wine color and a fine tart relish pleasing to the taste. Violets taken or prepared with honey cleanse more than they cool, and with sugar they do the opposite. The dried flowers of violets are accounted among the cordial drinks, powders, and other medicines, especially where cooling cordials are necessary. The green leaves are used with other herbs to make plasters and poultices for inflammations and swellings, and to ease any pains arising from heat, and for hemorrhoids also, being fried with egg yolks and applied to them.

# Viper's Bugloss.

<margin>Description]</margin>
*This has many long, rough leaves lying on the ground, from among which rise several hard, round stalks, very rough as if they were thickly set with prickles or hairs, upon which are set similar long, rough, hairy, or prickly dark green leaves, somewhat narrow; the middle rib is for the most part white. The flowers stand at the top of the stalks, branching forth into many long spikes of flowers, bowing or turning like the heliotrope, most of them opening on one side; they are long and hollow, turning up the rims a little, and are of a purplish violet color when they are fully in bloom, but more reddish while they are in the bud as well as when they decay and wither; but in some places they are of a paler purple color, with a long pistil in the middle, divided at the top. After the flowers have fallen, the seeds, as they ripen, are blackish, angular, and pointed somewhat like the head of a viper. The root is somewhat large, blackish, and hairy when it grows toward seed-time, and it dies in the winter.*

*There is another sort differing little from the former, except that it bears white flowers.*

<margin>Place]</margin>
The first grows wild almost everywhere. That with white flowers grows about the castle walls in Lewes in Sussex.

<margin>Time]</margin>
They flower in summer, and their seed is ripe quickly afterward.

<margin>Government and Virtues.] Venomous beasts, Poison, Heart, Sadness, Melancholy, Fevers, Milk,</margin>
It is a most excellent herb of the Sun; it is a pity it is no more in use than it is. It is a special remedy against the bite of the viper and all other venomous beasts or serpents, as also against poison and poisonous herbs. *Dioscorides* and others say that whoever takes the herb or root before they are bitten shall not be hurt by the poison of any serpent. ## Wall-Flowers, or Winter Gilly Flowers.

The garden kinds are so well known that they need no description.
*Description.]* The common single wall-flowers which grow wild outdoors have various small, long, narrow, and dark green leaves, set without order upon small, round, whitish, woody stalks which bear at the tops several single yellow flowers one above another, each having four petals <note>Early Modern botanical texts often refer to petals as "leaves"</note> and a very sweet scent; after these come long pods containing reddish seed. The root is white, hard, and fibrous.
*Place.]* It grows upon church walls, the old walls of many houses, and other stone walls in various places. The other sorts are in gardens only.
*Time.]* All the single kinds flower many times at the end of autumn, and if the winter is mild, all winter long, but especially in the months of February, March, and April, until the heat of the spring exhausts them. But the double kinds do not continue flowering in that manner all year long, although they flower very early sometimes, and in some places very late.
<margin>Obstructions, Liver, Provokes menstruation, after-birth, child, spleen, weakness, dislocation, gout, sinews, apoplexy, palsy.</margin>
*Government and Virtues.]* The Moon rules them. Galen, in his seventh book of *Simple Medicines*, says that the yellow wall-flowers work more powerfully than any of the other kinds and are therefore of more use in medicine. It cleanses the blood and frees the liver and kidneys from obstructions, provokes women's courses <note>menstruation</note>, expels the after-birth and dead child, helps the hardness and pains of the womb and of the spleen also, stops inflammations and swellings, comforts and strengthens any weak part or dislocation; it helps to cleanse the eyes from cloudiness and films, and to cleanse foul and filthy ulcers in the mouth or any other part, and is a singular remedy for the gout and all aches and pains in the joints and sinews. A conserve of the flowers is used as a remedy for both apoplexy and palsy.

The green husks will do the same when used in the same manner. A piece of the green husk put into a hollow tooth eases the pains. The catkins hereof taken before they fall off, dried, and given as a dram in powder with white wine, wonderfully help those that are troubled with the rising of the mother <note>hysteria or uterine disorders</note>. The young green nuts taken before they are half ripe and preserved with sugar are of good use for those that have weak stomachs or defluxions <note>discharges of fluid</note> upon them. The distilled water of the green husk, taken before they are half ripe, is of excellent use to cool the heat of agues when drunk an ounce or two at a time, as also to resist the infection of the plague if some of it is also applied to the sores thereof. ## Wold, Weld, or Dyers Weed.

<margin>Description.]</margin> *The common kind grows like a bush with many leaves, long, narrow, and flat upon the ground, of a dark bluish-green color, somewhat like woad, but not nearly so large, a little crumpled and as it were round-pointed, which remain this way the first year. And the next spring from among them rise several round stalks two or three feet high, set with many similar leaves on them, but smaller, and shooting forth some small branches, which with the stalks carry many small yellow flowers in a long spiked head at their tops, where afterwards the seed comes, which is small and black, enclosed in heads that are divided at the tops into four parts. The root is long, white, and thick, lasting through the winter. The whole herb changes to yellow after it has been in flower a while.*

<margin>Place.]</margin> It grows everywhere by the roadsides in moist grounds as well as dry, in corners of fields and by-lanes; and sometimes all over the field. In *Sussex* and *Kent* they call it Greenweed.

<margin>Time.]</margin> It is in flower about *June*.

<margin>Government and Virtues.]</margin>
<margin>Phlegm, Humors, Tumors, Venomous Beasts, Pestilence, Worms.</margin>
*Mathiolus* says that the root of this cuts tough phlegm, digests raw phlegm, thins thick humors, dissolves hard tumors, and opens obstructions. Some highly commend it against the bites of venomous creatures, to be taken internally and applied externally to the hurt place; as also for the plague or pestilence. The people in some parts of this land use to bruise the herb and lay it on cuts or wounds in the hands or legs to heal them.

# Woad.

*Description.*] It has various large leaves, long and somewhat broad as well, like those of the greater <term>plantain</term>, but larger, thicker, of a greenish color, and somewhat blue withal. From among these leaves rises a sturdy stalk three or four feet high, with various leaves set thereon; the higher the stalk rises, the smaller the leaves are. At the top, it spreads into various branches, at the end of which appear very pretty little yellow flowers; and after they pass away like other flowers of the field, there come husks, long and somewhat flat as well. In form, they resemble a tongue; in color, they are black, and they hang bobbing downwards. The seed contained within these husks (if it is a little chewed) gives an azure color. The root is white and long.

*Place*] It is sown in fields for its benefit, where those who sow it cut it three times a year.

*Time*] It flowers in June, but it is a long time after before the seed is ripe.

*Government and Virtues.*] It is a cold and dry plant of Saturn. Some people affirm the plant to be destructive to bees, which if it is, I cannot help; they say it affects bees with a <term>flux</term>, but I can hardly believe that unless bees are contrary to all other creatures. I should rather think it affects them with the contrary disease, the herb being exceedingly drying and binding. However, if any bees are diseased thereby, the cure is to set urine by them, but set it in such a vessel that they cannot drown themselves, which may be remedied if you put pieces of cork in it. I told you before the herb was drying and binding, and so drying and binding that it is not fit to be taken internally. An ointment made of it stanches bleeding. A plaster made of it and applied to the region of the spleen,

# Woodbind, or Honeysuckles.

It is a plant so common that everyone who has eyes knows them, and he who has none cannot read a description if I should write it.

*Time.]* They flower in *June*, and the fruit is ripe in *August*.

<margin>Lungs afflicted, asthma, spleen; provokes urine and speedy delivery in childbirth; cramps, convulsions, and palsies; freckles and sun-burning.</margin>
*Government and Virtues.]* Doctor *Tradition*, that grand introducer of errors, that hater of truth, that lover of folly, and that mortal foe to Doctor *Reason*, has taught the common people to use the leaves and flowers of this plant in mouthwashes; and by long continuance of time has so grounded it in the brains of the common people that you cannot beat it out with a mallet <note>A "beetle" was a heavy wooden mallet.</note>: All mouthwashes ought to be cooling and drying, but honeysuckles are cleansing, consuming, and digesting, and therefore in no way fit for inflammations: Thus says Doctor *Reason*. Again, if you please, we will leave Doctor *Reason* a while and come to Doctor *Experience*, a learned gentleman and his brother: Take a leaf and chew it in your mouth, and you will quickly find it more likely to cause a sore mouth or throat than to cure it. Well then, if it is not good for this, what is it good for? It is good for something, for God and Nature made nothing in vain: It is an herb of *Mercury*, and appropriated to the lungs; the Celestial *Crab* <note>The zodiac sign Cancer.</note> claims dominion over it, neither is it a foe to the *Lion* <note>The zodiac sign Leo.</note>: If the lungs are afflicted by *Jupiter*, this is your cure: It is fitting that a conserve made of its flowers be kept in every gentlewoman's house; I know no better cure for an asthma than this: Besides, it takes away the evil of the spleen, provokes urine, procures speedy delivery to women in travail <note>Labor/childbirth.</note>, helps cramps, convulsions, and palsies, and whatever griefs come of cold or blockages: If you please to make use of it in an ointment, it will clear your skin of morphew <note>A skin disease characterized by scurfy eruptions.</note>, freckles, and sun-burning, or whatever else discolors it, and then the maids will love it. I have done when I have told you what authors say, and caviled a little with them; they say the flowers are of more effect than the leaves, and that is true; but they say the seeds are the least effectual of all: but Dr. *Reason* told me that there was a vital spirit in every seed to beget its like; and Dr. *Experience* told me that there was a greater heat in a seed than there was in any other part of a plant, and withal, that heat was the mother of action. Then judge if old Dr. *Tradition* (who may well be honored for his age, but not for his goodness) has not so poisoned the world with his errors before I was born that it was never well in its wits since, and there is great fear it will die mad.

# Wormwood.

Three Wormwoods are familiar to us; one I shall not describe, another I shall describe, and the third I shall be critical of: And I do not care much if I begin with the last first.

Sea Wormwood has gotten as many names as virtues (and perhaps one more): *Seriphian, Santonicon, Belgicum, Narbonense, Xantomicum, Misnense*, and about twenty more which I will not stain paper with. A Papist got a whim in his head, and he called it Holy Wormwood; and in truth I am of the opinion that their giving so much holiness to herbs is the reason there remains so little in themselves. The seed of this Wormwood is what women usually give their children for worms. Of all Wormwoods that grow here, this is the weakest; aye, but doctors recommend it, and apothecaries sell it—the one must keep his credit and the other get money, and that is the key to the work. The herb is good for something, because God made nothing in vain. Will you give me leave to weigh things in the balance of reason? Then thus: The seeds of the common Wormwood are far more effective than the seed of this to expel worms in children or people of mature age. Of both, some are weak, some are strong. The *Seriphian* wormseed is the weakest, and perhaps may prove to be fittest for the weakest bodies (for it is weak enough, in all conscience). Let such as are strong take the common wormseed, for the other will do but little good. Again, near the sea many people live, and *Seriphium* grows near them, and therefore it is more fitting for their bodies because they are nourished by the same air; and this I had from Dr. *Reason*. In whose body Dr. *Reason* dwells not, dwells Dr. *Madness*, and he brings in his brothers, Dr. *Ignorance*, Dr. *Folly*, and Dr. *Sickness*, and these together make way for Dr. *Death*; and the end of that man is worse than the beginning. Pride was the cause of *Adam's* fall; Pride fathered a daughter—I do not know the father of it unless it was the Devil—but she christened it and called it *Appetite*, and sent her daughter to taste these Wormwoods. Finding this one the least bitter, she made the squeamish girl extol it to the skies, though its virtues never reached the middle region of the air. Its due praise is this: It is weakest, therefore fitter for weak bodies, and fitter for those bodies that dwell near it than those that live far from it. My reason is: The sea (as those who live far from it know when they come near it) does not cast such a smell as the land does. The tender mercies of God being over all his works, he has by his eternal providence planted *Seriphian* by the seaside as a fit medicine for the bodies of those who live near it. Lastly, it is known to all who know anything of the course of nature that the liver delights in sweet things; if so, it abhors bitter things. Then if your liver is weak, it is not the wisest course to plague it with an enemy. If the liver is weak, a consumption follows. Would you know the reason? It is this: A man's flesh is repaired by blood, through a third concoction <note>The final stage of digestion where blood is converted into tissue.</note> which transforms blood into flesh (it is well I said [concoction], for if I had said [boiling], every cook would have understood me). The liver

### SECT. I.

# The way of gathering, drying, and preserving Simples and their Juices.

## Chap. 1. *Of Leaves of Herbs, or Trees.*

1. Of leaves, choose only such as are green and full of juice; pick them carefully, and cast away such as are in any way declining, for they will putrefy the rest; so shall one handful be worth ten of those you buy in *Cheapside*.

2. Note in what place they most delight to grow, and gather them there, for Betony that grows in the shadow is far better than that which grows in the sun, because it delights in the shadow. So also, for such herbs as delight to grow near the water, let such be gathered as grow near the water, though perhaps you may find some of them upon dry ground. The treatise will inform you where every herb delights to grow.

3. The leaves of such herbs as go to seed are not so good when they are in flower as they were before (a few excepted, the leaves of which are seldom or never used). In such cases, if through ignorance they were not known, or through negligence forgotten, you had better take the top and the flower than the leaf.

4. Dry them well in the sun, and not in the shadow as the custom of physicians is; for if the sun draws away the virtues of herbs, it must necessarily do the like to hay by the same rule, which the experience of every country farmer will reject as a notable piece of nonsense.

5. To such as are skilled in astrology (and indeed none else are fit to be physicians), I advise: Let the planet that governs the herb be angular, and the stronger the better; if they can, in herbs of *Saturn*, let *Saturn* be in the ascendant; in the herbs of *Mars*, let *Mars* be in the mid-heaven, for in those houses they delight. Let the *Moon* apply to them by good aspect, and let her not be in the houses of their enemies. If you cannot well wait until she applies to them, let her apply to a planet of the same triplicity; if you cannot wait for that time either, let her be with a fixed star of their nature.

6. Having well dried them, put them up in brown papers, sewing the paper up like a sack, and do not press them too hard together; keep them in a dry place near the fire.

7. As for the duration of dried herbs, a precise time cannot be given, let authors prattle as they please. For:

First, Such as grow upon dry grounds will keep better than such as grow on moist.

Secondly, Such herbs as are full of juice will not keep so long as such as are drier.

<meta>Catchword: Thirdly</meta>

Thirdly, herbs that are well dried will keep longer than those that are poorly dried.

Yet I say this: you may know when they are corrupted, *namely*, by their loss of color, or smell, or both; and if they are corrupted, reason will tell you that they must necessarily corrupt the bodies of those people who take them.

8. Gather all leaves in the hour of the planet that governs them.

## Chap. 2. Of Flowers.

1. The flower, which is the beauty of the plant and of significant use in medicine, grows yearly, and it is to be gathered when it is in its prime.

2. As for the time of gathering them, let the planetary hour and the plant they come from be observed, as we showed you in the previous chapter. As for the time of day, let it be when the sun shines upon them so that they may be dry; for if you gather flowers when they are wet or dewy, they will not keep—a point I forgot to mention before.

3. Dry them well in the sun and keep them in papers near the fire, as I showed you in the previous chapter.

4. As long as they retain their color and smell, they are good; if either of them is gone, the virtue <note>medicinal potency</note> is gone as well.

## Chap. 3. Of Seeds.

1. The seed is that part of the plant which is endowed with a vital faculty to reproduce its own kind, and it contains potentially the whole plant within it.

2. As for the location, let them be gathered from the plants where they naturally prefer to grow.

3. Let them be fully ripe when they are gathered, and do not forget the celestial harmony mentioned before; for I have found by experience that their virtues are twice as great at such times as at others. There is an appointed time for everything under the sun.

4. When you have gathered them, dry them a little—but only a little—in the sun before you store them away.

5. You do not need to be as careful about keeping them so near the fire as the others mentioned before, because they are fuller of spirit <note>vital energy or essential essence</note> and therefore not so subject to decay.

6. As for the length of time they last, it is evident they will keep well for many years; yet I say this: they are best in the first year, and I can prove this with a good argument. They will grow most readily the first year they are planted; therefore, they are then in their prime, and it is an easy matter to renew them yearly.

## Chap. 4. Of Roots.

1. For roots, choose such as are neither rotten nor worm-eaten, but proper in their taste, color, and smell, and such as are neither too soft nor too hard.

2. Give me leave to be a little critical against the common received opinion, which is that the sap falls down into the root in autumn and rises again in spring, as men go to bed at night and rise in the morning; and this idle tale of untruth is so grounded in the heads not only of the common people but also of the learned, that a man cannot drive it out by reason. I pray, let such sap-mongers answer me this argument: if the sap falls into the root in the fall of the leaf and lies there all the winter, then must the root grow only in the winter, as experience witnesses; but the root grows not at all in the winter, as the same experience teaches, but only in the summer. Therefore, if you set an apple kernel in the spring, you shall find the root grows to a pretty bigness in that summer, and is not a whit bigger next spring. What does the sap do in the root all that while—pick straws? For God's sake, do not build your faith upon tradition; it is as rotten as a rotten post.
The truth is, when the Sun declines from the Tropic of *Cancer*, the sap begins to congeal both in root and branch; when he touches the Tropic of *Capricorn* and ascends toward us, it begins to grow thin again, by the same degrees as it congealed. But to proceed:

3. The drier the time you gather your roots in, the better they are, for they have less excrementitious <note>excess or waste</note> moisture in them.

4. Such roots as are soft, your best way is to dry in the sun, or else hang them in the chimney corner upon a string; as for such as are hard, you may dry them anywhere.

5. Such roots as are large will keep longer than such as are small, yet most of them will keep for a year.

6. Such roots as are soft, it is your best way to keep them always near the fire; and take this general rule for it: if in winter time you find any of your roots, herbs, or flowers begin to grow moist, as you shall many times, especially in the winter time (for it is your best way to look to them once a month), dry them by a very gentle fire; or if you can with convenience keep them near the fire, you may save yourself the labor.

7. It is in vain to dry such roots as may commonly be had, such as Parsley, Fennel, Plantain, etc.; gather them only for present need.

## Chap. 5. Of Barks.

1. Barks which physicians use in medicines are of these sorts: of fruits, of roots, and of boughs.

2. The barks of fruits are to be taken when the fruit is fully ripe, such as oranges, lemons, etc.; but because I have nothing to do with *exotics* <note>foreign plants</note> here, I shall pass them without any more words.

3. The barks of trees are best gathered in the spring, if it be from large trees like oaks or the like, because then they come off easiest; and so you may dry them if you please, but indeed your best way is to gather all barks only for present use.

4. As for the bark of roots, it is this and thus to be gotten: take the

Roots of such herbs as have a pith in them, as parsley, fennel, etc.; slit them in the middle, and when you have taken out the pith (which you may easily and quickly do), that which remains is called (though somewhat improperly) the bark, and indeed is the only part to be used.

### Chap. 6. Of Juices.

1. Juices are to be pressed out of herbs when they are young and tender, and also out of some stalks and tender tops of herbs and plants, and also out of some flowers.
2. Having gathered the herb you would preserve the juice of when it is very dry (for otherwise your juice will not be worth a button), bruise it very well in a stone mortar with a wooden pestle; then, having put it into a canvas bag (the herb, I mean, not the mortar, for that will yield but little juice), press it hard in a press; then take the juice and clarify it.
3. The manner of clarifying it is this: put it into a pipkin or skillet, or some such thing, and set it over the fire; and when the scum rises, take it off. Let it stand over the fire until no more scum rises; then you have your juice clarified. Cast away the scum as a thing of no use.
4. When you have thus clarified it, you have two ways to preserve it all year.

First, when it is cold, put it into a glass and put as much oil on it as will cover it to the thickness of two fingers. The oil will float at the top and so keep the air from reaching it and causing it to putrefy. When you intend to use it, do no more than this: pour out into a porringer a little more than you intend to use, and if any oil comes out with it (as it is a hundred to one it will if the glass is not full), you may easily skim it off with a spoon and put the juice you do not use back into the glass; it will quickly sink under the oil. This is the first way.

Secondly, the second way is a little more difficult, and the juice of fruits is usually preserved this way: when you have clarified the juice as before, boil it over the fire until (once cold) it is the thickness of honey. This is most commonly used for diseases of the mouth and is called <term>Rob</term> and <term>Sapa</term>.

And so much for the first section; the second follows.

# SECT. II.

## The way of making and keeping all necessary Compounds.

### Chap. 1. Of Distilled waters.

Hitherto we have spoken of medicines which consist in their own nature, which authors commonly call <term>Simples</term>, though somewhat improperly; for indeed and in truth, nothing is simple but the pure

pure Elements; all other things are compounded of them: We come now to treat of the Artificial Medicines, in the front of which (because we must begin somewhere) we place Distilled Waters; in which consider:

1. Waters are distilled out of herbs, flowers, fruits, and roots.
2. We do not treat of strong waters but of cold ones, as we are to play *Galen's* part and not *Paracelsus'*.
3. The herbs ought to be distilled when they are in their greatest vigor, and so ought the flowers also.
3. The common way of distillation which people use, because they know no better, is in a pewter still; and although distilled waters are the weakest of all artificial medicines, and good for little unless for mixtures with other medicines, yet distilled this way they are weaker by many degrees than they would be if they were distilled in sand. If I did not think it impossible to teach you the way of distilling in sand by writing, I would attempt it.
5. When you have distilled your water, put it into a glass, and having bound the top of it over with a paper pricked full of holes, so that the waste and fiery vapors may exhale (which indeed are those that cause that settling in distilled waters called "the Mother," which corrupts the waters and might this way be prevented), cover it closely and keep it for your use.
6. Stopping distilled waters with a cork makes them musty, and so will a paper also if it does but touch the water; your best way then is to stop them with a bladder, it being first wet in water and bound over the top of the glass.

Such cold waters as are distilled in a pewter still (if well kept) will last a year; such as are distilled in sand, as they are twice as strong, so will they last twice as long.

# Chap. 2. Of Syrups.

1. A syrup is a medicine of a liquid form, composed of infusion, decoction, and juice: And 1. for the more pleasant taste. 2. For the better keeping of it, with a certain quantity of honey or sugar (hereafter mentioned) boiled to the thickness of new honey.
2. You see at first view that this aphorism divides itself into three branches, which deserve to be treated of separately, namely:

> 1. *Syrups made by Infusion.*
> 2. *Syrups made by Decoction.*
> 3. *Syrups made by Juice.*

Of each of these (for the sake of your instructions, kind countrymen and women) I speak a word, or two or three, separately.

First, syrups made by infusion are usually made of flowers, and of such flowers as soon lose both color and strength by boiling, such as roses, violets, peach-flowers, etc. My translation of the *London Dispensatory* will instruct you in the rest: They are made thus; having picked your flowers clean, to every pound of them add three pounds (or three pints, whichever you prefer, for it is all one) of spring water made boiling hot by the fire; first put your flowers in a pewter pot with a cover, then pour the water to them,

then shutting the pot, let it stand by the fire to keep hot for twelve hours, then strain it out (in such syrups as purge, such as Damask Roses, Peach-Flowers, etc., the usual and indeed the best way is to repeat this infusion, adding fresh flowers to the same liquor several times so that it may be the stronger). Having strained it out, put the infusion into a pewter basin, or a well-glazed earthen one, and to every pint of it, add two pounds of fine sugar, which being only melted over the fire without boiling and skimmed, will produce the syrup you desire.

Secondly, syrups made by decoction are usually used for compounds, yet any simple herb may be thus converted into syrup; take the herb, root, or flower you would make into syrup and bruise it a little, then boil it in a convenient quantity of spring water. The more water you boil in it, the weaker it will be; a handful of the herb, root, etc., is a convenient quantity for a pint of water. Boil it until half the water is consumed, then let it stand until it is almost cold, and strain it (being almost cold) through a woolen cloth, letting it run out at leisure without pressing. To every pint of this decoction add one pound of sugar and boil it over the fire until it becomes a syrup, which you may know if you now and then cool a little of it in a spoon. Skim it all the while it boils, and when it is sufficiently boiled, strain it again through a woolen cloth while it is hot, but do not press it; thus you have the syrup perfected.

Thirdly, syrups made of juices are usually made of such herbs as are full of juice, and indeed they are better made into a syrup this way than any other; the operation is this: having beaten the herb in a stone mortar with a wooden pestle, press out the juice and clarify it as you were taught before in the section on juices; then let the juice boil away until a quarter of it (or nearly so) is consumed. To a pint of this add a pound of sugar, and boil it to a syrup, always skimming it; <unclear>and</unclear> when it is boiled enough, strain it through a woolen cloth as we taught you before, and keep it for your use.

3. If you make syrups of roots that are at all hard, such as parsley, fennel, and grass roots, etc., when you have bruised them, let them steep for some time in that water which you intend to boil them in while it is hot; in this way the medicinal virtue will come out better.

4. Keep your syrups either in glasses or stone pots, and do not stop them with cork or a bladder, unless you would have the glass break and the syrup be lost; as many opinions as there are in this nation, I suppose there are but few or none on this point: only bind a paper about the mouth.

5. All syrups, if well made, will last a year, with some advantage; yet of all types, those made by infusion keep for the shortest time.

# Chap. 3. Of Juleps.

1. Juleps were first invented, I suppose, in *Arabia*, and my reason is because the word *Juleb* is an *Arabic* word.

2. It signifies only a pleasant potion, and was commonly used (by those who were sick and wanted help, or those who were in health and had plenty of money) to quench thirst.

3. Nowadays it is commonly used:
->1. To prepare the body for purging.<-
->2. To open obstructions and the pores.<-
->3. To digest tough humors.<-
->4. To calm hot distempers, etc.<-

4. It is made this way (I mean simple juleps, for I have nothing to say about compounds here; all compounds have as many different ideas as men have whims in their brains). I say simple juleps are made thus: Take a pint of such distilled water as contributes to the cure of your ailment, which this treatise will plentifully furnish you with; to which add two ounces of syrup contributing to the same effect (I shall give you rules for it in the last chapter). Mix them together, and drink a portion of it at your pleasure. If you love tart things, add ten drops of oil of vitriol to your pint, and shake it together, and it will have a fine, pleasant taste.

5. All juleps are made for immediate use, and therefore it is pointless to speak of their shelf life.

## Chapter 4. Of Decoctions.

1. All the difference between decoctions and syrups made by decoction is this: syrups are made to be kept, while decoctions are only for immediate use. For you can hardly keep a decoction a week at any time, and if the weather is hot, not half so long.

2. Decoctions are made of leaves, roots, flowers, seeds, fruits, or barks, contributing to the cure of the disease you make them for; they are made in the same manner as we showed you for syrups.

3. Decoctions made with wine last longer than those made with water, and if you take your decoction to cleanse the urinary passages or open obstructions, your best way is to make it with white wine instead of water, because this is most penetrating.

4. Decoctions are of most use in such diseases as lie in the passages of the body, such as the stomach, bowels, kidneys, urinary passages, and bladder, because decoctions pass more quickly to those places than any other form of medicine.

5. If you wish to sweeten your decoction with sugar or any syrup fit for the occasion for which you take it, which is bitter, you may do so and no harm is done.

6. If in a decoction you boil roots, herbs, flowers, and seeds together, let the roots boil for a good while first, because they retain their virtue <note>medicinal potency</note> longest; then the next in order by the same rule: namely, 1. barks, 2. the herbs, 3. the seeds, 4. the flowers, 5. the spices (if you put any in), because their virtues come out soonest.

7. For such things as cause sliminess in a decoction by boiling, such as figs, quince seeds, linseed, etc., your best way is, after you have bruised them, to tie them up in a linen rag, as you tie up a calf's brains, and so boil them.

8. Keep all decoctions in a glass bottle closely stopped, and the cooler the place you keep them in, the longer they will last before they turn sour.

Lastly, the usual dose to be given at one time is usually two, three, four, or five ounces, according to the age and strength of the patient, the season of the year, the strength of the medicine, and the nature of the disease.

## Chapter 5. Of Oils.

1. Olive oil, which is commonly known by the name of salad oil—I suppose because it is usually eaten with salads by those who love it—if it is pressed out of ripe olives, according to *Galen*, is temperate and exceeds in no single quality.
2. Of oils, some are simple and some are compounds.
3. Simple oils are those made from fruits or seeds by pressing, such as oil of sweet and bitter almonds, linseed oil, and rapeseed oil, etc., regarding which see my *Dispensatory*.
4. Compound oils are made of olive oil and other simples—meaning herbs, flowers, roots, etc.
5. The way of making them is this: Having bruised the herbs or flowers you wish to make your oil from, put them in an earthen pot, and for every two or three handfuls of them, pour in a pint of oil. Cover the pot with a paper and set it in the sun for about a fortnight or less, according to the heat of the sun. Then, having warmed it very well by the fire, press out the herbs, etc., very hard in a press, and add just as many more bruised herbs (the herbs, I mean, not the oil) to the same oil in the same manner. Set them in the sun as before; the more often you repeat this, the stronger your oil will be. At last, when you believe it is strong enough, boil both the herbs and oil together until the juice is consumed—which you may know when it stops bubbling and the herbs become crisp. Then strain it while it is hot, and keep it in a stone or glass vessel for your use.
6. As for chemical oils, I have nothing to say in this treatise.
7. The general use of these oils is for pain in the limbs, roughness of the skin, the itch, etc., as well as for ointments and plasters.
8. If you have occasion to use it for wounds or ulcers, dissolve half an ounce of turpentine in two ounces of oil; the heat of the fire will quickly do it, for oil itself is irritating to wounds, and the turpentine tempers it.

## Chapter 6. Of Electuaries.

Physicians make more of a fuss than is necessary regarding electuaries; I shall prescribe but one general way of making them. As for the ingredients, you may vary them as you please and as you find occasion based on the last chapter.

1. So that you may make electuaries when you need them, it is necessary that you always keep herbs, roots, seeds, flowers, etc., ready dried in your house, so that you are prepared to beat them into powder when you need them.
2. Your better way is to keep them whole rather than powdered, for once powdered they

they are the more subject to lose their strength, because the air soon penetrates them.

3. If they are not dry enough to beat into *powder* when you need them, dry them by a gentle fire until they are so.

4. Having beaten them, sift them through a fine *tiffany sieve* <note>A sieve made of tiffany, a thin silk gauze.</note>, so that there may be no large pieces found in your *electuary*.

5. To one ounce of your *powder*, add three ounces of clarified *honey*; this quantity I hold to be sufficient. I confess *authors* differ about it. If you would make more or less *electuary*, vary your proportions accordingly.

6. Mix them well together in a *mortar*, and take this for a truth: you cannot mix them too much.

7. The way to clarify *honey* is to set it over the fire in a convenient vessel until the scum rises, and when the scum is taken off, it is clarified.

8. The usual dose of *cordial electuaries* is from half a dram to two drams; of *purging electuaries*, from half an ounce to an ounce.

9. The way to keep them is in a *pot*.

10. The time for taking them is either in the morning while fasting (and remaining fasting for an hour after them), or at night when going to bed, three or four hours after *supper*.

### Chap. 7. Of *Conserves*.

1. The way of making *conserves* is twofold: one of *herbs* and *flowers*, and the other of *fruits*.

2. *Conserves* of *herbs* and *flowers* are made like this: If you make your *conserves* of *herbs*, such as *scurvy-grass*, *wormwood*, *rue*, or the like, take only the *leaves* and tender tops (for you may beat your heart out before you can beat the *stalks* small). Having beaten them, weigh them, and to every pound of them add three pounds of *sugar*; beat them very well together in a *mortar*—you cannot beat them too much.

3. *Conserves* of *fruits*, such as *barberries*, *sloes*, and the like, are made like this: First, scald the *fruit*, then rub the *pulp* through a thick hair *sieve* made for the purpose, called a *pulping sieve*; you may do it in a pinch with the back of a *spoon*. Then take this *pulp* thus drawn and add to it its weight in *sugar* and no more. Put it in a *pewter vessel* and, over a *charcoal* fire, stir it up and down until the *sugar* is melted, and your *conserve* is made.

4. Thus you have the way of making *conserves*; the way of keeping them is in *earthen pots*.

5. The *dose* is usually the quantity of a *nutmeg* at a time, morning and evening, or (unless they are purging) whenever you please.

6. Of *conserves*, some keep for many years, such as *conserves* of *roses*; others keep for only a year, such as *conserves* of *borage*, *bugloss*, *cowslips*, and the like.

7. Take care regarding the "working" <note>Fermenting or bubbling up.</note> of some *conserves* immediately after they are made; look to them once a day and stir them around. *Conserves* of *borage*, *bugloss*, and *wormwood* have acquired an excellent knack for that activity.

8. You may know when your *conserves* are almost spoiled by this: you shall find a hard crust at the top with little holes in it, as though *worms* had been eating there.

## Chap. 8. Of Preserves.

Of Preserves there are sundry sorts, and since the operations of all are somewhat different, we will handle them all separately.
There are preserved with sugar:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;1 *Flowers.*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;2 *Fruits.*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;3 *Roots.*
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;4 *Barks.*

1. **Flowers** are but very seldom preserved; I never saw any that I remember, except only cowslip flowers, and that was a great fashion in *Sussex* when I was a boy. It is done thus: first, take a flat glass (we call them jar glasses), strew in a layer of fine sugar, on that a layer of flowers, on that another layer of sugar, on that another layer of flowers; do so until your glass is full; then tie it over with a paper, and in a little time you shall have very excellent and pleasant preserves.

There is another way of preserving flowers, namely with vinegar and salt, as they pickle capers and broom buds, but because I have little skill in it myself, I cannot teach you.

2. **Fruits**, such as quinces and the like, are preserved two ways.
First, boil them well in water, and then pulp them through a sieve as we showed you before; then with the equal quantity of sugar, boil the water they were boiled in into a syrup, *namely*, a pound of sugar to a pint of liquor; to every pound of this syrup add four ounces of the pulp, then boil it with a very gentle fire to the right consistency, which you may easily know if you drop a drop of it upon a <term>trencher</term>; if it is enough, it will not stick to your fingers when it is cold.

Secondly, another way to preserve fruits is this: First, pare off the rind, then cut them in halves and take out the core; then boil them in water until they are soft (if you know when beef is boiled enough, you may easily know when they are); then boil the water with its equal weight of sugar into a syrup, put the syrup into a pot, and put the boiled fruit in as whole as you left it when you cut it, and let it remain so until you have occasion to use it.

3. **Roots** are preserved thus: First, scrape them very clean, and cleanse them from the pith if they have any, for some roots do not, such as <term>eryngo</term> and the like; boil them in water until they are soft, as we showed you before with the fruits, then boil the water you boiled the roots in into a syrup as we showed you before; then keep the roots whole in the syrup until you use them.

4. **As for Barks**, we have but few that come to our hands to be done, and of those few that I can remember, they are oranges, lemons, citrons, and the outer bark of walnuts which grows outside the shell, for the shells themselves would make but poor preserves. These are the ones I can remember; if there are any more, add them to the number.

The way of preserving these is not all the same among authors, for some are bitter and some are not; those that are bitter, say authors, must be soaked in warm wa-

5. They are kept in glasses or glazed pots.
6. The preserved flowers will keep a year if you can forbear eating them; the roots and barks much longer.
7. This art was plainly and clearly at first invented for delicacy, yet it later came to be of excellent use in medicine: for,
First, by this means medicines are made pleasant for sick and queasy stomachs, which otherwise would loathe them.
Secondly, by this means they are preserved from decaying for a long time.

## Chap. 9. Of Lohochs.

1. That which the *Arabians* call *Lohoch*, and the *Greeks* *Eclegma*, the *Latins* call *Linctus*, and in plain English, signifies nothing else but a thing to be licked up.
2. Their first invention was to prevent and remedy afflictions of the breast and lungs, to cleanse the lungs of phlegm, and make it fit to be cast out.
3. They are in body thicker than a syrup, and not as thick as an electuary.
4. The manner of taking them is to often take a little with a licorice stick and let it go down at leisure.
5. They are easily made thus: make a decoction of any pectoral herbs—this treatise will furnish you with enough—and when you have strained it, boil it with twice its weight of honey or sugar to a lohoch. If you are troubled with tough phlegm, honey is better than sugar; and if you add a little vinegar to it, you will do well; if not, I consider sugar to be better than honey.
6. It is kept in pots, and may be kept for a year or longer.
7. Its use is excellent for roughness of the windpipe, inflammations of the lungs, ulcers in the lungs, difficulty of breathing, asthma, coughs, and distillation of humors <note>The discharge or dripping of bodily fluids, such as mucus or catarrh</note>.

## Chap. 10. Of Ointments.

1. Various are the ways of making ointments which authors have left to posterity, which I shall omit, and quote one which is easiest to be made and therefore most beneficial to people who are ignorant in medicine, for whose sakes I write this. It is done thus:

Bruise those herbs, flowers, or roots you would make an ointment of, and to two handfuls of your bruised herbs add a pound of hog's grease, rendered <note>Melted and clarified</note> or cleansed from the skins. Beat them very well together in a stone mortar with a wooden pestle, then put it in a stone pot (the herbs and grease, I mean,

Then take it out and boil it a little; then, while it is hot, strain it, pressing it out very hard in a press. To this grease, add as many more bruised herbs as before; let them stand in the same manner for just as long, then boil them as you did the former. If you think your ointment is not strong enough, you may do this a third and fourth time; yet I tell you this: the fuller of juice your herbs are, the sooner your ointment will be strong. The last time you boil it, boil it so long until your herbs are crisp and the juice is consumed; then strain it, pressing it hard in a press. To every pound of ointment, add two ounces of turpentine and as much wax, because grease is as offensive to wounds as oil is.

2. Ointments are commonly known to be kept in pots, and will last over a year, or even over two years.

## Chap. 11. Of Plasters.

1. The Greeks made their plasters from various simples <note>Medicinal plants or single-ingredient remedies</note> and put metals in most of them, if not in all; for having reduced their metals into powder, they mixed them with that fatty substance of which the rest of the plaster consisted while it was still hot, continually stirring it up and down lest it should sink to the bottom. They stirred it continually until it was stiff; then they made it up into rolls, which they could melt by the fire again when they needed to use them.

2. The Arabians made theirs with meals, oil, and fat, which did not need such long boiling.

3. The Greeks' plasters consisted of these ingredients: metals, stones, various sorts of earth, dregs, juices, liquors, seeds, roots, herbs, animal excrements, wax, rosin, and gums.

## Chap. 12. Of Poultices.

1. Poultices are those kinds of things which the Latins call *Cataplasmata*, and our "learned fellows"—who, if they can read English, that is all—call them *cataplasms* because it is a difficult word few understand; it is indeed a very fine kind of medicine to ripen sores.

2. They are made of herbs and roots suited to the disease and the afflicted limb, being chopped small and boiled in water almost to a jelly. Then, by adding a little barley meal, or lupin meal, and a little oil or rough sheep suet (which I consider to be better), they are spread upon a cloth and applied to the painful area.

3. Their use is to ease pain, to break open sores, to cool inflammations, to dissolve hardness, to ease the spleen, to mature humors, and to dissipate swellings.

4. I beseech you to take this caution with you: use no poultices (if you can help it) that are of a heating nature before you have first cleansed the body, because they are liable to draw the humors to them from every part of the body.

## Chap. 13. *Of Troches.*

1 The Latins call them *Placentulæ*, or little cakes (and you might have seen what the Greeks call them too, had the last edition of my *London’s Dispensatory* not been so hellishly printed; that is all the public gets by one stationer printing another's copies: namely, to plague the country with false prints and disgrace the author). The Greeks call them τροχίσκοι <note>trochiskoi</note>, κυκλίσκοι <note>kykliskoi</note>, and ἀρτίσκοι <note>artiskoi</note>. They are usually little, round, flat cakes, though you may make them square if you will.

2 Their first invention was so that powders, being kept in this way, might resist the entry of air and thus stay pure for longer.

3 Besides, they are more easily carried in the pockets of those who travel. Many a man (for example) is forced to travel whose stomach is too cold, or at least not as hot as it should be—which is most proper, for the stomach is never cold until a man is dead. In such a case, it is better and more convenient for him to carry troches of wormwood or of galanga <note>a root similar to ginger</note> in a paper in his pocket, than to lug a gallipot <note>a small earthenware jar</note> along with him.

4 They are made this way: At night when you go to bed, take two drams of fine gum tragacanth and put it into a gallipot. Add half a quarter of a pint of any distilled water suited to the purpose you would make your troches for. Cover it, and the next morning you shall find it has become such a jelly as physicians call mucilage. With this you may (with a little effort) make any powder into a paste, and that paste into little cakes called troches.

5 Having made them, dry them well in the shade and keep them in a pot for your use.

## Chap. 14. *Of Pills.*

1 They are called *Pilulæ* because they resemble little balls; the Greeks call them *Catapotia*.

2 It is the opinion of modern physicians that this way of making up medicines was invented only to deceive the palate, so that by swallowing them whole, the bitterness of the medicine might not be perceived, or at least that it might not be unbearable; and indeed most of their pills, though not all, are very bitter.

3 I am of a completely contrary opinion to this. I rather think they were prepared in this hard form so that they might take longer to digest, and my opinion is grounded upon reason as well, not upon fancy or hearsay. The first invention of pills was to purge the head. Now, as I told you before, such infirmities as lie near the passages were best removed by decoctions because they pass to the afflicted part soonest. So here, if the infirmity lies in the head or any other remote part, the best way is to use pills because they are longer in digestion and therefore better able to draw the offending humor to them.

4 If I should tell you here a long tale of medicines working by sympathy and antipathy, you would not understand a word of it; those who are fit to be physicians may find it in the Treatise. All modern physicians know

...did not know what belonged to a Sympathetic Cure, any more than a cuckoo knows what belongs to flats and sharps in music, but they follow the common road and call it a "Hidden Quality" because it is hidden from the eyes of dunces; and indeed none but astrologers can give a reason for it, and medicine without reason is like a pudding without fat.

5 The way to make pills is very easy, for with the help of a pestle and mortar, and a little diligence, you may make any powder into pills, either with syrup or the jelly I told you of before.

### Chap. last. *The way of mixing Medicines according to the Cause of the Disease and the part of the Body afflicted.*

This being indeed the key of the work, I shall be somewhat more diligent in it: I shall express myself thus,

1 To the common people.
2 To those who study astrology, or those who study medicine astrologically.

First, to the common people: Kind souls, I am sorry it has been your hard misfortune to have been so long trained in such Egyptian darkness—even darkness which, to your sorrow, may be felt. The common road of medicine is not my practice, and I am therefore the more unfit to give you advice; and I have now published a little

<margin>*Galen's Art of Physic.*</margin>

*book which will fully instruct you, not only in the knowledge of your own bodies, but also in fit medicines to remedy each part of it when afflicted; in the meantime, take these few rules to satisfy you.

1 Along with the disease, consider the cause and the part of the body afflicted: for example, suppose a woman is subject to miscarrying because of wind; do this:

1 Look up [*Abortion*] in the Table of Diseases, and you shall be directed by that as to how many herbs prevent miscarriage.
2 Look up [*Wind*] in the same table, and you shall see how many of those herbs expel wind.

->These are the medicinal herbs for your ailment.<-

2 In all diseases, strengthen the part of the body afflicted.
3 In mixed diseases, there lies some difficulty; for sometimes two parts of the body are afflicted with contrary humors, one to the other; sometimes one part is afflicted with two contrary humors—as sometimes the liver is afflicted with choler <note>yellow bile</note> and water, such as when a man has both a dropsy <note>edema</note> and the yellow jaundice, and this is usually fatal.

In the former case, suppose the brain is too cold and moist, and the liver is too hot and dry; do this:

1 Keep your head warm on the outside.
2 Accustom yourself to smell hot herbs.
3 Take a pill that heats the head at night when going to bed.
4 In the morning, take a decoction <note>a concentrated liquor made by boiling herbal material</note> that cools the liver, for that quickly passes the stomach and reaches the liver immediately.

You must not think (courteous people) that I can spend time to give you examples of all diseases; these are enough to let you see as much light as you, without art, are able to receive. If I should set you to look upon the sun, I should dazzle your eyes and make you blind.

Secondly, to those who study astrology (who are the only people I know who are fit to study medicine—medicine without astrology being like a lamp without oil): you are the people I respect greatly. I will provide you with such instructions as my brain can offer at present (being away from my study), and an example to prove them.

1 Strengthen the body with herbs of the nature of the lord of the Ascendant; it does not matter whether he is a Fortune or an Infortune in this case.
2 Let your medicine be something antipathetic to the lord of the Sixth House.
3 Let your medicine be something of the nature of the ascending sign.
4 If the lord of the Tenth House is strong, make use of his medicines.
5 If this cannot easily be done, make use of the medicines of the "light of time" <note>The Luminary, either Sun or Moon, ruling the day or night of the chart</note>.
6 Always be sure to strengthen the afflicted part of the body with sympathetic remedies.

7. Pay attention to the heart; keep it "upon the wheels" <note>Keep it functioning and active</note> because the Sun is the fountain of life. Therefore, those universal remedies *Aurum potabile* <note>Drinkable gold</note> and the *Philosopher's Stone* cure all diseases simply by strengthening the heart.

But so that this may appear to you as clear as the sun when it is at the meridian, I quote an example here which I performed when I was as far from my study as I am now; yet I am not ashamed that the world should see how much or little of my lesson I have learned by heart.

On July 25, 1651, a letter came to me from *Bedfordshire* from a gentleman (at that time) altogether unknown to me, though since well known, who was a student of both *astrology* and *medicine*. The words are these:

->*Mr. Culpeper,*<-

<margin>L</margin>
> *My regards to you. Although I do not know you by face, because I greatly respect that pretty little lark you so lately let fly into the world, which you call* Semiotica Uranica <note>Culpeper's book on the astrological judgment of diseases</note>, *which I have lately taken into my cage, I am therefore emboldened to write to you on behalf of a neighbor's wife. She is afflicted with a violent disease which began in the lower parts of her body, but has now ascended upwards and torments her in her breast, throat, tongue, and lips. This disease took possession of her (as she relates to me) about a fortnight before last Michaelmas, but she is unable to name the exact day and hour. She sent for me and inquired whether she was under an "ill tongue" <note>A curse or hex</note> or not, or what the nature of the disease was. I have sent you the enclosed chart. I could find only one testimony of fascination or witchcraft, which was one sign possessing the cusps of the Twelfth and First Houses; this, to me, indicates nothing more than a strong suspicion on the part of the <term>querent</term>. However, I am confident there is a natural disease which causes much harm, because the lord of the Sixth House, which usually indicates natural diseases, is now placed in the Ascendant. But at present I refrain from making any long discourse on my own opinions, being desirous that you would apply your skill to this cure; for there is not a doctor among them all, far or near, who has been skillful enough to find the disease, much less to effect the cure. Sir, I expect your answer; meanwhile, I bid you farewell and remain yours in affection, etc.*

# My answer to the letter was to this effect:

Sir,
I received yours on July 25, in which I find your enclosed scheme and (I suppose) the nature of the disease, and I have sent you such an answer as I could, being far from my study, which I entreat you to take in good part, as it was written with a hurried pen <note>Festinanti calamo Conscripta: Written with a hurried pen</note>. As for the ignorance of your country doctors, their lack of the true judgment of astrology is in no way surprising to me. I perceive you to be a young man by the time of your birth chart <note>Genesis refers to a birth chart or the moment of birth</note>, which you also sent me; beware whom you trust with that. He who knows your nativity knows when bad directions operate, and if he is an enemy, he knows when to do you harm. If Cecil had not possessed Essex's nativity, he would never have gotten his head off; but to instruct you as a young student, I shall give you my judgment methodically.

<margin>Diagnostic signs.]</margin> You say you can find no evidence of witchcraft, except for only one sign occupying the cusps of both the Twelfth and the Ascendant houses; but if you had considered the proximity of Venus to Saturn, you would have found another reason for that. Yet I do not think he is bewitched, because of other more prevalent testimonies;
